Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the role of assessment in diagnosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1 — Introduction to assessment; basic assessment methods; physical assessment as a screening tool; Unit 6a — functional assessment

★ Memory hook — Assessment = data; Diagnosis = its interpretation; PT diagnosis = a movement-system label. Reason in a cycle: history → hypotheses → tests → PT diagnosis (ICF) → treat → re-assess, screening red flags at every step.

1Introduction

Assessment is the systematic, hypothesis-driven collection of data about a patient's status — the subjective history, the physical examination, functional testing and outcome measures. Diagnosis is the label reached by interpreting that data. In physiotherapy, assessment does not end in a medical diagnosis but in a physiotherapy (movement-system) diagnosis — a cluster of signs and symptoms that identifies the dysfunction the therapist is qualified and licensed to treat (for example, “subacromial pain syndrome with scapular dyskinesis and loss of thoracic extension”). It is distinct from, yet always linked to, the medical diagnosis.

Assessment is the foundation of every clinical decision that follows: it decides whether the patient is safe to treat, what the problem is, what the treatment targets are, and whether treatment is working. In direct-access or first-contact practice the physiotherapist is the entry point to care, so the role of assessment widens to include screening for serious pathology and timely referral.

2Physiology

The “physiology” of assessment is the clinical-reasoning process itself. In a well-conducted assessment the therapist runs a hypothetico-deductive cycle (Jones & Rivett): generate two or three competing hypotheses (differential diagnoses) from the history; design physical tests that can confirm or refute each hypothesis; commit to a working diagnosis by weighing the findings; treat and re-assess to validate the reasoning. Assessment is thus the “input” and diagnosis the “output” of a closed loop.

Physiologically, the examination works by stressing tissues in a controlled way — passive movement loads capsule and ligament, resisted movement loads muscle–tendon, and neural tension loads the nerve — to reproduce the patient's symptom and so localise the structure at fault. The value of the data depends on standardised technique, valid outcome measures and a consistent sequence, so that today's findings can be compared with tomorrow's. Because no test is perfect, each result merely shifts the pre-test probability of a diagnosis up or down rather than proving it.

3Pathophysiology

When assessment is incomplete, hurried or biased, the process fails. Hypotheses are never tested, red flags are missed, and a medical masquerader — fracture, infection, malignancy or visceral referral — is treated as a musculoskeletal problem. Diagnostic error is compounded by cognitive biases: anchoring on the first impression, confirmation bias (seeking only data that supports the favoured diagnosis) and availability bias (over-weighting recent cases).

Incomplete assessment also means no baseline, so change cannot be measured and treatment cannot be justified to the patient, the referrer or an insurer. The clinical cost is delayed correct treatment, unnecessary investigations and, in the worst case, harm to a patient with serious pathology.

4Answer

Assessment serves several linked roles in diagnosis, best shown by mapping each component of the examination to its diagnostic contribution:

ComponentContribution to diagnosis
Subjective history + red/yellow-flag screenGenerates roughly 80% of the hypothesis list; localises and characterises symptoms; screens for serious pathology
Observation and gaitConfirms visible dysfunction — posture, deformity, protective gait
Objective tests (AROM/PROM, MMT, joint play, special tests, neurological screen)Confirms or refutes each hypothesis and localises the tissue at fault
Functional and outcome measuresQuantifies impact at the ICF activity and participation levels and sets the baseline
Interpretation / clusteringConverts findings into a physiotherapy diagnosis and a ranked differential list
Documentation and re-assessmentMeasures change and provides the medico-legal record of autonomous practice

Stated as roles, assessment therefore:

  • Determines safety — it screens for red flags (fracture, infection, malignancy, cauda equina, vascular disease) and decides whether to treat or refer.
  • Localises and labels — it converts the patient's story into a defensible movement-system (physiotherapy) diagnosis.
  • Differentiates — it separates the working diagnosis from a ranked list of alternatives, each eliminated by a named finding.
  • Maps to the ICF — findings are recorded as body structure/function (restricted flexion, weak abductors), activity (unable to squat) and participation (unable to work as a farmer), which defines both the treatment targets and the outcome measures for re-assessment.
  • Sets the baseline and measures change — it provides the yardstick against which progress, plateau or deterioration is judged.
  • Justifies and documents — it is the professional and legal record that protects autonomous practice and communicates with referrers and insurers.

In Indian practice this process must accommodate a busy OPD and a high burden of tuberculosis, osteoporosis and diabetic neuropathy — red-flag screening is not optional.

Conclusion

Assessment is not a preliminary ritual but the diagnostic instrument of physiotherapy: done as a hypothesis-driven cycle it converts the patient's story into a defensible movement-system diagnosis and a measurable plan; done as a checklist it merely collects data without producing a diagnosis.

5Recent advances

  • Jones (1992) — Proposed the hypothetico-deductive model of clinical reasoning for physiotherapists, describing five categories of hypotheses (source of symptoms, contributing factors, etc.) that direct the assessment and testing sequence.
  • Edwards et al. (2004) — Qualitative study of expert physiotherapists identified eight clinical reasoning strategies (diagnostic, narrative, procedural, interactive, collaborative, predictive, teaching and ethical) and the idea of dialectical reasoning, broadening physiotherapy diagnosis beyond hypothesis testing.
  • Rivett & Higgs (1997) — Study of manual-therapy physiotherapists found they generated working hypotheses within the first minute of the examination, supporting the hypothetico-deductive model and informing how reasoning is taught to physiotherapy students.
  • Rushton et al. (2023) — The IFOMPT International Framework for Examination of the Cervical Region has clinicians systematically generate and test vascular and red-flag hypotheses during the history and physical examination, embedding screening into physiotherapy assessment.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 1 & 6.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (syllabus reference 4).
  3. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. (reference 2)
  4. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. (standard clinical-reasoning text)
  5. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier (2nd ed., 2019).
  6. International Federation of Orthopaedic Manipulative Physical Therapists (IFOMPT). Cervical Framework, 2020 (updated).
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe the screening of neck following C3-C4 disc prolapse.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2a — Screening the Head, Neck and Back

★ Memory hook — Myotome ladder: C5 abduct, C6 wrist extend, C7 elbow extend, C8 finger flex, T1 finger abduct; Spurling (compression) pairs with distraction (relief).

1Introduction

C3–C4 cervical disc prolapse is a posterolateral disc herniation at the third–fourth cervical level that can compress the exiting C4 nerve root. Screening the neck in this situation is a focused, hypothesis-driven examination that localises the neurological level, excludes myelopathy and red flags, and establishes a baseline for management.

2Physiology

Neurological screen — the C4 root

Myotome C4: scapular elevation (shoulder shrug) and diaphragm (C3–C5 — "C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive"); test resisted shrug. Reflex: no pure C4 DTR — biceps jerk (C5) and brachioradialis (C6) are tested to exclude adjacent-root involvement. Sensation: pinprick/light touch over the neck, clavicle and upper shoulder cap. Complete the screen of the upper limb for a broader deficit pattern.

Fig 2 — The C3–C4 'high-collar' dermatome map with myotome, reflex and special-test annotations parked beside it. The whole answer's neurological screen in one drawing.

3Pathophysiology

A C3–C4 prolapse narrows the intervertebral foramen and compresses the C4 nerve root, producing radicular pain in the C4 "high-collar" distribution (suboccipital/neck → clavicle → shoulder cap), paraesthesia and, in a minority, myotomal weakness of shoulder shrug and diaphragm. Adjacent-root involvement (C5, C6) must be excluded because there is no pure C4 deep-tendon reflex. A central, cord-compressing herniation produces myelopathy (gait change, hand clumsiness, bowel/bladder symptoms) — a red flag needing urgent referral.

4Answer

History & observation

C3–C4 prolapse typically compresses the C4 nerve root: pain in the suboccipital/neck region radiating to the shoulder cap and clavicular area (C4 dermatome — a "high-collar" distribution, with C3 giving occipital/sub-occipital referral). Ask onset, trauma, posture/occupation (prolonged laptop flexion), night pain, and screen red flags: myelopathy signs (gait change, hand clumsiness, bowel/bladder), fever, weight loss, trauma.

Palpation, ROM & mobility
  • Observation: forward head posture, loss of cervical lordosis, antalgic tilt.
  • Palpation: paraspinal muscle spasm/guarding, segmental tenderness at C3–C4 level, upper trapezius trigger points.
  • ROM: flexion/extension, side-flexion, rotation — painful arcs, capsular vs non-capsular pattern; extension combined with ipsilateral rotation reproduces radicular symptoms in the affected dermatome.
  • Segmental mobility: central and unilateral posterior-anterior glides (PAIVMs) at C3–C4 for stiffness vs pain response; intersegmental movement testing (PPIVMs).
Special tests

Spurling's test (extension + ipsilateral rotation + axial compression — radicular reproduction), cervical distraction test (relief is confirmatory), shoulder-abduction (bakery) relief sign, ULNT/neurodynamic testing for mechanosensitivity, Hoffman's test for myelopathy, and quadriceps/Babinski if cord signs are suspected.

Close

Integrate findings into a working PT diagnosis and baseline (NDI — Neck Disability Index), referring urgently for MRI if myelopathy or red flags appear.

The examiner's trap: writing a generic neck exam. Anchor EVERY neurological line to C3/C4 — dermatome map, shrug myotome, "no C4 reflex — test C5/C6 adjacent." That specificity is what separates 8+/10 from 5/10.

5Recent advances

  • Wainner et al. (2003) — Landmark physiotherapy diagnostic-accuracy study: a four-test cluster (upper-limb neurodynamic test 1, cervical rotation <60° to the involved side, distraction test and Spurling test A) gives a positive likelihood ratio of 30.3 when all four are positive, and ULNT1 was the best single test for ruling out cervical radiculopathy.
  • Blanpied et al. (2017) — The APTA/JOSPT neck pain clinical practice guideline classifies neck pain with radiating pain and recommends neurodynamic testing, the Spurling test, the distraction test and the Valsalva test, used in combination rather than in isolation.
  • Yousif et al. (2025) — Scoping review found reduced tendon reflexes the most specific single neurological sign, while the full neurological examination is highly specific but has low sensitivity for cervical radiculopathy.
  • NICE (2023) and NASS — Guidance is to diagnose cervical radiculopathy from arm pain with a matching neurological deficit; the Spurling test is specific but insensitive and is best used in a cluster with the cervical distraction and upper-limb neurodynamic tests.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2a.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (reference 4) — cervical spine chapter.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1)
  4. Thoomes EJ et al. Value of physical tests in diagnosing cervical radiculopathy: a systematic review. Spine J. 2018;18:179–189.
  5. NICE. Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral (NG127, 2023).

On the evaluation form — Q2: Cervical disc prolapse C3-C4 with C4 radiculopathy

I. Subjective examination

Female, 34 years, desk worker. Chief complaint: neck pain radiating to the outer shoulder and upper scapular region for 6 weeks, with associated tingling over the shoulder cap. Symptom analysis — site: lower cervical/parascapular region, referring to the lateral neck and mid-deltoid (C4 dermatome); onset: gradual, after long hours at a computer; duration: 6 weeks; type: deep ache with sharp shooting pain into the shoulder; severity: NPRS 6/10. Aggravating factors: neck extension, side-flexion toward the painful side, prolonged static postures, coughing and sneezing. Relieving factors: rest, a supported shoulder, hand-behind-head posture. Red-flag screen negative (no trauma, fever, weight loss, gait change or bladder involvement). Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Forward head posture, protracted rounded shoulders and protective elevation of the shoulder girdle; no wasting or scars.

On palpation. Tenderness over the C3-C4 facet region and the paraspinals; increased deep-tissue tension (hypertonicity) of the upper trapezius and levator scapulae; no crepitus or swelling.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: cervical extension and rotation to the affected side reduced to about half range; PROM shows the same limitation with a muscle-spasm end-feel. Resisted isometrics of neck side-flexion reproduce the scapular pain. MMT (MRC 0-5): shoulder shrug (upper trapezius, C4) 4/5 on the affected side; shoulder abduction (C5), wrist extension (C6), triceps (C7) and finger flexion (C8) 5/5. Reflexes: biceps, brachioradialis, triceps and lower-limb reflexes normal. Arm girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment. Dermatomes: diminished light touch and pinprick over the C4 dermatome (lateral neck, clavicular area, mid-deltoid); C2-T1 screen otherwise intact. Myotomes: C4 weakness as above; no upper motor neurone signs.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Sitting tolerance limited to 20-30 minutes; overhead reach and driving affected. Outcome measures: Neck Disability Index (NDI, 0-50) baseline items scored; NPRS 0-10; PSFS 0-10 for reading, desk work and sleeping; cervical ROM by goniometry.

4. Gait analysis. Gait normal.

5. Balance. No balance deficit.

6. Hand function. Overhead reaching and driving affected; hand-behind-head posture used for symptom relief.

7. Coordination. No upper motor neurone signs on the neurological screen.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Spurling's testExtend and side-flex the neck to the symptomatic side, then apply axial compressionReproduction of radicular shoulder painForaminal compression of the C4 nerve root — positive in this patient
Cervical distractionSupine; cradle the occiput and distract the headReduction of radicular painConfirms a compressive origin of symptoms — positive in this patient (relief with distraction)
Shoulder abduction (Bakody) testPatient rests the hand on top of the headRelief of radicular painReduces tension on the compressed nerve root — positive in this patient (relief in the hand-behind-head posture)
Upper limb neurodynamic test 1Shoulder abduction, elbow extension, forearm supination, wrist/finger extension, neck side-flexion awaySymptom reproduction with an inter-side difference of about 10°Mechanosensitivity of the brachial plexus/nerve root — positive in this patient
Hoffmann's signFlick the tip of the relaxed middle fingerReflex thumb and finger flexionMyelopathy screen, refer if positive — negative in this patient (no upper motor neurone signs)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Neck and radicular pain
  • Reduced cervical ROM
  • C4 dermatomal sensory change
  • Paraspinal (upper trapezius and levator scapulae) spasm

Functional limitations

  • Reduced sitting tolerance
  • Limited overhead activity

Disabilities

  • Unable to sustain full-time desk work
11. Functional diagnosis

Cervical disc prolapse at C3-C4 with C4 nerve-root compression, causing radicular pain, reduced cervical ROM, C4 dermatomal sensory change and paraspinal muscle spasm, limiting sitting tolerance and overhead activity and preventing full-time desk work.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce pain from 6/10 to 3/10 on NPRS; gain 25% more painless cervical rotation; sleep through the night.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): full-time desk tolerance with hourly posture breaks; full painless AROM; NDI reduced by at least 10 points.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1-2): intermittent cervical traction, cryotherapy/TENS, pain-free gentle ROM. Stage 2: manual therapy and mobilisation as tolerated, scapular stabilisation, craniocervical (deep neck flexor) training, posture and workstation ergonomics.

14. Home programme

Chin tucks, shoulder-blade setting, posture diary, activity pacing.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe the screening of upper back for fibromyalgia.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 (b, e) — Screening the shoulder/upper extremity and chest; musculoskeletal screening

★ Memory hook — Fibromyalgia numbers: ACR 1990 — 18 sites, 4 kg pressure, ≥11 needed; ACR 2016 — WPI + SSS, no palpation. Trigger point = taut band (local); tender point = systemic (central sensitisation).

1Introduction

Fibromyalgia is a chronic nociplastic pain syndrome of central sensitisation, defined by widespread pain present for more than 3 months together with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms. Screening the upper back is the practical core of the examination because four of the nine paired ACR 1990 tender-point sites lie in and around the upper trunk.

2Physiology

In normal nociception, peripheral tissue injury activates nociceptors whose signals are processed and modulated in the dorsal horn and brain; pain is proportional to the stimulus, localised to the injured tissue, and resolves as healing proceeds. Light touch and deep pressure over muscle and bone are not normally painful, and "control" sites such as the forehead, mid-deltoid and thumbnail are non-tender.

3Pathophysiology

What you are diagnosing

Fibromyalgia: chronic widespread pain (axial + bilateral, above and below waist) for >3 months, with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms. ACR 1990: ≥11 of 18 tender points on ~4 kg thumb pressure. ACR 2010/2016 revision: Widespread Pain Index (0–19) + Symptom Severity Scale — criteria now usable without a tender-point count; both are worth quoting.

4Answer

Screening the upper back
  • History: female predominance (7:1), ages 30–50; pain "all over" and migrating; sleep disturbance, morning stiffness >30 min, irritable bowel/bladder, mood symptoms; absence of mechanical relieving postures.
  • Observation: often normal posture but "hurting everywhere" on light touch; guarded, protective posturing.
  • Palpation of the 9 paired sites (4 in/around the upper trunk): suboccipital muscle insertions; low-cervical (C5–C7) interspinous ligaments; mid-upper trapezius; supraspinatus at the medial scapular border. Complete the set with 2nd rib costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, gluteal and greater-trochanteric sites — thumb pressure ≈4 kg, positive when the patient winces ("jump sign").
  • ROM & chest: thoracic mobility, chest expansion (normal ≥5 cm; markedly restricted suggests ankylosing spondylitis, not fibromyalgia), scapulothoracic rhythm.
Differentials & associated screen

Distinguish myofascial trigger points (local, taut band, reproducible referral — fibromyalgia points are systemic tender points with no taut band), hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica (age >50, raised ESR), inflammatory arthritis and cervical/thoracic spondylosis. Screen for central sensitisation features (allodynia to light touch), and quantify with the FIQR (Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire) and pain diagram.

Conclusion

Document a body map of positive sites, score FIQR for baseline, and coordinate a multidisciplinary plan — education, graded aerobic exercise, sleep and stress management — since physiotherapy is a cornerstone of fibromyalgia management.

Fig 3 — Tender-point map: upper-body sites in red; complete the 9 pairs with 2nd rib, lateral epicondyle, gluteal and trochanteric sites (blue) to reach the ACR 1990 count of 18.
State BOTH criteria sets (1990 tender-point count AND 2010 WPI + SSS) — this shows current knowledge, and quoting 4 kg thumb pressure is the practical detail examiners remember.

5Recent advances

  • Macfarlane et al. (2017) — EULAR revised recommendations make exercise the only "strong for" therapy-based recommendation for fibromyalgia and position non-pharmacological management (education plus exercise) as first-line care.
  • Bidonde et al. (2017) — Cochrane review of 13 RCTs (839 adults) found aerobic exercise probably improves health-related quality of life and may slightly reduce pain and improve physical function in fibromyalgia.
  • Bidonde et al. (2019) — Cochrane review of 29 RCTs (2088 adults) found mixed (aerobic, resistance and flexibility) exercise improves quality of life, physical function and fatigue and may reduce pain, with no serious adverse events.
  • Arnold et al. (2019) — The ACTTION-APS (AAPT) criteria simplified fibromyalgia diagnosis to pain in at least 6 of 9 body regions with moderate-to-severe fatigue or sleep disturbance, aiding early screening.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4).
  3. Wolfe F et al. The American College of Rheumatology 1990 / 2010/2016 criteria for fibromyalgia. Arthritis Rheum / Semin Arthritis Rheum. (primary)
  4. McCarty DJ, Koopman WJ. Arthritis and Allied Conditions. (syllabus reference 11).
  5. Arnold LM et al. AAPT diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia. J Pain. 2019;20:611–628.
  6. Wolfe F et al. 2016 revisions to the 2010/2011 fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2016;46:319–329.

On the evaluation form — Q3: Fibromyalgia (upper back screening)

I. Subjective examination

Female, 42 years. Chief complaint: widespread aching pain, worst in the neck and upper back, for over 3 years — above and below the waist, bilateral and axial (Widespread Pain definition met). Past medical history: prior investigations normal; no inflammatory joint disease. Symptom analysis — site: widespread, worst in the neck and upper back; duration: over 3 years; type: aching with morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes; severity: average NPRS 7/10. Aggravating factors: poor sleep, physical or emotional stress, cold weather. Relieving factors: warmth, rest. Associated features: fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, poor concentration ("fibro fog"), tension headaches and irritable bowel symptoms. Vitals and BMI recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Guarded round-shouldered posture; no swelling, deformity or wasting; gait mildly slowed by pain.

On palpation. The 1990 ACR tender-point sites examined with about 4 kg of thumb-pad pressure — bilateral suboccipital insertions, low cervical (C5-C7 anterior), mid-upper trapezius, supraspinatus above the scapular spine, second costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, greater trochanters and medial knee fat pads; control sites (mid-forehead, mid-deltoid, thumbnail) non-tender, indicating widespread allodynia rather than local pathology.

1. Motor assessment. AROM/PROM of the cervical spine, thoracic spine and shoulders full but slow and painful; no capsular end-feel. MMT: give-way (breakaway) weakness on sustained effort rather than a true deficit. Resisted isometrics of the upper trapezius reproduce the upper-back pain. Reflexes and girth symmetrical.

2. Sensory assessment. No dermatomal loss; hyperaesthesia and allodynia to light touch and clothing over the upper back; peripheral nerve screen normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Reduced activity tolerance with pacing difficulty; a two-week activity pacing diary issued to identify boom-bust cycles. Outcome measures: Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ-R) for the overall impact of fibromyalgia on function and symptoms; WPI and SSS as below; NPRS 0-10; PSFS 0-10 for sleep, walking and household work; six-minute walk test for aerobic capacity; timed 30-second sit-to-stand.

4. Gait analysis. Gait mildly slowed by pain; gait speed recorded.

5. Balance. Not formally documented at this assessment.

6. Hand function. Not formally documented at this assessment.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Prior investigations as per the medical records were normal, with no evidence of inflammatory joint disease; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
ACR 1990 tender point countDigitally palpate the 18 defined sites with about 4 kg pressurePain reported at 11 or more of 18 sitesClassifies widespread hyperalgesia — the defined sites were tender on palpation in this patient (exact count not documented)
Widespread Pain Index (WPI)Patient marks painful areas on a body chart (19 zones)WPI ≥7 with SSS ≥5 (or WPI 4-6 with SSS ≥9), symptoms ≥3 monthsSupports fibromyalgia (2010/2016 criteria) — the Widespread Pain definition is met in this patient
Symptom Severity Scale (SSS)Rate fatigue, waking unrefreshed, cognitive and somatic symptomsScore 5 or moreCombined with WPI confirms fibromyalgia — corresponding symptoms present in this patient (score not documented)
Control-site palpationPalpate non-tender control sitesTenderness at control sites tooGeneralised allodynia, not local pathology — control sites were non-tender in this patient
Beighton scoreScore 9 joint hypermobility manoeuvres4 or more in adultsScreens associated joint hypermobility — result not documented in this patient
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Widespread pain
  • Allodynia
  • Fatigue
  • Unrefreshing sleep

Functional limitations

  • Reduced activity tolerance
  • Pacing difficulty

Disabilities

  • Household and occupational roles disrupted
11. Functional diagnosis

Fibromyalgia syndrome with widespread pain, allodynia, fatigue and unrefreshing sleep, reducing activity tolerance and disrupting household and occupational roles.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce average pain by 1 point on NPRS; establish a paced 10-minute walk twice daily.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): graded aerobic progression to 30 minutes of brisk walking most days; better sleep quality; return to family and occupational routines using pacing.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: education on central sensitisation, sleep hygiene, pacing diary. Stage 2: graded aerobic training (walking, cycling, warm-water pool exercise) and gentle stretching of the upper back and neck. Stage 3: light progressive resistance training, relaxation and breathing retraining; physician co-management and cognitive-behavioural therapy referral.

14. Home programme

10-minute walking bouts, stretch breaks at work, fixed sleep-wake timings.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Describe the importance of direct access in Physiotherapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 3 — Direct access and self-referral; primary care; autonomous practice; decision making

★ Memory hook — Direct access = patient → physio first. Benefits spell E-C-A-P-S: Earlier treatment, Cost-effective, Autonomy, Patient satisfaction, System decongestion — earned by red-flag rigour.

1Introduction

Direct access means that patients may seek physiotherapy assessment and treatment without a physician's referral — the physiotherapist acts as a first-contact, autonomous practitioner, with patient self-referral as its operational form. It is the fullest expression of autonomous practice: the therapist examines, diagnoses within the physiotherapy scope, plans and delivers treatment, and decides on discharge or referral independently.

Its importance lies in what it changes for the patient, the profession and the health system — and in the clinical responsibility that this freedom transfers to the therapist.

2Physiology

In the conventional referral-based model the patient first consults a physician, who triages, may order imaging or medication, and then refers to physiotherapy. This pathway preserves the physician's gatekeeper role but inserts a waiting step between symptom onset and physiotherapy. Physiologically and prognostically this matters: the first weeks after an acute musculoskeletal injury are the window in which appropriate loading and education prevent the transition from acute to persistent pain, and in which fear-avoidance and deconditioning either take root or are prevented. Delayed access wastes precisely that window.

A health system that routes every musculoskeletal problem through a physician also concentrates demand on scarce specialist time — a poor match, since most musculoskeletal problems need no physician at all.

3Pathophysiology

The “pathology” of the referral-only model is delay and inefficiency. Time lost waiting for a physician appointment and referral allows acute musculoskeletal problems to become chronic, and the pathway generates more imaging, medication and secondary referrals than is clinically necessary — with their own costs and harms (radiation, opioid exposure, medicalisation). Direct access removes this bottleneck: the patient reaches a first-contact physiotherapist, who screens red flags and either treats within scope or refers appropriately. The dysfunction being corrected is therefore not the patient's tissue but the access pathway itself — a systems “lesion” that produces avoidable disability and cost.

4Answer

The importance of direct access is best shown as its benefit for each stakeholder:

StakeholderBenefit of direct access
PatientEarlier treatment and faster recovery; shorter pathways and fewer consultations; better access in underserved areas; greater choice and satisfaction
ProfessionRecognition of the physiotherapist's competence to diagnose within scope, screen red flags and refer; foundation of the primary-care and doctor-of-physiotherapy models; a marker of professional maturity
Health systemCost-effectiveness — fewer physician visits, less imaging and medication, no worse outcomes; frees physician time for complex disease; eases the specialist-burden crisis

Evidence. Systematic and scoping reviews of direct access report clinical outcomes equal or superior to physician-first care, with 10–30% fewer general-practitioner consultations, reduced imaging and medication use, and no increase in adverse events; patient satisfaction is consistently higher. Self-referral pilots in the UK NHS and US military health systems showed the same pattern.

Scenario in India. Direct access is legal in all 50 US states, the UK, Australia, the Netherlands and much of the EU. In India it remains partial: some state practice and the Indian Association of Physiotherapists support autonomous practice, but referral culture, insurance rules and variable implementation of the Clinical Establishments Act leave it an evolving frontier.

Responsibilities it imposes. First-contact practice demands competence in differential diagnosis and red-flag screening (cancer, fracture, infection, visceral referral), strict referral criteria, indemnity insurance, meticulous documentation and continuing competency. Autonomy is earned by clinical rigour, not demanded.

Conclusion

Direct access matters because it shortens the path to effective, conservative musculoskeletal care, raises the professional standing of physiotherapy and reduces system cost — but only where the therapist can screen, diagnose within scope and refer safely, so that autonomy and patient safety advance together. An answer that only celebrates autonomy and never mentions red-flag screening reads as naive to an examiner.

5Recent advances

  • Maselli et al. (2023) — Systematic review concluded that direct-access physiotherapy is safe, more cost-effective and higher in patient satisfaction than physician-first care, with less imaging and medication and no reported adverse events.
  • Cattrysse et al. (2024) — Scoping review found direct access reduced general-practitioner workload by 10–30% and lowered imaging and prescribing, with clinical outcomes comparable to GP-referred care.
  • Severijns et al. (2024) — Systematic review of physiotherapy-led versus physician-led low-back-pain care reported higher satisfaction, fewer physician visits and lower total costs without increased harm.
  • World Physiotherapy (2023) — Direct access is now legal in most high-income health systems; in India it remains partial, with referral culture and insurance rules still evolving.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 3 (a–d).
  2. World Physiotherapy (2011/2019) policy statement — Description of physiotherapy / direct access and patient self-referral.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  4. Gallotti M et al. Effectiveness and consequences of direct access in physiotherapy: a systematic review. J Clin Med. 2023;12(18):5832.
