Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. A 30-year-old female comes with a history of ankle injury. Describe the various special tests for the ankle.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4b — Special tests used in musculoskeletal examination

★ Memory hook — Ankle ligament tests: plantarflexion → ATFL (drawer), 90° → CFL (talar tilt); syndesmosis trio = Squeeze, Kleiger, Cotton.

1Introduction

Setting the scene

A 30-year-old woman with an inversion injury most likely sprains the lateral ligament complex — anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) first, then calcaneofibular (CFL), rarely posterior talofibular (PTFL). Grade I (stretch), II (partial), III (complete). Acutely effusion and pain limit testing — examinations are more reliable at day 4–5.

2Physiology

The lateral ligament complex of the ankle comprises three ligaments: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL). The ATFL resists inversion with the foot plantarflexed and is the weakest and most commonly injured; the CFL resists inversion in neutral dorsiflexion; the PTFL is rarely injured. Normal talar translation and tilt are minimal and symmetrical between sides.

Fig 5 — Lateral ligament complex and the anterior drawer. Draw the ATFL/CFL pair and mark the drawer arrow — the two sketches the evaluator expects side by side.

3Pathophysiology

An inversion injury forces the talus into plantarflexion and internal rotation, loading the lateral complex: the ATFL ruptures first, then the CFL, and rarely the PTFL. The resulting lateral ankle sprain is graded I (ligament stretch), II (partial tear) or III (complete tear). Acute effusion, swelling and pain limit reliable testing — mechanical examination is most valid at day 4–5. Chronic ankle instability (perceived "giving way") develops in about 40% of cases.

4Answer

Lateral ligament tests
  • Anterior drawer — for ATFL integrity: patient prone/supine, foot relaxed in ~10–15° plantarflexion, one hand stabilises the tibia while the other draws the talus forward on the fibula; >4–5 mm anterior translation (or a clunk/soft end-feel) suggests ATFL rupture.
  • Talar-tilt (inversion stress) — for CFL: foot at 90°, invert the talus in the mortise; compare sides — >5–10° asymmetry or soft end-feel indicates CFL injury.
  • Squeeze test at the mid-calf and cross-over pain help localise ligament territory.
Syndesmosis tests
  • Calf/squeeze test — compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calf; distal syndesmotic pain is positive.
  • External rotation (Kleiger) test — stabilise the leg, dorsiflex + externally rotate the foot — syndesmotic and deltoid pain.
  • Cotton (fibular translation) test — anteroposterior fibular glide; and the point-toe (plantarflex–external rotation) test.
Others that complete the screen
  • Deltoid ligament (eversion stress) — medial pain/valgus laxity; implies possible syndesmosis/fracture.
  • Ottawa ankle rules (not laxity but fracture triage): X-ray if pain over malleolar zone plus bone tenderness over posterior edge/tip, or inability to bear weight 4 steps.
  • Thompson/Simmonds test for an intact Achilles, anterior impingement test, and peroneal-tendon subluxation screen complete the ankle work-up.
Conclusion

Cluster the tests by structure (lateral ligaments → syndesmosis → medial → tendon/fracture screen), grade the sprain, and baseline the patient with the FAAM/Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool.

Position details separate grades: drawer in 10–15° plantarflexion for ATFL, 90° for CFL in talar tilt. Mentioning that acute-day testing is unreliable (test day 4–5) is a hallmark of clinical sense.

5Recent advances

  • Vuurberg et al. (2018) — The BJSM evidence-based clinical guideline update states that severity of ligament damage is assessed most reliably by delayed physical examination 4–5 days after trauma, and that supervised exercise-based functional treatment is preferred over immobilisation, with braces for prevention of recurrence.
  • Martin et al. (2021) — The JOSPT clinical practice guideline (lateral ankle ligament sprains revision) adds the reverse anterolateral drawer test and anterolateral talar palpation, and recommends the weight-bearing lunge test, single-limb balance and the Star Excursion Balance Test with FAAM, LEFS and PROMIS as outcome measures.
  • Gribble et al. (2016) — The International Ankle Consortium consensus standardised the definition and selection criteria for chronic ankle instability, recommending the CAIT (≤24) or IdFAI (≥11) to confirm self-reported instability.
  • Doherty et al. (2016) — Longitudinal data show about 40% of people with a first-time lateral ankle sprain progress to chronic ankle instability, for which the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool or IdFAI should be used.
  • Ottawa ankle rules — Remain the standard clinical decision rule for fracture triage before ligament stress testing.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4b.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — ankle & foot chapter.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — ankle biomechanics.
  4. Stiell IG et al. Ottawa ankle rules. JAMA. 1993 (primary, for triage).
  5. Martin RL et al. Ankle stability and movement coordination impairments: lateral ankle ligament sprains revision 2021. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2021;51(4):CPG1–CPG80.
  6. Gribble PA et al. International Ankle Consortium position statement on chronic ankle instability. Br J Sports Med.

On the evaluation form — Q5: Acute lateral ankle sprain (30-year-old female)

I. Subjective examination

Female, 30 years, badminton player. Chief complaint: left ankle pain and swelling. Symptom analysis — site: left lateral ankle; onset: 2 days ago, sudden inversion injury on landing, felt a "pop" over the outer ankle; duration: 2 days; type: sharp lateral ankle pain; severity: NPRS 7/10 at rest, 9/10 on stairs. Aggravating factors: weight bearing, stairs, uneven ground. Relieving factors: ice, elevation, rest. History: able to bear weight to the chair immediately after the injury (recorded for the Ottawa ankle rules); no previous sprain. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Anterolateral swelling with ecchymosis spreading to the lateral foot; antalgic gait; unable to hop on the left; limb held in slight plantarflexion-eversion for comfort; no deformity.

On palpation. Marked tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament and mild tenderness over the calcaneofibular ligament; no tenderness over the malleoli, navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal (Ottawa ankle rules negative for radiography); mild warmth; no crepitus.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: plantarflexion and inversion limited and painful; dorsiflexion and eversion near full. PROM shows the same pattern with a pain-limited end-feel. MMT: eversion (peronei) 3/5 due to pain; other motions 4/5. Resisted isometric inversion painful. Figure-of-eight girth 2 cm more on the left. Reflexes and myotomes (L4-S1) normal.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact over the sural and superficial peroneal territories; distal pulses and capillary refill normal; no paraesthesia.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Stair descent needs support; currently off play and unable to commute normally. Outcome measures: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) for foot and ankle function in daily living and sport; LEFS (0-80); NPRS 0-10; girth by figure-of-eight tape.

4. Gait analysis. Antalgic gait with reduced stance time on the left.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance held for 5 seconds only; unable to hop on the left (dynamic balance impaired).

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this lower-limb case.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Radiography not indicated — the Ottawa ankle rules were negative (no bony tenderness at the malleoli, navicular or base of the fifth metatarsal, and the patient could bear weight immediately after injury); no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawer testStabilise the tibia, grasp the heel with the ankle in 20° plantarflexion, glide the talus anteriorlyExcessive anterior translation of the talusAnterior talofibular ligament laxity — result not documented at this acute (2-day) presentation
Talar tilt testAnkle in neutral; invert the talus on the tibiaExcessive lateral tilt or a soft end-feelCalcaneofibular ligament laxity — result not documented at this acute presentation
Squeeze testCompress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calfPain over the anterior tibiofibular areaSyndesmotic (high ankle) injury — result not documented in this patient
External rotation (Kleiger) testStabilise the tibia, externally rotate the foot with the knee at 90°Pain over the syndesmosisSyndesmosis disruption — result not documented in this patient
Thompson testProne; squeeze the calf muscleAbsent ankle plantarflexionAchilles tendon rupture — performed as a rule-out; no rupture signs recorded in this patient
Tinel's test at fibular neckPercuss over the fibular neckTingling along the lateral leg/dorsumCommon peroneal nerve involvement — negative in this patient (sensation intact, no paraesthesia)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Pain
  • Swelling
  • Restricted AROM
  • Weak peronei
  • Impaired single-leg balance

Functional limitations

  • Altered gait
  • Stair difficulty

Disabilities

  • Off play
  • Unable to manage daily commuting
11. Functional diagnosis

Acute left lateral ankle sprain (inversion injury) with anterolateral pain, swelling, restricted and painful ankle ROM, peroneal weakness and impaired single-leg balance, producing an antalgic gait and stair difficulty and currently preventing sport and daily commuting.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): pain from 7/10 to 3/10; swelling reduced by 1 cm on figure-of-eight measurement; full pain-free AROM; normal-speed independent gait.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): single-leg stance for 30 seconds; peroneal strength 5/5; return to badminton drills with LEFS within 10 points of the pre-injury score.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (days 1-7): protection, relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, isometric peroneal sets. Stage 2 (weeks 1-3): graded AROM in all planes, stationary cycling, eversion strengthening with a band, wobble-board and single-leg balance. Stage 3 (weeks 4+): proprioceptive and agility drills, lateral movements, sport-specific rehabilitation, taping/bracing for return to play.

14. Home programme

RICE schedule, alphabet tracing with the foot, band exercises, balance progressions.

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for osteoporosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4d — Investigation methods / diagnostic imaging in musculoskeletal disease

★ Memory hook — T-score ladder: above −1 normal · −1 to −2.4 osteopenia · ≤−2.5 osteoporosis; a fragility fracture upgrades to severe. DEXA sites: L1–L4 + hip.

1Introduction

Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease of low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration that increases bone fragility and fracture risk. Because it is clinically silent until a fragility fracture occurs, it is diagnosed by imaging (DXA) and risk algorithms rather than symptoms — hence the central role of investigations.

2Physiology

Bone is continuously remodelled by osteoclastic resorption and osteoblastic formation. Peak bone mass is reached in the third decade; thereafter resorption exceeds formation and bone mineral density (BMD) falls, steeply after menopause. BMD is measured as areal density (g/cm²) and compared with a young-adult mean (T-score) or an age-matched mean (Z-score).

3Pathophysiology

In osteoporosis, trabecular thinning and perforation and cortical thinning reduce bone strength, so a low-energy ("fragility") fracture occurs. A T-score of −1 to −2.4 defines osteopenia and ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis; a fragility fracture with a T-score ≤ −2.5 is "severe" osteoporosis. Plain radiographs show bone loss only after 30–40% of bone mass is lost, which is why DXA and fracture-risk tools are used for early diagnosis.

Fig 6 — The T-score ruler. One glance, three zones — draw it exactly like this in the exam.

4Answer

DEXA — the gold standard

Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry measures areal bone mineral density (g/cm²) at the lumbar spine (L1–L4) and proximal femur with minimal radiation (~1/10 of a chest X-ray). Results as T-score (comparison with young-adult mean, WHO cutoffs in postmenopausal women & men ≥50: ≥ −1 normal; −1 to −2.4 osteopenia; ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis; with fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis) and Z-score (age-matched; ≤ −2 = "below expected for age" in premenopausal women/younger men).

Fracture-risk algorithms

FRAX computes 10-year probability of major osteoporotic and hip fracture from BMD plus clinical risk factors (age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parent hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, alcohol, secondary causes) — treatment thresholds (e.g., hip-probability ≥3% in Indian guidelines adapt WHO/NOF cut-points) are FRAX-based, not BMD alone.

Other imaging
  • Plain radiographs — show complications (vertebral compression, cortical thinning, trabecular rarefaction) only after 30–40% bone loss; vertebral fracture assessment morphometry.
  • Quantitative CT — true volumetric BMD, sensitive but higher dose; pQCT for peripheral sites.
  • Quantitative ultrasound (heel) — radiation-free screening (SOS/BUA), not for diagnosis.
  • MRI/bone scan — for occult fracture, malignancy differentiation.
Laboratory work-up

To exclude secondary causes and mark turnover: serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH, TSH, renal/liver profile; in men testosterone; markers of resorption (serum/urine CTx) and formation (P1NP) for monitoring therapy.

Three numbers decide the grade band: the cutoffs −1 / −2.5, the ~30–40% X-ray invisibility threshold, and "BMD is a risk factor, FRAX converts it into fracture probability." No answer gets full marks without DEXA sites (L1–L4 + hip).

5Recent advances

  • Giangregorio et al. (2014) — The Too Fit To Fracture international consensus strongly recommends a multicomponent exercise programme combining progressive resistance and balance training for people with osteoporosis or vertebral fracture, with physiotherapist consultation for those with vertebral fracture.
  • Howe et al. (2011) — Cochrane review of 43 RCTs (4320 postmenopausal women) found exercise, especially progressive resistance and combination training, produces small but significant improvements in bone mineral density at the spine and hip.
  • Giangregorio et al. (2013) — Cochrane review of exercise after osteoporotic vertebral fracture found exercise and physical activity should be encouraged with attention to spine-sparing technique rather than generic activity restriction.
  • ISCD/ESCEO-IOF (2023) — Guidance incorporates trabecular bone score (TBS) and TBS-adjusted FRAX into fracture-risk assessment, refining who is referred for rehabilitation and fracture-prevention exercise.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4d.
  2. McKinnis LN. Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging. FA Davis (reference 8).
  3. Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach. (reference 9).
  4. WHO Technical Report / Kanis JA. FRAX — Assessment of osteoporotic fracture risk (primary).
  5. Shevroja E et al. Update on the clinical use of trabecular bone score (TBS) in the management of osteoporosis. Osteoporos Int. 2023;34:1501–1529.
  6. Gregson CL et al. The 2024 UK clinical guideline for the prevention and treatment of osteoporosis. Arch Osteoporos. 2024.

On the evaluation form — Q6: Postmenopausal osteoporosis work-up

I. Subjective examination

Female, 58 years, 8 years post-menopause. Chief complaint: intermittent mid-thoracic back pain for 1 year, with two severe episodes after lifting, and a documented height loss of about 4 cm. Risk-factor review: early menopause, thin build, low dietary calcium, sedentary lifestyle, no steroid use, mother had a hip fracture. No previous fracture. Red-flag screen negative (no fever, weight loss or features of malignancy). Severity: NPRS 4/10 at baseline. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Increased thoracic kyphosis with a developing Dowager's hump; reduced rib-pelvis distance; standing height reduced versus young-adult height; mild increase in occiput-to-wall distance; slow gait with short steps.

On palpation. Mid-thoracic paraspinal tenderness and spasm; no step-off or radicular signs.

1. Motor assessment. Thoracolumbar AROM limited by pain in extension and rotation; PROM with a pain-limited end-feel. MMT: back extensors 4/5; hip abductors and knee extensors 4/5. Timed Loaded Standing and sit-to-stand performance reduced for age. Reflexes normal.

2. Sensory assessment. Dermatomes intact; peripheral neuropathy screen negative; no saddle anaesthesia.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Independence in household mobility and transfers documented; reduced lifting, bending and walking tolerance. Outcome measures: TUG and gait speed for fall risk; Berg Balance Scale (0-56) if balance is impaired; functional reach; 30-second sit-to-stand; QUALEFFO-41 questionnaire for quality of life in vertebral osteoporosis; serial height measurement; NPRS 0-10 and PSFS 0-10.

4. Gait analysis. Slow gait with short steps; gait speed recorded for fall risk.

5. Balance. Reduced balance; fall risk screened with TUG, functional reach and the Berg Balance Scale (0-56) as above.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this case.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations
  • Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA): low-radiation scan of the lumbar spine and proximal femur; a T-score of ≤ -2.5 confirms osteoporosis, and -1 to -2.5 indicates low bone mass.
  • Vertebral fracture assessment / lateral spine radiograph: lateral image of the thoracolumbar spine; a wedge or compression deformity indicates a prevalent vertebral fracture — the strongest predictor of future fracture.
  • FRAX tool: country, age, BMI and clinical risk factors entered, with or without femoral-neck BMD; a high 10-year major osteoporotic/hip fracture probability guides pharmacological treatment decisions.
  • Serum 25-hydroxy vitamin D (fasting blood sample): deficiency per the laboratory reference is a correctable secondary cause of bone loss and myopathy.
  • Bone turnover markers: serum CTX (resorption) and P1NP (formation); values above the premenopausal reference indicate high turnover and are mainly used to monitor therapy.
  • Secondary-cause panel: serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, PTH, TSH, CBC, ESR/CRP and renal function, screening for hyperparathyroidism, thyroid disease, malignancy and other secondary causes.
9. Special tests

No musculoskeletal special tests are documented for this case; the diagnostic work-up for this patient (DXA, vertebral fracture assessment, FRAX and the laboratory panel) is detailed under Investigations above.

10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Low bone density with kyphosis
  • Thoracic pain
  • Weak back extensors
  • Reduced balance

Functional limitations

  • Reduced lifting, bending and walking tolerance

Disabilities

  • Fear of falls with activity restriction and social withdrawal
11. Functional diagnosis

Postmenopausal osteoporosis with thoracic kyphosis, back-extensor weakness and reduced balance, limiting lifting, bending and walking tolerance and leading to fear of falls, activity restriction and social withdrawal.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): pain 2/10 or less; independent, safe home programme; family-involved fall-risk reduction plan.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): back and leg strength to 5/5; balance retrained to age norms; 30 minutes of daily walking; adherence to calcium, vitamin D and prescribed anti-resorptive therapy with follow-up DXA.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1: pain relief with electrotherapy/heat, posture care, avoidance of loaded spinal flexion and high-impact activity. Stage 2: site-specific loading — prone back extension, progressive resisted hip and knee work with cuffs/bands, weight-bearing walking. Stage 3: balance and fall-prevention training, home-hazard modification, nutrition counselling, medication education, and annual height and DXA follow-up with the physician.

14. Home programme

Prone back extensions, resisted hip and knee exercises with cuffs/bands, weight-bearing walking, balance and fall-prevention exercises, and home-hazard modification as trained.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative assessment following supracondylar fracture of elbow.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5a — Assessment of fractures (pre- & post-operative)

★ Memory hook — Supracondylar alarm: the 5 Ps + pain on passive finger extension = compartment syndrome — the earliest sign. NEVER force extension (myositis ossificans); Baumann angle ≈ 75–80°.

1Introduction

Context

Supracondylar humerus fracture (Gartland I–III) is the commonest elbow fracture of children (fall on outstretched hand); displaced types are treated by closed/open reduction and K-wire fixation, cast 3–4 weeks. Post-op assessment begins the day after surgery.

2Physiology

The distal humerus forms the elbow with the ulna and radius. The carrying angle is the normal valgus of the extended, supinated elbow — about 11° in men and 13° in women (range 11–14° / 13–16°). In children the capitellum ossifies first; Baumann's angle (the humeral-capitellar angle, normally ~75–80°) is used to judge reduction, and the anterior humeral line should intersect the capitellum on the lateral radiograph.

3Pathophysiology

A supracondylar fracture disrupts this alignment and threatens the neurovascular bundle. Displaced Gartland III fractures risk brachial-artery injury and compartment syndrome (the 5 Ps — pain, pallor, paraesthesia, pulselessness, paralysis — with pain on passive finger extension the earliest sign); if missed it causes Volkmann's ischaemic contracture. Malunion produces cubitus varus (gunstock deformity), and forceful passive stretching predisposes to myositis ossificans.

Fig 7 — The post-op elbow sketch: K-wires in place, the carrying angle marked, and the 5-P compartment-syndrome box beside it — the safety half of the answer in one glance.

4Answer

Neurovascular — the first priority
  • Vascular: radial pulse, capillary refill, colour/temperature of the hand — brachial-artery injury/kinking threatens the limb; watch for Volkmann's ischaemic contracture — the 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis), especially pain on passive finger extension.
  • Neural: test anterior interosseous (median — OK sign), main median, radial (wrist/thumb extension) and ulnar nerves — all are at risk from both injury and K-wires.
  • Compartment syndrome screen: tense forearm, pain out of proportion.
Local, ROM & radiology
  • Wound/pin sites — discharge, infection; cast/splint condition.
  • ROM elbow flexion–extension, pronation–supination once the cast is off (expect stiffness; grade objectively by goniometer).
  • Carrying angle — normal valgus ~11° in men, ~13° in women (Dutton: 11–14° / 13–16°); loss = cubitus varus ("gunstock", the classic malunion). Baumann's angle on radiograph (humeral capitellar angle, ~75–80°; a falling value warns of varus) plus callus formation define union progression.
Strength, function, complications

MMT of elbow/forearm/wrist musculature once pain allows; circumference for atrophy; functional tasks (writing, feeding); outcome instruments (QuickDASH, pediatric PROMIS). Hunt for complications: pin-tract infection, myositis ossificans (calcification anteriorly — avoid forceful passive stretching!), stiffness, malunion (varus), nerve palsy, growth disturbance.

Conclusion

Assessment findings set the rehabilitation stage — early gentle active motion, no forced passive stretching, progressive strengthening — re-assessed every visit against a documented baseline.

The sentence that earns the safety mark: "NEVER force passive extension in a post-supracondylar elbow — myositis ossificans." Examiners invariably probe it in viva.

5Recent advances

  • Schmale et al. (2014) — Randomised controlled trial (61 children) found a short course of hospital-based physiotherapy gave no added benefit over cast removal alone for elbow motion or function after uncomplicated paediatric supracondylar humeral fracture, challenging routine referral.
  • Keppler et al. (2005) — Prospective randomised study found weekly physiotherapy improved elbow range of motion at 12–18 weeks but showed no difference at one year, concluding postoperative physiotherapy is unnecessary in children without neurovascular injury.
  • Ducic et al. (2015) — Prospective randomised study found physiotherapy improved early range of motion after supracondylar fracture but groups were equal by 12 months, showing full recovery takes about a year and is largely spontaneous.
  • Flynn et al. (1974) — Flynn's criteria (loss of carrying angle and loss of motion) remain the standard grading system for assessing elbow outcome after supracondylar fracture, guiding when residual stiffness warrants physiotherapy.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5a.
  2. Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. (reference 16).
  3. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — elbow chapter.
  4. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13).
  5. Duffy S et al. Interventions for treating supracondylar elbow fractures in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022;6:CD013290.
  6. Vaquero-Picado A et al. Management of supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children. EFORT Open Rev. 2018;3(10):526–540.

On the evaluation form — Q7: Post-operative supracondylar humerus fracture (child, K-wires)

I. Subjective examination

Boy, 7 years, right-hand dominant. Chief complaint: stiff left elbow. History: fall on an outstretched hand 5 weeks ago; displaced (Gartland III) supracondylar fracture treated with closed reduction and percutaneous K-wiring; above-elbow cast and K-wires removed 1 week ago. The mother reports that the child holds the arm close and prefers the right hand for writing and eating. Pain evaluation: faces scale 3/10 on movement, none at rest. Red-flag screen: no night pain, fever or fresh trauma.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Healed pin-site scars on the lateral elbow; mild loss of left upper-arm bulk; limb carried in a guarded, slightly flexed attitude; carrying angle compared with the right.

On palpation. Mild scar tenderness with mobile scar tissue; no warmth, swelling or palpable bony mass over the distal triceps (myositis ossificans screen).

1. Motor assessment. AROM: elbow flexion 40-100° with a 40° extension lag; pronation-supination about half range. PROM: flexion to 110° with a firm end-feel; extension limited by a capsular feel. MMT (MRC 0-5): elbow flexors and extensors 4/5; wrist and hand muscles 5/5. Girth: left arm 1.5 cm less than the right at mid-arm. Reflexes (biceps, brachioradialis, triceps) present and symmetrical; no limb-length discrepancy.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact in the median, radial and ulnar territories; anterior interosseous nerve screen (tip-to-tip pinch, OK circle) normal; no Tinel's over the scar; hand vascular status normal.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Left-arm use in age-appropriate tasks — writing, eating, dressing and play — recorded, with school participation restrictions documented on the ICF-CY framework. Outcome measures: goniometric ROM (flexion-extension, pronation-supination); MRC grades 0-5; girth; Pediatric Outcomes Data Collection Instrument (PODCI) for paediatric function and participation.

4. Gait analysis. Gait unaffected.

5. Balance. Not affected in this upper-limb case.

6. Hand function. The child holds the left arm close and prefers the right hand for writing and eating; reaching, grasping and releasing with the left during age-appropriate tasks is reduced.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

Follow-up radiographs per the orthopaedic records, including Baumann's angle (the angle between the capitellar physis and the long axis of the humerus on X-ray; deviation from the normal side by more than about 5° predicts the final carrying angle); no current films reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Carrying angle measurementGoniometry with the elbow extended and forearm supinated, compared side-to-sideLoss of valgus or a varus angle versus the normal sideCubitus varus malunion, the commonest late deformity — compared with the right side; deviation not documented in this patient
Anterior interosseous nerve screenAsk the child to make an OK circle or pick up a small coin with tip-to-tip pinchUnable to flex the thumb IP and index DIP jointsAIN palsy associated with supracondylar fracture — negative in this patient (screen normal)
Tinel's over pin sitesPercuss along the scar and pin-site tracksReproducible tingling in a nerve territoryNeuroma or nerve irritation — negative in this patient (no Tinel's over the scar)
Palpation for myositis ossificansPalpate the distal triceps and anterior elbow for a firm massFirm, tender bony lumpMyositis ossificans limiting extension, avoid forceful stretching — negative in this patient (no palpable bony mass)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Elbow ROM restriction
  • Mild weakness
  • Disuse atrophy

Functional limitations

  • Difficulty writing, dressing and playing

Disabilities

  • Reduced school participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Post-operative left supracondylar humerus fracture (Gartland III, treated by closed reduction and percutaneous K-wiring, wires removed 1 week ago) with elbow ROM restriction, mild weakness and disuse atrophy, limiting writing, dressing, play and school participation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): flexion to 120° with an extension lag of 20°; painless self-care with the left arm.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): elbow arc of 0-130°; pronation-supination within 10° of the right side; symmetrical carrying angle; full school and play participation.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1-2 after wire removal): active and active-assisted exercises, gravity-eliminated flexion-extension in side-lying, pronation-supination with a bat or rolling pin; no passive stretching. Stage 2 (weeks 3-6): strengthening with putty, light weight-bearing through the arm, play-based reach activities. Stage 3: graded return to sports.

14. Home programme

10 repetitions of each movement 3-4 times daily as a game; hot packs before exercise; weekly girth and ROM checks; parents counselled to avoid forceful stretching (myositis ossificans risk); orthopaedic follow-up for the carrying angle.

Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe in detail the assessment following below-knee amputation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 5d — Assessment of amputations; Unit 6 — functional assessment

★ Memory hook — Ideal stump: gently cylindrical, firm, healed, volume-stable by 3–6 months, scar mobile, soft-tissue pad over bone. Assess with AMP / LCI-5 for mobility prediction.

1Introduction

Below-knee (transtibial) amputation removes the foot and ankle but retains the knee, which is preserved deliberately because knee retention improves prosthetic function and reduces energy cost compared with transfemoral amputation. Assessment is a staged process: residual limb → proximal joints → prosthesis → gait → function → psychosocial status.

2Physiology

In normal gait the ankle plantarflexors provide the push-off that drives forward progression; the knee and hip extensors control loading and the hip abductors stabilise the pelvis in single-limb stance. An intact, pain-free knee with full extension is central to transtibial prosthetic gait; even a 10° knee flexion contracture impairs prosthetic alignment and increases energy cost.

3Pathophysiology

After transtibial amputation the residual limb remodels: oedema resolves, volume shrinks and the stump matures over 3–6 months, while nerve transection may produce a neuroma (Tinel-positive) and phantom-limb phenomena. Hip and knee weakness, a knee flexion contracture, or an immature, oedematous stump all degrade prosthetic fitting and gait, and the sound limb is overloaded and at risk of degenerative change.

4Answer

Residual limb

Residual-limb shape (ideal: firm — cylindrical for total-surface-bearing sockets, conical for traditional patellar-tendon-bearing — matured by 3–6 months post-op), skin (scars, grafts, moisture, breakdown over bony points), wound healing, adherent vs mobile scar, sensation (hyper-sensitivity, neuroma — Tinel's), oedema/volume fluctuation (circumferential measurements; test socks), limb length and soft-tissue padding over the bone end.

Musculoskeletal

Hip and knee ROM — flexion contracture of the knee is the enemy of prosthetic gait (even 10° matters); strength of hip flexors/extensors, abductors, quadriceps and hamstrings (MMT); knee stability; upper-limb strength (crutch/transfer readiness) and trunk control/balance.

Pain & prosthetic/gait
  • Pain: differentiate phantom-limb pain (painful sensations in the absent foot) from residual-limb pain (neuroma, bone spur, socket pressure) and back pain.
  • Prosthesis: socket fit (pistoning, pressure marks, redness that doesn't fade in 10–15 min), suspension, alignment in standing and walking; component condition (foot category, SACH etc.).
  • Gait: observe for vaulting, circumduction, lateral trunk bending, knee instability and unequal step length — each names a fitting or weakness problem.
Functional assessment

Standardised instruments: Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) (with/without prosthesis), Locomotor Capabilities Index-5, Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire, 2-minute/6-minute walk test, TUG, and the SIGAM mobility grades; K-levels (0–4) classify mobility potential. Also energy expenditure (O₂ cost of amputee gait is higher — relevant to rehab planning).

Psychosocial

Body image, depression screening, motivation, family support, occupation and financial access to prosthetic services — decisive in the Indian setting for prosthetic success.

Fig 8 — The below-knee stump sketch with the full assessment checklist beside it. Draw the limb, label six points, then list what each label tells you.
Structure wins: residual limb → proximal joints → prosthesis → gait → scales → psychosocial. Name-dropping AMP or LCI-5 with one-line purpose lifts a generic answer into the top band; "differentiate phantom pain from residual-limb pain" is the viva's pet question.

5Recent advances

  • Chan et al. (2007) — Landmark randomised, sham-controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine found mirror therapy markedly reduced phantom limb pain after leg amputation, establishing the technique in amputee rehabilitation.
  • Barbin et al. (2016) — First systematic review of mirror therapy for phantom limb pain concluded the evidence is insufficient to recommend it as first-line treatment and that protocols need standardising.
  • Al Muderis et al. (2024) — Observational study showed transtibial osseointegration (bone-anchored prosthesis) improved K-level, Timed Up-and-Go, six-minute walk distance, prosthesis wear time and quality of life, with an acceptable safety profile.
  • VA/DoD (2024) — The Lower-Limb Amputation guideline recommends a rigid or semi-rigid residual-limb dressing after transtibial amputation, osseointegration as an option for eligible patients, and patient-reported plus performance-based measures to assess function.
  • Gailey et al. (2002) — The Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) and Locomotor Capabilities Index-5 remain the core validated mobility measures for prosthetic rehabilitation.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 5d & 6.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10) — amputation chapters.
  3. Chui KC et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. (reference 18).
  4. Gailey RS et al. Amputee Mobility Predictor. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. (primary)
  5. VA/DoD. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Rehabilitation of Individuals with Lower Limb Amputation. 2024.
  6. Gailey RS et al. The Amputee Mobility Predictor: an instrument to assess determinants of the lower-limb amputee's ability to ambulate. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2002.

On the evaluation form — Q8: Below-knee (transtibial) amputation assessment

I. Subjective examination

Man, 55 years. Chief complaint: right residual-limb pain with phantom sensations. History: right transtibial amputation 6 weeks ago after a road-traffic crush injury; stump healed and sutures removed. Pain evaluation distinguishes residual-limb pain (stump) from phantom limb pain (shooting foot pain, 4/10, worse at night) and from non-painful phantom sensation. Risk factors: smoker, borderline diabetic. Personal and social history: mobility by hop transfers and walker use at home. Goal: shop-floor work with a prosthesis. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Residual-limb shape (conical versus cylindrical — of prosthetic relevance), well-healed scar, skin colour, oedema and redundant distal tissue; sound limb inspected for vascular and trophic changes; hop-to gait with a walker.

On palpation. Distal tenderness, scar mobility, tissue tone at the stump end (firm distal padding is needed for weight bearing), tibial and fibular ends not prominent, neuroma tenderness; pulses in the sound limb.

1. Motor assessment. AROM/PROM: knee flexion-extension full with a normal end-feel (no flexion contracture); hip motions full. MMT (MRC 0-5): right hip flexors, abductors and extensors 4/5; stump knee extensors/flexors 4/5; sound limb 5/5. Stump girth measured circumferentially at fixed intervals from the tibial tuberosity for shrinkage charting, with stump length recorded.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation over the residual limb with hypersensitivity at the scar; Semmes-Weinstein 10-g monofilament testing of protective sensation on the sound foot; sound-limb dermatomes and myotomes intact.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Medicare Functional Classification Levels (K0-K4) assigned; transfers and bed mobility; hop and walker distance; stairs. Outcome measures: Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) for prosthetic mobility potential; Locomotor Capabilities Index for walking capabilities with the prosthesis; Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire for satisfaction and quality of life; 6-minute walk test and TUG; stump-pain and phantom-pain NPRS 0-10.

4. Gait analysis. Hop-to gait with a walker at home; once prosthesis is fitted, stump weight bearing and gait parameters (velocity, cadence, step length) to be assessed.

5. Balance. Standing balance on the sound limb; further balance testing not documented at this pre-prosthetic stage.

6. Hand function. Upper-limb use required for walker handling (assistive device); no hand dysfunction recorded.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

No imaging or laboratory investigations reviewed at this assessment; stump-healing status as per the surgical records.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Distal Tinel's testPercuss along the scar and distal tibial/fibular nerve tractsReproducible electric tingling into the phantom footNeuroma at the nerve ending, refer if painful — neuroma tenderness present on palpation in this patient
Knee flexion contracture assessmentSupine; heel on the plinth, attempt full knee extensionExtension lag with a firm end-feelContracture will impair prosthetic alignment and gait — negative in this patient (full extension with a normal end-feel)
Thomas testSupine; one hip flexed to flatten the lumbar spine, test the other hipLack of full hip extensionHip flexion contracture affecting prosthetic stance — negative in this patient (hip motions full)
Prone hip extension (gluteal) testProne; lift the limb into extension against gravity/resistanceWeak extension with trunk substitutionWeak hip extensors/abductors, predicting a Trendelenburg prosthetic gait — positive for weakness in this patient (hip extensors 4/5)
Stump maturity assessmentSerial circumferential girth, volume and skin checksContinued shrinkage over weeksDetermines readiness for the definitive socket — serial charting initiated; stump not yet mature at 6 weeks post-amputation
10-g monofilament (sound foot)Apply the filament to plantar sitesFailure to feel at any siteLoss of protective sensation in the remaining limb — testing performed; result not documented
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Phantom and residual-limb pain
  • Hip-muscle weakness
  • Stump oedema/immaturity
  • Sound-limb overload risk

Functional limitations

  • Mobility dependent without a prosthesis

Disabilities

  • Unable to resume work and community ambulation
11. Functional diagnosis

Right transtibial amputation 6 weeks post-operative, with residual-limb and phantom pain, hip-muscle weakness and an immature, oedematous stump, causing mobility dependence without a prosthesis and preventing return to work and community ambulation.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): independent hop transfers; phantom pain 2/10 or less; elastic stump-wrapping regime established; hip and knee strength 5/5.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): mature stump for a definitive prosthesis; independent prosthetic gait without aids on level ground; 6-minute walk distance consistent with community ambulation; return to work.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (pre-prosthetic): elastic stump wrapping or shrinker sock, desensitisation (towel rubbing, textured materials), mirror therapy and TENS for phantom pain, graded hip/knee strengthening, sound-limb conditioning and stump skin-care education. Stage 2 (prosthetic training): stump weight tolerance, donning/doffing, standing balance, then gait training from parallel bars to level ground, ramps and stairs, with falls training.

14. Home programme

Bandaging, daily stump and sound-foot inspection, strengthening sets, graded walking.

Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for shoulder pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6 (b, c) — Functional assessment scales; selection of outcome measures

★ Memory hook — One measure per ICF level: body function (goniometry · dynamometry · VAS) + activity (SPADI · DASH · ASES · Constant) + participation (PSFS). MCID: SPADI 8–10, DASH 10–15.

1Introduction

Outcome measures for shoulder pain are the standardised, validated instruments used to quantify the patient's status at baseline and to detect real change after intervention. Because shoulder pain spans pain, movement, strength, activity and participation, no single tool is sufficient: a defensible evaluation combines an impairment measure (ROM, strength, pain) with a self-report function scale.

Choosing measures is itself a skill — select by ICF level, by region- versus condition-specificity, by psychometric quality in the target population, and by responsiveness with a known minimal clinically important difference (MCID).

2Physiology

Normal shoulder function depends on the integrated action of the glenohumeral, scapulothoracic, acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints with the rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers. This function is best described across the ICF levels — body function/structure (ROM, strength, pain), activity (reaching, dressing) and participation (work, sport) — and outcome measures are chosen to capture each level.

In the healthy shoulder, pain-free movement sits within defined norms (flexion ~180°, abduction ~180°, external rotation at 90° abduction ~90°), strength is symmetric within about 10%, and scapulohumeral rhythm is roughly 2:1. Outcome measures are anchored to these norms so that deviation and change can be quantified.

3Pathophysiology

Shoulder pain arises from a spectrum of pathology — rotator-cuff tendinopathy and tears, subacromial impingement, adhesive capsulitis, instability and glenohumeral arthritis — each producing a characteristic pattern of pain, restricted movement (a painful arc of 60–120° or a capsular pattern of external rotation > abduction > internal rotation) and functional loss.

Because the underlying pathology and the expected treatment effect differ, the outcome measure must match the condition and be responsive to change. A measure that is valid in frozen shoulder may ceiling out in a young overhead athlete with instability, and psychosocial factors (fear-avoidance, catastrophising) call for a biopsychosocial measure alongside the region-specific one.

4Answer

Body structure and function (impairment): ROM by goniometry or inclinometry (note the 60–120° painful arc); strength by handheld dynamometry or MMT of the cuff and scapular muscles; pain by VAS/NRS at rest and on provocation, plus a pain diary.

Self-report scales — the core of the answer:

ScaleItems / rangeBest forPsychometrics
SPADI13 items (5 pain, 8 disability), 0–100General shoulder pain; sensitive in frozen shoulderICC ~0.99; MDC ~6; MCID ~8–10
DASH / QuickDASH30 / 11 items, 0–100Upper-limb-wide disability; multiple jointsMCID ~10–15
ASES13 items, 0–100Rotator-cuff pathology; physician- and self-ratedMCID ~6–7
Constant–Murley100 pts (35 subjective + 65 objective)European standard including ROM and strengthMCID ~10
SST / UCLA / WORC / WOSIvariedSingle-answer / general / cuff disease / instabilityGood reliability
PSFS3 patient-chosen activities, 0–10Individualised and very responsiveMCID ~2

Interpretation. Report baseline → discharge change against the MCID of the chosen scale (SPADI ≈ 8–10 points; DASH ≈ 10–15 points), and use two complementary levels (one impairment measure plus one self-report scale) for a defensible, ICF-rounded evaluation. Never write “VAS is the gold standard for shoulder function” — VAS measures pain intensity, not function.

Conclusion

Outcome measurement in shoulder pain should be deliberate, not habitual: pick measures that match the condition and the ICF level, know their MCID, and combine an impairment measure with a self-report scale so that both the tissue and the person's function are tracked.

5Recent advances

  • Furtado et al. (2022) — Overview of systematic reviews found strong reliability and validity for the DASH, SPADI, ASES, WORC and Simple Shoulder Test, and proposed them as a core clinical outcome set for shoulder disorders.
  • Lafrance et al. (2022) — The JOSPT clinical practice guideline for rotator cuff disorders recommends an active, task-oriented rehabilitation programme (exercise plus education) and use of patient-reported outcome measures to guide care and return to work.
  • Venturin et al. (2023) — Validation study confirmed the SPADI has excellent test–retest reliability (ICC ≈ 0.99) and a minimal detectable change of about 6.3 points in frozen shoulder.
  • Padua et al. (2021) — Review recommends combining a region-wide measure (DASH) with a condition-specific measure — ASES for rotator-cuff pathology and osteoarthritis, SPADI for stiffness and unspecified shoulder pain.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 6.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  3. Roach KE et al. SPADI. Arthritis Care Res. 1991 (primary).
  4. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4).
  5. Reid S et al. Patient-reported outcome measures used for shoulder disorders: an overview of systematic reviews. J Hand Ther. 2022.
  6. Briggs E et al. Choosing patient-reported outcome measures for shoulder pathology. EFORT Open Rev. 2021.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total hip replacement.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4f / 6 — Exercise testing & functional assessment in musculoskeletal dysfunction

★ Memory hook — THR fitness = painless independent gait + abductors ≥4/5 (no Trendelenburg) + TUG ≤12 s + gait speed ≥1 m/s + safe stairs — re-test at 3 / 6 / 12 months.

1Introduction

Total hip replacement (THR) is offered for end-stage hip osteoarthritis. After surgery, "fitness" means the patient has the impairments, gait, balance and functional capacity needed to resume independent community ambulation, work and low-impact activity safely, without threatening the implant.

2Physiology

In normal walking the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) hold the pelvis level in single-limb stance; their failure produces a Trendelenburg drop or trunk lurch. Functional hip motion for daily life is roughly 110° flexion, 30° abduction and adequate rotation, and community ambulation requires a gait speed of about 1.0 m/s and a Timed Up-and-Go under ~12 s.

3Pathophysiology

THR relieves arthritic pain but leaves post-operative impairments: hip-abductor weakness and Trendelenburg gait, reduced hip ROM, thigh atrophy and, with a posterior approach, dislocation precautions. These impairments limit cane-free walking, stairs and return to work, and define the criteria that must be met — and re-tested — before the patient is declared fit.

4Answer

Surgical & safety screening

Confirm radiological implant position and stability, healed wound, absence of infection/HO; note surgical approach (posterior precautions vs direct-anterior fewer restrictions); pain level (≤3/10 on activity); medical clearance if cardiac comorbidity.

Impairment criteria
  • ROM: functional range needed for daily life — hip flexion ≥110°, abduction ≥30°, ER in abduction; documented risk-relevant limits per approach.
  • Strength: abductors grade ≥4/5 (no Trendelenburg sign in single-leg stance for 10–30 s), extensors and flexors ≥4/5; no pain on resisted tests.
  • Leg-length equality within 1–1.5 cm; no fixed contracture.
Gait & balance

Independent gait without assistive device, symmetrical cadence and step length, no limp/Trendelenburg lurch, single-limb balance ≥10 s (eyes open), Stork/functional reach within norms; stairs with rail ascending and descending reciprocally.

Functional performance tests
  • Timed Up-and-Go — community ambulation benchmark ≤12–14 s; ≤8–10 s for near-normal.
  • Six-minute walk test — compare with age-norms (roughly 400–600 m healthy adults; a post-THR patient should exceed ~70% predicted).
  • 10-metre walk (gait speed ≥1.0 m/s = community standard), stair test, sit-to-stand ×5 <12 s; self-reports: Harris Hip Score, Oxford Hip Score, HOOS for QoL confirmation.
Fitness verdict

The adult is declared fit for independent community ambulation/work when: painless independent gait, abductor strength 4/5+, negative Trendelenburg, functional ROM, TUG ≤12 s, safe stairs, and stable 6MWT performance — criteria graded on reassessment at 3, 6 and 12 months.

Fig 10 — The THR fitness decision chain: impairments → gait/balance → functional tests → fit or continue. Any criteria question can be answered with this pattern.
Numbers decide this answer: TUG ≤12 s, gait speed ≥1 m/s, Trendelenburg-negative single-leg stance. Also name ONE patient-reported scale (Harris/Oxford/HOOS) to complete the ICF triangle.

5Recent advances

  • Klein et al. (2007) — Hip Society/AAHKS consensus guidelines frame return to sport after total hip arthroplasty in three tiers — low-impact activity recommended, intermediate-impact with experience, high-impact generally not recommended — with most surgeons advising a 3–6 month wait.
  • Hoorntje et al. (2018) — Systematic review and meta-analysis found most patients return to sport after total hip arthroplasty within about 28 weeks and to work within about 17 weeks, with a shift from high- to low-impact activity.
  • Mooiweer et al. (2022) — Systematic review confirmed consensus for low-impact activity after hip or knee arthroplasty, non-recommendation of contact and high-impact sport, and applicability of the WHO recommendation of 150–300 minutes of moderate activity per week.
  • Ohio State CPG (2022) — Lists return-to-recreation criteria: strength greater than 90% of the uninvolved limb, single-leg leg press above 90% body weight, patient-reported outcome scores of 90% or more, and physician clearance.

6References

  1. RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 4f & 6.
  2. Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13) — THR criteria.
  3. Wilk KE et al. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. (reference 14).
  4. ACSM. Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. (reference 12).
  5. Meftah M et al. Return to sport after hip and knee arthroplasty: counseling the patient on resuming an active lifestyle. Curr Rev Musculoskelet Med. 2023.
  6. Klemt C et al. Being active with a total hip or knee prosthesis: a systematic review. Eur Rev Aging Phys Act. 2022.

On the evaluation form — Q10: Fitness evaluation after total hip replacement (adult)

I. Subjective examination

Man, 62 years, 8 weeks after a right primary total hip replacement (posterior approach, cementless prosthesis) for advanced osteoarthritis. Chief complaints: mild anterior thigh pain after walking (NPRS 3/10) and a feeling of the hip "giving way". Functional history: walks indoors with a single cane and needs the rail on stairs. Post-operative precautions followed. Red-flag screen negative (no dislocation, wound discharge or fever). Past medical history: controlled hypertension. Vitals recorded.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Well-healed posterior-lateral scar; no gluteal wasting; mild Trendelenburg with trunk lurch over the right and a shortened right stance phase.

On palpation. Mild scar tenderness; no trochanteric tenderness; abductors non-tender but weak on testing; no warmth.

1. Motor assessment. AROM: hip flexion 0-90° (within the precaution range), abduction 25°, rotations within precaution limits; PROM similar, with a slightly firm end-feel in abduction. Resisted isometrics: abductors and extensors 3+/5. MMT: hip flexors 4/5, extensors 4/5, knee extensors 4/5; handheld dynamometry used for objective abductor values. Reflexes normal; thigh girth 1.5 cm less on the right; mild apparent shortening of the right limb.

2. Sensory assessment. Sensation intact; sciatic and superior gluteal territory screen normal; no foot drop or dermatomal loss.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). FIM (18 items, score 18-126) for transfers, locomotion and stairs; 30-second chair stand and step-up/step-down tests for lower-limb functional strength and stair readiness. Outcome measures: Harris Hip Score (0-100); Oxford Hip Score (0-48); Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) for pain, symptoms, function, sport and quality of life; SF-36; NPRS 0-10 and PSFS 0-10 for walking, stairs and sleeping.

4. Gait analysis. Velocity, cadence, step-length symmetry and cane dependence recorded; mild Trendelenburg with trunk lurch over the right and a shortened right stance phase; TUG and 6-minute walk test for endurance.

5. Balance. Single-leg stance, Functional Reach and Berg Balance Scale (0-56).

6. Hand function. Single cane used for indoor walking and the rail needed on stairs (assistive-device dependence); no other hand dysfunction recorded.

7. Coordination. Not formally documented at this assessment.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Trendelenburg testStand on the operated leg for 30 secondsPelvis drops on the sound side or the trunk leans over the stance limbWeak hip abductors, not ready for unsupported walking — positive in this patient (mild Trendelenburg with trunk lurch)
Thomas testSupine; flex the sound hip to flatten the lumbar spine, test the operated hipOperated hip lifts off the plinthFlexion contracture affecting gait — negative in this patient (hip flexion 0-90°; no contracture recorded)
Single-leg stance testBarefoot, stand on one leg, arms freeUnable to hold 10 seconds or marked swayDynamic balance and abductor deficit — result not documented in this patient (assessed under balance)
30-second chair standRise fully and sit from a standard chair as many times as possible in 30 secondsRepetitions below age normsLower-limb functional strength below fitness level — result not documented in this patient
Step-up/step-down testStep onto and off a standard 20 cm stepPain, substitution or handrail dependenceReadiness for stairs and community ambulation — positive in this patient (handrail dependence on stairs)
10. Problem list

Impairments

  • Weak hip abductors (3+/5) with positive Trendelenburg
  • Reduced hip ROM
  • Thigh atrophy

Functional limitations

  • Cane-dependent gait
  • Stair difficulty

Disabilities

  • Unable to resume community walking, driving and work
11. Functional diagnosis

Right total hip replacement 8 weeks post-operative, with residual hip-abductor weakness (3+/5, positive Trendelenburg), reduced hip ROM and thigh atrophy, causing cane-dependent gait and stair difficulty and preventing return to community walking, driving and work.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): hip abduction 4/5; Trendelenburg-free gait with a single cane; TUG within 12 seconds; pain 2/10 or less.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): pain-free independent gait without an aid with symmetrical step length; hip flexion 100° and abduction 30° with strength 4+/5 or better; independence on stairs; return to driving and work; Harris Hip Score in the good range.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (up to 6 weeks): precaution education, gait retraining with a cane, scar mobilisation, isometric then active abductor/extensor work in side-lying, ankle pumps. Stage 2 (6-12 weeks): progressive resistance with bands and cuff weights, dynamometer reassessment, single-leg balance, step-ups, treadmill endurance. Stage 3 (3 months+): low-impact fitness (swimming, cycling); avoid high-impact sports.

14. Home programme

Daily abductor sets, bridges, heel raises, mini-squats within precautions, walking increased by 5 minutes weekly up to 30 minutes daily.

Last-Hour Sheet · Paper III — Physical & Functional Diagnosis

QP 8131 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Role of assessment in diagnosis

  • Cycle: history → hypotheses → objective exam → PT diagnosis (ICF) → treat → re-assess; red flags screened at every step.
  • Assessment = data collection; diagnosis = its interpretation; PT dx = movement-system label (e.g., subacromial impingement + scapular dyskinesis).

2C3–C4 screening

  • C4 dermatome: neck → clavicle → shoulder cap (C3 suboccipital). Myotome C4: shrug + diaphragm (C3-5).
  • No C4 DTR — test biceps (C5), brachioradialis (C6). Spurling, distraction, ULNT, Hoffman's.

3Fibromyalgia screening

  • Widespread pain >3 months. ACR 1990: ≥11/18 tender points at ~4 kg thumb pressure.
  • ACR 2010/2016: WPI (0–19) + symptom severity. Upper-trunk pairs: suboccipital, low cervical, mid-trapezius, supraspinatus.
  • Differentiate myofascial trigger point (taut band, referral) vs tender point (systemic, no band); FIQR for baseline.

4Direct access

  • Patient → physio first, no referral: earlier treatment, fewer visits/imaging, cost-effective, professional autonomy — with red-flag competence and referral criteria.

5Ankle special tests

  • Anterior drawer (10–15° PF) = ATFL, >4–5 mm positive; talar tilt (90°) = CFL, >5–10°.
  • Syndesmosis: squeeze, Kleiger (ER), Cotton. Ottawa rules for X-ray triage; FAAM/Cumberland for outcome.

6Osteoporosis investigations

  • DEXA L1–L4 + hip, ~1/10 chest X-ray dose. WHO T-score: ≥ −1 / −1 to −2.4 / ≤ −2.5 (+ fracture = severe); Z-score for the young.
  • FRAX = 10-year fracture probability. X-ray shows loss only after 30–40%. Labs: Ca, PO₄, ALP, vitamin D, PTH, TSH.

7Post-op supracondylar elbow

  • 5 Ps of compartment syndrome (pain on passive finger extension first!); AIN/median/radial/ulnar screens.
  • Carrying angle ~11° valgus (loss = cubitus varus); Baumann ~75–80°; NEVER force passive extension — myositis ossificans.

8Below-knee amputation

  • Stump: shape, skin, scar, sensation (Tinel), volume, knee ROM (no flexion contracture).
  • Phantom vs residual-limb pain; socket fit/pistoning; gait: vaulting, circumduction, trunk bend.
  • Scales: AMP, LCI-5, 2MWT/6MWT, TUG; psychosocial + vocational readiness.

9Shoulder outcome measures

  • Pair one per ICF level: body function (goniometry, dynamometry, VAS) + activity/participation (self-report).
  • SPADI 13 items; DASH 30 / QuickDASH 11; ASES; Constant (35 subjective + 65 objective); UCLA; SST; PSFS. MCID: SPADI 8–10, DASH 10–15.

10THR fitness criteria

  • Impairment: ROM functional, abductors ≥4/5, Trendelenburg negative, leg length ≤1–1.5 cm.
  • Function: independent painless gait, stairs reciprocal, TUG ≤12 s, gait speed ≥1 m/s, 6MWT ≥~70% predicted; HHS/Oxford/HOOS.
Numbers to carry into the hall: 20–30° drawer, 4 kg thumb pressure, ≥11/18, T-score −1/−2.5, ~11° carrying angle, TUG ≤12 s, gait speed 1 m/s. Six numbers, six questions.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Enumerate basic assessment methods for joint play movements.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 1a — Introduction to assessment: basic assessment methods

★ Memory hook — Roll, Spin, Glide, Traction — four circles and two rules (convex–concave); then the nine-item enumeration: PAIVM, PPIVM, spring, end-feel.

1Introduction

Joint play is the accessory, involuntary component of joint movement that a patient cannot perform voluntarily. Assessment of joint play examines that accessory layer — the roll, spin, glide, traction and compression between joint surfaces — which voluntary range and imaging cannot show. It is the bridge between diagnosis and manual therapy.

2Physiology

Every joint moves in two layers. The layer the patient controls is osteokinematics — flexion, abduction, rotation. Beneath it runs the layer the patient cannot command: arthrokinematics, or joint play — the accessory roll, spin and glide of the surfaces plus traction and compression between them. A knee that bends to 120° can still be restricted by a stiff posterior glide, and a shoulder that abducts fully may hide a hypomobile inferior glide.

Two principles guide the examination. First, if voluntary range looks normal but the joint hurts or feels tight, the problem often sits in the accessory layer. Second, the convex–concave rule tells you the direction to test and treat: a convex surface moving on a fixed concave one glides opposite to its roll, while a concave surface moving on a fixed convex one glides in the same direction as the movement.

3Pathophysiology

When the accessory layer is lost the joint becomes either hypomobile — a firm or hard end-feel with reduced glide, as in capsular tightness or osteoarthritis — or hypermobile — a soft, spongy end-feel with excessive travel, as in ligamentous laxity. A restriction that reproduces the patient's symptom at grade I points to an irritable, pain-dominant joint; reproduction only near the limit points to a stiffness-dominant joint. That distinction sets the grade of mobilisation chosen.

4Answer

The basic assessment methods for joint play, enumerated:

  1. Passive accessory intervertebral and peripheral joint movements (PAIVMs) — central and unilateral glides for the spine, translatoric glides for peripheral joints.
  2. Passive physiological intervertebral movements (PPIVMs) — the therapist moves the joint through its voluntary arc and grades the feel.
  3. Assessment of roll, spin and glide in the loose-packed (resting) position.
  4. Long-axis traction and distraction.
  5. Compression and joint-springing to reproduce the patient's symptom.
  6. End-feel assessment at the physiological limit — bony, capsular, soft-tissue approximation, springy block or empty.
  7. Maitland's grading of the oscillation — grades I to IV, small-to-large amplitude within or up to the limit.
  8. Ligamentous stress tests for stability of the accessory restraint system.
  9. Hypermobility screening on the other side of the spectrum — the Beighton score.

How to perform and interpret. Position the joint close to its loose-packed position so the capsule is slack; stabilise the proximal segment with one hand and apply the glide with the other, taking up the slack before grading the oscillation. Compare with the contralateral side — the patient is their own control. Ask two questions of every glide: how far does it travel, and does it reproduce the familiar pain? A firm or hard end-feel with reduced glide indicates hypomobility (this joint wants mobilisation); a soft, spongy end-feel with excessive travel indicates hypermobility (this joint wants control, not stretching).

In Indian OPDs the classic example is knee osteoarthritis lacking the last 15° of extension: the missing movement is a restricted anterior tibial glide, and graded anterior glides become the treatment.

Conclusion

Assessment of joint play is not an extra skill but the bridge between diagnosis and manual therapy: it quantifies the accessory layer, defines the direction and grade of treatment, and is interpreted from end-feel and symptom reproduction rather than from range alone.

“Enumerate” means a numbered list — nine one-line items score better than three long paragraphs. Learn the numbers, write the list, then add one sentence of interpretation.

5Recent advances

  • O'Donohue & Wise (2021) — the Mobil-Aider device gave objective, reliable measurement of accessory glide (intra-rater ICC 0.771 for glenohumeral posterior glide and 0.904 for radiocarpal volar glide), allowing joint-play deficits to be quantified rather than judged by feel alone.
  • Gorgos et al. (2014) — a systematic review found strong evidence that intra-clinician reliability of joint mobilisation force application is good but inter-clinician reliability is only poor to moderate, so standardising applied force (for example with feedback devices) matters when testing accessory motion.
  • Pfluegler et al. (2020) — a systematic review found passive joint mobilisation immediately alters local muscle function, decreasing superficial muscle activity and improving motor patterns in symptomatic individuals.
  • Staes et al. (2009) — intra- and inter-rater reliability of accessory motion testing at the carpal joints was acceptable, with end-feel agreement very good, supporting accessory-motion testing as a usable clinical joint-play assessment.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — principles chapter and regional chapters.
  2. Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function — arthrokinematics chapters.
  3. Maitland GD. Peripheral Manipulation — grades of movement.
  4. Evaluation of lumbar segmental motion using ultrasound imaging following common joint mobilization techniques. J Man Manip Ther. 2025;33(4):343-355.
  5. Gulick DT. Measurement of accessory motion of the glenohumeral and radiocarpal joints: intra-rater reliability of the Mobil-Aider device. 2020.
Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Explain screening the head and neck in upper cross syndrome.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2a — Screening regions: head, neck and back

★ Memory hook — Tight, Weak, Forward, Rounded — pair every tight muscle you name with its weak opponent.

1Introduction

Upper cross syndrome is Janda's classical muscle-imbalance pattern of the head, neck and shoulder girdle, and screening it means reading a crossed pattern of tightness and weakness from posture and a small set of endurance and length tests. This answer sets out that screen in the order it is performed: pattern, observation, tests, interpretation.

2Physiology

The head, neck and shoulder girdle work as a balanced system. The deep cervical flexors (longus colli and capitis) and the scapular stabilisers (lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior) hold the head and scapulae against gravity, while the upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals and pectorals provide movement and postural set. In balance the ear sits over the acromion and the cervico-thoracic angle is preserved.

3Pathophysiology

Upper cross syndrome is a crossed pattern of imbalance. The tight line runs through the upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals and pectoralis major and minor; the weak/inhibited line runs through the deep neck flexors, lower and middle trapezius, and serratus anterior. The postural result is a forward head, loss of the cervico-thoracic angle, rounded shoulders with protracted and elevated scapulae, and a chin that pokes forward. For the eyes to stay level the upper cervical spine extends and the lower cervical spine flexes, so the suboccipitals shorten while the deep flexors are held long and weak.

4Answer

Screening the head and neck in upper cross syndrome follows a fixed sequence:

StepWhat is donePositive finding
1. Observation / plumb lineStand the patient in profile; check that the ear sits over the acromionEar falls forward of the acromion; prominent C7; protracted, elevated, winged scapulae; pectoral prominence
2. PalpationUpper trapezius and levator scapulae for tone and tendernessHypertonicity and tenderness
3. Cervical AROM with overpressureClear the joints themselvesMovement-related pain or restriction
4. Craniocervical flexion testSupine; patient nods in five graded stages of 2 mmHg from a 20 mmHg biofeedback baselineSuperficial flexor (SCM) substitution; failure to hold the stage — the heart of the screen
5. Deep neck flexor endurance testChin tuck, head lifted 2–3 cm, held while quality is timedEndurance far below expected duration
6. Muscle length testsPectoralis minor length supine (acromion-to-couch distance), pectoralis major, suboccipital and upper-trapezius/levator length in side-lyingPectoralis minor more than the normal few centimetres from the couch; tight suboccipitals
7. Janda's shoulder abduction testPatient abducts the arms slowlyImmediate scapular hitching before 60° confirms upper-trapezius/levator dominance over weak lower stabilisers

Interpretation. No single test is the screen — the diagnosis rests on a cluster: chin juts and SCM visibly tightens during craniocervical flexion, endurance holds fall short, pectoralis minor is short, and the scapula hikes early in abduction.

The screen feeds directly into treatment: deep neck flexor retraining with the biofeedback cuff, lengthening of the pectorals and suboccipitals, lower trapezius and serratus strengthening, and ergonomic correction of the desk and mobile-phone posture. In the Indian clinic this presentation is everywhere — students with heavy shoulder bags, young IT professionals, and long hours of floor-level sitting with the neck flexed.

Conclusion

Screening the head and neck in upper cross syndrome is a postural and endurance assessment that pairs every tight muscle with its weak opponent — forward head, rounded shoulders, tight upper trapezius/levator/pectorals, weak deep flexors and lower scapular stabilisers — and converts that cluster into a targeted corrective programme.

The four words that score: tight, weak, forward, rounded. Pair every tight muscle you name with its weak opponent — examiners look for the pairing, not the shopping list.

5Recent advances

  • Seidi et al. (2020) — an 8-week comprehensive corrective exercise programme improved alignment, muscle activation and scapular movement in men with upper crossed syndrome, and the gains were maintained after four weeks of detraining.
  • Aneis et al. (2022) — a multimodal programme (muscle energy technique plus cervical and scapulothoracic stabilisation and postural correction with ergonomic advice) outperformed muscle energy technique alone for craniovertebral angle, sagittal shoulder angle, pain and disability.
  • Chaudhuri et al. (2023) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found physiotherapy significantly improves craniovertebral angle, kyphotic angle and rounded shoulder versus no treatment.
  • Yaghoubitajani et al. (2022) — a randomised trial in office workers with upper crossed syndrome found online-supervised corrective exercise improved neck-shoulder pain, postural angles, workability and upper-trapezius activity, supporting telerehabilitation for screening and correction.
  • Nitayarak & Charntaraviroj (2021) — a randomised controlled trial showed scapular stabilisation exercises improved posture and muscle imbalance in women with upper crossed syndrome.

6References

  1. Janda V. Evaluation of muscular imbalance, in Liebenson C. Rehabilitation of the Spine.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — cervical spine chapter.
  3. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — posture chapters.
  4. Bayattork M, Seidi F, Minoonejad H, Andersen LL, Page P. The effectiveness of a comprehensive corrective exercise program on alignment, muscle activation and movement pattern in men with upper crossed syndrome: RCT. Sci Rep. 2020.
  5. Physiotherapeutic interventions for upper cross syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis. 2023.

On the evaluation form — Q2: Upper cross syndrome / forward head posture

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: young to middle-aged adult, typically a desk/IT worker or student. Chief complaints: insidious-onset neck and suboccipital ache, often bilateral, present for months; frequently reported suboccipital headache, fatigue on reading, and sometimes tingling over the upper limb with sustained postures. Past medical/personal history: prolonged screen exposure, ergonomically poor workstation, stress. Symptom analysis: site — suboccipital region, cervical spine, interscapular area; onset — insidious; duration — months; type — dull ache with occasional "tight band" feeling; severity 4-6/10 on NPRS; aggravating factors — prolonged computer or smartphone use, sustained forward head postures, driving; relieving factors — posture change, rest, mild activity, heat. Pain evaluation: NPRS 4-6/10 with the mechanical, posture-related behaviour described above. Red-flag screen: trauma, night pain, fever and neurological deficit screened for. Vital signs: usually within normal limits.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Forward head posture with protracted chin; increased cervicothoracic angle; elevated and protracted scapulae with rounded shoulders (pectoralis tightness); increased thoracic kyphosis; visible upper trapezius hypertrophy; attitude of head held in slight flexion.

On palpation. Tenderness and trigger points in upper trapezius, levator scapulae, suboccipitals, sternocleidomastoid and pectoralis minor; increased deep tissue tension over the cervical extensors; reduced mobility (hypomobility) of the upper cervical segments on palpation.

1. Motor assessment

AROM/PROM of the cervical spine — reduced extension and rotation; flexion is full, giving a flexion-dominated movement pattern; end-feel typically of muscular tightness. MMT: deep neck flexors (longus colli/capitis) weak (3/5 or less on cranio-cervical flexion); lower and middle trapezius weak; scapular retractors inhibited. Resisted isometrics: cervical rotation/flexion painful at end range in the tight structures. Postural photograph with goniometry/inclinometry for the craniovertebral angle.

2. Sensory assessment

Dermatomes C4-T2 screened if radicular symptoms are reported; myotomes C5-T1 tested. In classic postural syndrome the screen is normal — abnormal findings suggest concurrent cervical radiculopathy and alter management.

3. Functional assessment (FIM)

Functional findings: ability to sustain sitting posture over 30 minutes (desk simulation), functional reach, and posture during gait; condition-relevant tests — timed reading/computer tolerance and sit-to-stand with head position noted. Outcome measures: Neck Disability Index (NDI, 0-50; higher scores indicate greater disability), NPRS (0-10), craniovertebral angle by photogrammetry, cervical ROM by goniometer/inclinometer.

4. Gait analysis

Posture during gait observed as part of the functional assessment; no gait deviation specific to this postural syndrome is expected.

5. Balance

Static and dynamic balance are not typically affected in this postural syndrome; balance is observed informally during gait and desk-task simulation.

6. Hand function

Reaching, grasping and releasing are not affected in this condition, though tingling over the upper limb may be reported with sustained postures; no assistive devices are required for hand tasks.

7. Coordination

Coordination is not impaired in upper cross syndrome; upper limb coordination is screened within the neurological examination, and abnormal coordination would suggest a different diagnosis.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests

Findings below describe the expected pattern for this condition; each test is recorded individually as positive or negative for the patient on testing — no result is assumed.

TestProcedurePositive signInference
Cranio-cervical flexion test (CCFT, Jull)Supine; inflatable pressure sensor under cervical spine inflated to 20 mmHg; patient performs gentle head-nod to five incremental levelsUnable to hold 10 s at lower pressure levels; substitution with superficial neck flexorsDeep neck flexor motor-control impairment
Deep neck flexor endurance testSupine chin-tuck with head lifted 2–3 cm off plinth, heldTremor, neck extension, or hold time below expectedWeakness/low endurance of deep neck flexors
Pectoralis minor length testSupine; distance from posterior shoulder to plinth, or pectoralis minor indexPosterior shoulder rests well off the tableAdaptive pectoralis minor shortening
Pectoralis major wall testStanding facing wall with shoulder abducted 90° and elbow flexed 90°, forearm to wallInability to keep forearm in contact with the wall without compensatory lumbar extensionAdaptive pectoral tightness
Cervical flexion-rotation testSupine, maximal cervical flexion, then passive rotationRotation restricted by >10° from the contralateral sideC1-C2 (suboccipital) joint dysfunction
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Forward head posture with deep neck flexor and scapular stabilizer weakness
  • Pectoral and suboccipital tightness
  • Upper cervical hypomobility
  • Trigger points

Functional limitations:

  • Inability to sustain upright sitting/reading tasks
  • Reduced tolerance for computer work
  • Headache

Disabilities:

  • Reduced work productivity
11. Functional diagnosis

Reduced tolerance for sustained sitting, reading and computer work due to forward head posture with deep neck flexor and scapular stabilizer weakness, pectoral and suboccipital tightness, upper cervical hypomobility and trigger points.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1-2 weeks): reduce pain from 5/10 to 2/10 on NPRS; achieve independent self-correction of head position in sitting; begin deep neck flexor training at a tolerated level.

Long-term goals (6-12 weeks): normal deep neck flexor endurance on CCFT; symmetrical scapular control during overhead and desk tasks; measurable improvement in craniovertebral angle; NDI reduction by at least 5 points; return to full-time desk work with ergonomic modifications.

13. Treatment plan
