Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe various outcome measures used for knee pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 6 — Functional assessment, outcome scales and ICF

★ Memory hook — WOMAC 24 (high = bad), KOOS 42 (high = good), Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — the score direction is the mark most candidates lose.

1Introduction

An outcome measure converts the patient's knee into a number that can be tracked across visits and reported to surgeons, insurers and researchers. Because knee pain spans impairment, activity and participation, a defensible evaluation combines a self-report scale with objective impairment measures.

A usable instrument needs reliability (same score on repeat testing), validity (measures what it claims), responsiveness (detects real change) and interpretability — the minimal clinically important difference (MCID), which for KOOS subscales is roughly 8–10 points. Each tool is mapped to the ICF: impairment-level measures such as VAS, activity-level measures such as WOMAC and KOOS, and participation-level measures such as the Tegner activity scale. That single sentence ties this answer to the Paper III Unit 6 framework.

2Physiology

Normal knee function is a modified-hinge movement of the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral joints, stabilised by the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments, the medial and lateral collaterals and the capsule, and driven by the quadriceps and hamstrings. Normal values are 0° of extension to about 135° of flexion, a pain-free, symmetric gait, and knee-extensor strength within about 10% of the opposite side.

Knee function spans the levels of the ICF — impairment (pain, stiffness, weakness, reduced range), activity limitation (walking, stairs, squatting, rising from a chair) and participation restriction (sport, work) — so a good outcome measure captures one or more of these levels and lets change be tracked objectively across visits.

3Pathophysiology

Different knee pathologies demand different instruments. Osteoarthritis and post-arthroplasty care are dominated by pain and function; ligament and sports injuries by instability, sport and quality of life; patellofemoral pain by anterior-knee and squatting symptoms; and inflammatory arthritis by systemic disease activity alongside joint function.

Mechanistically, OA is a whole-joint disease with cartilage loss, subchondral sclerosis, synovitis and arthrogenic muscle inhibition; ligament rupture produces laxity, giving-way and altered joint mechanics; and patellofemoral pain reflects maltracking and load intolerance. Because the clinical picture differs, the choice of scale follows the pathology — the selection logic that the answer must demonstrate.

4Answer

WOMAC — the osteoarthritis classic

The Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index: 24 items in three domains — pain (5 items), stiffness (2 items) and physical function (17 items) — scored 0-100 where higher means worse. Validated in knee osteoarthritis, available in translated Indian-language versions, responsive to change. Its limits: no sport or quality-of-life domain, ceiling effects in younger or higher-function patients, and poor performance in patellofemoral problems.

KOOS — the expanded successor

The Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score: 42 items across five subscales — symptoms, pain, activities of daily living, function in sport and recreation, and knee-related quality of life — each scored 0-100 where higher means better (note the reversal from WOMAC; examiners love this trap). It captures the young athletic patient where WOMAC ceilings out, making it the preferred measure after ACL reconstruction and for sports injuries.

Lysholm score and the Tegner activity scale

The Lysholm knee scoring scale, originally for ligament injuries and later broadened, is a knee-specific 8-item questionnaire — limp, support, locking, instability, pain, swelling, stair climbing, squatting — scored 0-100, higher is better. It is short, so it suits busy Indian OPDs, but it has a ceiling in high-functioning athletes. It pairs with the Tegner activity level scale, which grades current and pre-injury activity from 0 (sick leave, desk work) to 10 (competitive sports at national level): together they answer two different questions — how the knee feels and what the patient can do.

Fig 8 — Item counts on one bar chart with the scoring-direction note beneath; that note is the mark most candidates lose.

Kujala score — the patellofemoral tool

The Kujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale: 13 items covering limp, walking, stairs, squatting, running, jumping, prolonged sitting, pain and swelling, all weighted to patellofemoral complaints, scored 0-100 with higher being better. It is the instrument of choice for patellofemoral pain and patellar instability studies.

Generic anchors and the complete toolkit

The Visual Analogue Scale (0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable) or its numeric cousin is the universal impairment measure — quick, repeatable, but one-dimensional. The Knee Society Score (Insall, 1989) combines a knee score (pain, range, stability, alignment — clinician-rated) with a functional score (walking, stairs), originally built for total knee arthroplasty follow-up. Selection logic closes the answer: osteoarthritis or post-arthroplasty means WOMAC or KSS; sports injury or young active knee means KOOS with Lysholm-Tegner; patellofemoral pain means Kujala; and every patient gets a pain scale plus objective measures (goniometry, manual muscle testing, timed walk or stair tests) — because patient-reported and performance-based numbers together tell the whole story.

Examiner's tip: score direction and item counts are the discriminating marks: WOMAC 24, KOOS 42, Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — and opposite directions of "better".

Selection summary:

ConditionPreferred measure(s)
Knee osteoarthritis / post-arthroplastyWOMAC, Knee Society Score
Sports injury / young active knee (ACL, meniscus)KOOS with Lysholm + Tegner
Patellofemoral pain / instabilityKujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale
Every patientPain scale (VAS/NRS) + objective measures (goniometry, MMT, timed walk or stair test)

Patient-reported and performance-based numbers together tell the whole story; report baseline → discharge change against the MCID of the chosen scale.

Conclusion

Outcome measurement for knee pain should match the instrument to the pathology and the ICF level — WOMAC/KSS for arthritis and arthroplasty, KOOS with Lysholm–Tegner for sports injury, Kujala for patellofemoral pain, and a pain scale plus objective tests for everyone — so that change is measured, not assumed.

5Recent advances

  • Gandek et al. (2019) — This study developed and validated KOOS-12, a 12-item short form cutting respondent burden by 70% while preserving pain, function and quality-of-life domain scores and a summary knee-impact score.
  • Baré et al. (2021) — This multicentre study found KOOS-12 shows no ceiling effect, good construct validity and responsiveness after total knee arthroplasty, where the full-length KOOS and KOOS-JR did show ceiling effects.
  • Roos (2023) — This 30-year review of the KOOS documented the KOOS-12 and established minimal-important-difference and patient-acceptable symptom-state thresholds (KOOS-12 MID about 14–16 points at six months after knee arthroplasty).
  • Quintana et al. (2024) — This factor-analytic study found the original KOOS did not meet structural-validity criteria and proposed a refined 12-item structure as a more psychometrically sound instrument.
  • Lyman et al. (2019) — Culturally adapted versions (for example the JKOOS+) now add floor-based activities such as squatting and using a squat toilet, relevant to Asian populations.

6References

  1. Bellamy N et al. Validation study of WOMAC. J Rheumatol. 1988.
  2. Roos EM et al. KOOS — Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther / JBJS. 1998.
  3. Lysholm J, Gillquist J. Evaluation of knee ligament surgery results. Am J Sports Med. 1982.
  4. Tegner Y, Lysholm J. Rating systems in the evaluation of knee ligament injuries. Clin Orthop. 1985.
  5. Kujala UM et al. Scoring of patellofemoral disorders. Arthroscopy. 1993.
  6. Insall JN et al. Rationale of the Knee Society clinical rating system. Clin Orthop. 1989.
  7. Roos EM, Lohmander LS. 30 years with the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS). Osteoarthritis Cartilage. 2023.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe screening of the ankle following ankle subluxation.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 2 — Screening: lower quadrant (ankle and foot)

★ Memory hook — Inversion failure order: ATFL first, CFL second, PTFL last — drawer tests the ATFL, talar tilt the CFL, and never forget the pulses.

1Introduction

An ankle subluxation is a momentary partial dislocation of the talus in the mortise, usually during an inversion episode, that signals failure of the lateral ligament complex. Screening after such an episode asks which ligaments are torn, what else is injured, and whether the dynamic stabilisers can compensate.

2Physiology

The lateral ankle is stabilised by three ligaments — the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL) — supported by the peroneal muscles and the proprioceptive system. The ATFL is the weakest and is tested by the anterior drawer; the CFL crosses both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints and is tested by talar tilt.

3Pathophysiology

Anatomy and mechanism: what a subluxation tells you

An ankle subluxation — a momentary partial dislocation, almost always the talus shifting under the tibiofibular mortise during an inversion or eversion episode — means the restraining ligaments failed: the anterior talofibular ligament (weakest, fails first in inversion), the calcaneofibular ligament (next, crosses both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints), and the posterior talofibular ligament (last). Repeated subluxation equals chronic instability, so screening asks three questions: which ligaments are loose, what else is injured, and can the dynamic stabilisers compensate.

4Answer

History and observation

Mechanism (inversion-plantarflexion for lateral), previous episodes — the single strongest predictor of chronic instability — inability to bear weight, swelling and bruising pattern, and functional giving way on uneven ground or stairs. Observe swelling, ecchymosis over the lateral ligaments, hindfoot alignment, arch posture, and gait (antalgic, avoidant push-off). Palpate systematically: distal fibula, ATFL and CFL course, base of the fifth metatarsal (avulsion), anterior syndesmosis, deltoid, and the proximal fibula — a Maisonneuve pattern referred up the leg.

Anterior drawer test — the ATFL test

Patient sitting with leg hanging, ankle relaxed in about 10 to 20 degrees of plantarflexion; the examiner stabilises the tibia with one hand and grips the calcaneus with the other, drawing the hindfoot forward while the talus is distracted from the mortise. Excessive anterior translation with a soft end-feel compared with the other side indicates ATFL insufficiency. Best after five to seven days, once acute spasm has settled; a side-to-side difference of about 3 mm or more on stress imaging is the laboratory counterpart, and manual grading is subjective — hence always compare with the uninjured ankle.

Fig 9 — Lateral ligament map with the two stress-test arrows; knowing ATFL fails first and CFL second turns a drawing into marks.

Talar tilt (inversion stress) test

Stabilise the tibia and calcaneus together, then invert (adduct) the talus in the mortise — a comparison test for the CFL and subtalar restraint. Increased tilt with a soft end-feel against the other side indicates lateral ligament laxity; pure talar tilt also loads the subtalar joint, so attribute carefully. Both tests can be done with an arthrometer or stress ultrasound/radiographs for objectivity when surgery is contemplated.

Clearing the rest of the ring

After a subluxation the examiner must clear the neighbours: the squeeze test (compress the calf mid-shaft; pain distally at the syndesmosis is positive) and external rotation test (dorsiflex the ankle and externally rotate — syndesmotic pain) rule out a high sprain; deltoid palpation and eversion stress rule out the medial side; the Ottawa ankle rules guide radiography (malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness plus inability to bear four steps); the Thompson test clears the Achilles; and the neurovascular check (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulse, sensation) is mandatory after any subluxation episode.

Functional screening and conclusion

Test what the instability actually steals: single-leg balance with eyes open and closed, the Star Excursion Balance Test, hopping and figure-of-eight running, stair descent. Quantify with the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool or FAAM for outcome tracking. Conclude the screening by grading: mechanical laxity (positive stress tests) plus functional instability (positive balance and giving-way) with muscle weakness means a structured proprioceptive-peroneal rehabilitation programme; bony avulsion, syndesmotic injury or neurovascular deficit means immediate referral. That closing sentence is what a 10-mark answer is judged by.

Examiner's tip: "compare with the other ankle" after each stress test, and never forget the pulses — the viva question hiding at the end of this paper.

5Recent advances

  • Delahunt et al. (2019) — The International Ankle Consortium ROAST consensus defined a structured, equipment-free clinical assessment of acute lateral ankle sprain (mechanism, bony and ligamentous integrity, swelling, range, strength, balance, gait) to identify impairments that lead to chronic instability.
  • Vasconcelos et al. (2018) — This meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials found proprioceptive/balance training reduced the incidence of ankle sprains by 38% and improved dynamic neuromuscular control (Star Excursion Balance Test) in athletes.
  • Jiang et al. (2022) — This meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials found balance training significantly improves dynamic postural stability (Star Excursion Balance Test) in people with chronic ankle instability.
  • Mollà-Casanova et al. (2021) — This meta-analysis found balance training significantly improves function, instability and dynamic balance in chronic ankle instability, outperforming strength training for the functional outcome.
  • Tang et al. (2023) — This systematic review found elastic orthoses, kinesiotaping and textured insoles can improve postural stability in chronic ankle instability, although evidence for semi-rigid braces and arch-support insoles remains mixed.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  2. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
  3. Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott.
  4. Jiang C, Huang D, Li X, et al. Effects of balance training on dynamic postural stability in patients with chronic ankle instability: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2022;62(12):1707-1715.

On the evaluation form — Q9: Recurrent ankle instability / subluxation

I. Subjective examination

Demographics: 21-year-old female college basketball player. Chief complaints: repeated giving way of the right ankle on uneven ground with the joint slipping out and back; persistent lateral swelling; apprehension on landing and cutting; walks with slight antalgia on uneven ground. History: three right-sided inversion sprains in 14 months, the latest 3 weeks ago. No other past medical, personal, family or socioeconomic history is given. Symptom analysis: site — anterolateral aspect of the right ankle; onset — after the initial sprain 14 months ago, recurrent since; duration — current episode 3 weeks; type — sharp pain; severity — 3/10 on the NPRS; aggravating factors — uneven surfaces, jumping and flat unsupportive chappals; relieving factor — taping. Red-flag screen: no red-flag features documented. Vital signs: normal.

II. Objective examination

On observation. Mild anterolateral swelling with resolving ecchymosis; slight pes planus with dynamic valgus on single-leg stance; the patient watches her foot during stance (visual dependency of chronic instability).

On palpation. Tenderness over the anterior talofibular ligament, milder over the calcaneofibular ligament; the fifth metatarsal base, syndesmosis and medial structures are non-tender; no effusion or crepitus.

1. Motor assessment. AROM full, with pain at end-range inversion; dorsiflexion 5–10° less than on the left side. PROM: increased inversion laxity. MMT: peroneals 4/5 (the key finding in chronic instability); other muscles 5/5. Resisted isometrics painful for eversion. Ankle jerk intact; calf girth 1 cm less on the right.

2. Sensory assessment. Light touch and pinprick intact in the L4–S1 dermatomes, including the peroneal territories; ankle position sense commonly impaired after repeated sprains; eyes-closed single-leg stance reduced on the right — the proprioceptive deficit central to functional instability.

3. Functional assessment (FIM). Running, cutting, jumping and landing are limited; single-leg hop is limited by apprehension; the LEFS documents the overall activity limitation. Outcome measures: Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool — a condition-specific questionnaire for chronic ankle instability; Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) with ADL and sport subscales; NPRS (0–10); LEFS (0–80); Patient-Specific Functional Scale (0–10); single-leg stance time and Star Excursion Balance Test as performance measures.

4. Gait analysis. Slight antalgia on uneven ground; dynamic valgus on stair descent.

5. Balance. Eyes-open single-leg stance normal; eyes-closed single-leg stance clearly reduced; Star Excursion Balance Test reach reduced posteromedially and anteriorly.

6. Hand function. Not relevant to this presentation.

7. Coordination. Not separately tested; the proprioceptive and balance deficits above are the relevant coordination-related findings.

8. Investigations

X-rays and relevant blood investigations as per medical records; no imaging reviewed at this assessment.

9. Special tests
TestProcedurePositive signInference
Anterior drawer test (result not documented)Ankle relaxed in about 20° plantarflexion; stabilise the tibia, translate the talus anteriorlyExcessive anterior translation or soft end-feelAnterior talofibular ligament laxity
Talar tilt (inversion stress) test (positive — increased inversion laxity on PROM in this patient)Ankle neutral; stabilise the leg, invert the hindfootExcessive inversion laxity versus the sound sideCalcaneofibular ligament laxity / subluxation
Squeeze test (negative — syndesmosis non-tender)Compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calfPain over the syndesmosisSyndesmotic (high ankle) injury
External rotation (Kleiger) test (negative — no syndesmotic or medial joint pain)Stabilise the leg, externally rotate the foot with the knee at 90°Syndesmotic or medial joint painSyndesmosis injury, possible deltoid involvement
Thompson / Simmonds test (result not documented)Prone; squeeze the calfNo plantarflexionAchilles rupture (exclude in ankle trauma)
Cotton test (result not documented)Anteroposterior drawer with the ankle in neutralIncreased translation with a mushy end-feelGeneralised talar instability
Single-leg balance, eyes closed (positive — clearly reduced on the right)Timed unilateral stance, eyes closedReduced time or increased sway versus the leftProprioceptive deficit of functional instability
10. Problem list

Impairments:

  • Anterolateral ligament laxity with recurrent subluxation
  • Peroneal weakness
  • Impaired proprioception and balance
  • Dorsiflexion tightness

Functional limitations:

  • Running, cutting, jumping and landing

Disabilities:

  • Reduced basketball and college outdoor participation
11. Functional diagnosis

Decreased ability to perform running, cutting and single-leg stability tasks secondary to chronic ankle instability.

12. Goals

Short-term goals (1–2 weeks): pain reduced from 3/10 to 1/10; swelling controlled; peroneal isometric activation; eyes-closed single-leg balance progressing toward 30 seconds.

Long-term goals (6–12 weeks): peroneal strength 5/5; Star Excursion Balance Test within 5–10% of the left side; confident hop, side-hop and cutting; full return to basketball with preventive bracing.

13. Treatment plan

Stage 1 (weeks 1–2): relative rest; balance retraining from single-leg stance to eyes-closed and foam surfaces; peroneal isometrics; taping. Stage 2 (weeks 2–4): elastic-band peroneal strengthening, wobble-board balance, calf stretching, reactive peroneal drills, hopping in place. Stage 3 (weeks 4–8): plyometrics, agility ladder, cutting and landing mechanics, uneven-surface training, sport reintegration with a semi-rigid orthosis. Stage 4 (weeks 8–12): full return with a twice-weekly prevention programme and footwear advice (supportive shoes rather than loose sandals).

14. Home programme

Band eversion, single-leg balance progressions, heel raises off a step; surgery is considered only after failed 3–6-month rehabilitation.

Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Write in detail about clinical reasoning in manual therapy.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III Unit 4 — PT diagnosis, special tests and red flags; Unit 3 — decision making

★ Memory hook — Hypothesis → test → treat → re-assess: reasoning is a cycle, not a list, with the red-flag gate at the top.

1Introduction

What clinical reasoning is

Clinical reasoning is the thinking process that converts patient data into decisions — diagnosis, prognosis and intervention. Modern understanding is dual-process: System 1 is fast, automatic pattern recognition born of experience; System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytic hypothesis testing. The novice must live in System 2 deliberately; the expert runs System 1 and audits it with System 2 when the pattern does not fit. In manual therapy, reasoning decides not only which technique, but whether manual therapy belongs in the plan at all.

2Physiology

Hypothesis-oriented examination

The Jones model structures the examination around hypotheses generated from the very first history sentence. From the referral, demographics and opening complaint the clinician frames candidate hypotheses across categories: the pain source (pathology, tissue), movement impairment, contributing factors (biomechanical, psychosocial), precautions and contraindications, prognosis, and management. Each question and each test then deliberately seeks information that confirms or rejects a hypothesis, and the therapist reweights with every finding. In manual therapy this shows as: does the movement reproduce the pain (a concordant sign), does repeated movement centralise or abolish it, which direction of mobilisation changes it immediately. Hypothesis orientation is what separates an examination from a checklist.

3Pathophysiology

Red flags and the reasoning to refer

Before any mobilisation, reasoning screens for red flags: unexplained weight loss and night pain, fever, history of malignancy, sphincter disturbance or saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, trauma in the osteoporotic, anticoagulated or pregnant patient, upper cervical ligament laxity (RA), and vascular claudication. Manual therapy is contraindicated or requires modification in osteoporosis, acute fracture, inflammatory flare, hypermobility and vertebrobasilar insufficiency for cervical techniques. The clinician's reasoning must distinguish nociceptive mechanical pain from systemic or visceral mimicry — in the Indian clinic, spinal tuberculosis and malignancy present late, so vigilance is high.

4Answer

Schools of thought and their reasoning fingerprints

The Maitland concept (Australian) is hypothesis-driven, movement-based, with Maitland's famous dictum that the therapist needs a hypothesis only until the next piece of data arrives; grades I-IV of oscillation are chosen by irritability and stiffness versus pain. The McKenzie method (mechanical diagnosis and therapy) classifies by directional preference — derangement responds to repeated movements in one plane, dysfunction to end-range loading, postural syndrome to education. The Kaltenborn-Evjenth/OMPT tradition reasons by arthrokinematics and grades of translation to restore roll-glide. Paris's reasoning emphasises segmental dysfunction and soft-tissue signs. The modern synthesis (Jones and Rivett) makes reasoning itself explicit: narrative, diagnostic, procedural, interactive, collaborative and predictive reasoning streams run in parallel during one consultation.

Fig 10 — The reasoning cycle with the red-flag gate at the top; the loop from re-assessment back to cues is the sentence that earns full marks.

Re-assessment: the manual therapist's stethoscope

Immediate re-assessment after a treatment trial is the core manual-therapy reasoning skill: the pre-post comparison of the concordant sign — pain on movement, range, or the patient's functional task. Improvement validates the hypothesis and the technique; no change rejects it and redirects the reasoning. Sustained reassessment over visits separates real progress from short-term analgesic effects, and treatment-based classification systems (for example, the Pittsburgh low-back classification) formalise this logic into subgroups: mobilisation responders, specific-exercise responders, centralisation, control-dysfunction groups.

Expert versus novice, and the honest conclusion

Experts reason by organised patterns, tolerate uncertainty, self-monitor for bias, and change course early; novices gather indiscriminately and anchor on first impressions. Clinical reasoning in manual therapy, concluded properly, is not the decoration of technique selection — it is the safety system that decides who should be mobilised, who should be exercised, and who should be sent to a surgeon today.

Examiner's tip: name Jones, Maitland, McKenzie and Kaltenborn in one paragraph with one reasoning idea each, then close with "immediate re-assessment validates every hypothesis". That paragraph alone is a third of the marks.

5Recent advances

  • Blanpied et al. (2017) — This APTA clinical practice guideline (Neck Pain: Revision 2017) recommends manual therapy (thoracic and cervical manipulation/mobilisation) combined with targeted exercise for neck pain, with the technique chosen according to the patient's impairment classification.
  • Beyer et al. (2022) — This summary review placed the overall evidence for manual medicine/manual therapy at EBM level III, with manipulation and mobilisation more effective than no treatment, placebo or usual care for neck and low back pain.
  • Short et al. (2023) — This clinical commentary argued that the value of manual therapy lies in reasoned, individualised symptom modification alongside exercise, rather than as a standalone passive treatment.
  • Veenstra et al. (2024) — This cross-sectional study using the Diagnostic Thinking Inventory found hypothetical-deductive reasoning skills develop with professional experience and education, supporting structured reasoning training.

6References

  1. Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
  2. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  3. Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
  4. A clinically-reasoned approach to manual therapy in sports physical therapy. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2023.
  5. Evidence (-based medicine) in manual medicine/manual therapy: a summary review. Manuelle Medizin. 2022.
Last-Hour Sheet · Paper III

QP 8131 · 03-Jun-2024 · the 60-minute sheet — one line per idea, the night before the exam. Cover a column and test yourself.

1Elbow special tests

  • Cozen's = resisted wrist extension, pain at lateral epicondyle
  • Mill's = passive stretch (elbow ext, forearm pronated, wrist flexed)
  • Reverse both for golfer's elbow (medial)
  • Valgus at ~25 deg = MCL; varus = LUCL
  • Tinel cubital tunnel = ulnar; Maudsley = radial tunnel trap

2Decision-making steps

  • Examine, evaluate, diagnose, prioritise, prognose (SMART), intervene, re-examine, modify
  • Novice = analytic; expert = pattern recognition + audit
  • Bias list: anchoring, confirmation, availability

3Both-bone forearm fracture

  • ORIF plate = motion-first rehab
  • Phase 1 (0-2 wk): protect, elevate, finger/shoulder AROM, watch 6 Ps
  • Phase 2 (2-6 wk): elbow, wrist, pro-sup, scar mob
  • Phase 3 (6-12 wk): resistance; 3-6 months: work/sport
  • Enemies: stiffness, radioulnar synostosis, compartment syndrome, re-fracture after plate removal

4SCI investigations

  • ASIA: 10 key muscles 0-5, 28 dermatomes x 2 modalities 0-2, plus DAP and VAC
  • AIS A = no sacral sparing; C = less than half key muscles 3 or more; D = half or more
  • 2019 revision: ZPP now allowed in incomplete injuries; star tag for non-SCI deficits
  • MRI = cord (haemorrhage = poor prognosis); CT = bone and canal
  • Myelography when MRI contraindicated or unavailable
  • SSEP tests dorsal columns, gives prognosis; urodynamics protects the kidneys

5PCL screening

  • Posterior drawer at 90 deg = gold standard (about 90 percent sensitive, 99 percent specific)
  • Grade I anterior (0-5 mm), Grade II flush (5-10 mm), Grade III behind (over 10 mm + suspect PLC)
  • Sag sign: tibia drops by gravity; quadriceps active: tibia shifts forward on quad contraction
  • Dashboard mechanism; sag makes ACL drawer falsely positive — reduce first

6Symes amputation

  • Ankle disarticulation, malleoli removed, heel pad over tibia end
  • Advantages: end bearing, long lever, self-suspending, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing
  • Socket: posterior door or expandable wall; thin SACH foot
  • Assess: pad migration, bulbous diameter, knee ROM, quads strength

7Demographics and history

  • Every variable must rule something in or out (age, sex, occupation, dominance, locality)
  • Inflammatory pain: rest + second half of night + morning stiffness over 1 hour
  • Red flags: weight loss, night pain, fever, sphincter loss, saddle anaesthesia, progressive deficit
  • India context: spinal TB with evening fever and weight loss

8Knee outcome measures

  • WOMAC 24 items (5 pain, 2 stiffness, 17 function); high = worse
  • KOOS 42 items, 5 subscales; high = better
  • Lysholm 8 items x 100; Tegner 0-10 activity level; Kujala 13 items patellofemoral
  • KSS = knee score + function score (arthroplasty); VAS 0-10 for all

9Ankle after subluxation

  • Inversion order of failure: ATFL first, CFL second, PTFL last
  • Anterior drawer in 10-20 deg plantarflexion tests ATFL; talar tilt tests CFL
  • Squeeze + external rotation = syndesmosis; Ottawa rules for X-ray
  • Pulses and sensation after every subluxation episode

10Clinical reasoning in manual therapy

  • Hypothesis categories: pain source, movement impairment, contributing factors, precautions, prognosis, management
  • Schools: Maitland (movement, grades), McKenzie (directional preference), Kaltenborn (arthrokinematics), Paris (segmental)
  • Immediate re-assessment of the concordant sign = validate or reject the hypothesis
  • Red flag gate before any mobilisation
keep-if-nothing-else: the minimum cargo for the exam hall.

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Explain the basic assessment method used for the musculoskeletal system diagnosis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit I — Fundamentals of musculoskeletal assessment

★ Memory hook — History tells you where to look, the physical exam tells you what is wrong, and outcome measures tell you how much it matters.

1Introduction

Musculoskeletal (MSK) assessment is the systematic process by which a clinician collects data, forms and tests hypotheses, and arrives at a working diagnosis for a disorder of muscle, bone, joint, tendon, ligament or peripheral nerve. It is not a random collection of tests; it is a structured clinical-reasoning sequence that moves from the patient's story to a targeted physical examination and finally to a diagnosis and problem list.

The modern physiotherapy assessment is built on the World Health Organization's biopsychosocial model and the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), so findings are recorded not only as tissue pathology but also as activity limitation and participation restriction. Its purpose is to localise the structure at fault, to grade the impairment, to screen for serious pathology and to set a measurable baseline.

2Physiology

Normal MSK function depends on the integrated behaviour of four tissues: bone (load-bearing scaffold), cartilage (low-friction articulating surface), muscle–tendon (force generation and shock absorption) and ligament–capsule (passive restraint and proprioceptive feedback). Movement is produced by muscle contraction acting across joints and controlled by neural feedback from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint mechanoreceptors.

The clinician's examination is designed to stress each of these tissues in a controlled way — passive movement loads capsule and ligament, resisted movement loads muscle and tendon, and neural tension loads the nerve — so as to reproduce the patient's symptom and localise the structure at fault. Normal reference values (full, pain-free range; symmetric strength within about 10%; normal reflexes and sensation) provide the yardstick against which abnormality is judged.

3Pathophysiology

When a tissue is overloaded or injured, the pathological process dictates the clinical picture. Acute injury produces inflammation, swelling, pain and protective muscle spasm; chronic overload produces tendon degeneration, cartilage loss or a stress reaction in bone. Pain may be nociceptive (from tissue damage), neuropathic (from nerve compression such as radiculopathy) or centrally sensitised (amplified by psychological and social factors).

Because different pathologies produce overlapping findings, the assessment must distinguish, for example, referred pain from a hip or cervical spine source from a local knee or shoulder lesion. In Indian practice the differential must also keep tuberculosis, osteoporotic fragility fracture and diabetic neuropathy in view.

4Answer

The basic method follows a fixed, reproducible sequence:

  1. Subjective examination (history): demographics, chief complaint, mechanism of injury, onset, site, nature and behaviour of symptoms (aggravating/easing factors, 24-hour pattern), past history, medication, and functional and social history. Screen specifically for red flags (unexplained weight loss, night pain, fever, neurological deficit, cancer history, trauma) and yellow flags (fear-avoidance, catastrophising).
  2. Observation and inspection: posture, alignment, deformity, swelling, wasting, skin changes and gait.
  3. Objective examination: active and passive range of motion (goniometry), muscle strength and length (MMT, dynamometry), joint play and accessory movement, palpation, neurological screen (dermatomes, myotomes, reflexes, neural tension tests) and, where indicated, the relevant special tests.
  4. Functional and outcome measures: region-specific questionnaires (DASH, KOOS, PRTEE, ODI) and performance tests (gait, sit-to-stand, 6-minute walk).
  5. Analysis: cluster findings, form a working diagnosis and a differential list, and link each problem to the ICF domains.
  6. Documentation and re-assessment: record baseline data so progress can be measured objectively.
ComponentPurposeExample tools
SubjectiveLocalise and characteriseBody chart, red-flag screen
ObservationDetect visible abnormalityPostural/gait analysis
ROM & strengthQuantify impairmentGoniometer, dynamometer
Special testsConfirm tissue at faultLachman, Hawkins–Kennedy
Outcome measuresMeasure impact and changeKOOS, DASH, NPRS

Findings are interpreted as a pattern rather than in isolation, because no single test is perfectly sensitive or specific.

Conclusion

The basic MSK assessment method is a fixed sequence — history and red-flag screen, observation, objective tests, functional measures, analysis and documentation — whose value lies in structured reasoning and ICF-based interpretation, not in the number of tests performed.

5Recent advances

  • Cella et al. (2010) — the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) item banks allow rapid, computer-adaptive measurement of pain and function with less respondent burden than fixed questionnaires.
  • Hill et al. (2016) — the Arthritis Research UK Musculoskeletal Health Questionnaire (MSK-HQ) was developed and validated with community physiotherapy patients as a single, cross-condition outcome measure usable across the whole musculoskeletal pathway.
  • Jones et al. (2014) — validated a smartphone goniometry app against the universal goniometer, giving low-cost, reliable range-of-motion measurement for clinic and telerehabilitation use.
  • Hill et al. (2008) — developed the Keele STarT Back screening tool (later extended to STarT MSK), so that prognostic screening at first contact can match patients to the right intensity of care.
  • Maarseveen et al. (2025) — built a machine-learning pipeline that prioritised musculoskeletal referrals better than manual triage, showing such decision-support models are adjuncts to, not replacements for, clinical reasoning.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Discuss about the role of screening the shoulder joint in overhead injury.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit III — Screening of the shoulder complex

★ Memory hook — In the overhead athlete, screen the scapula, the rotator cuff and the range of rotation — the three Rs.

1Introduction

Overhead sports — throwing, swimming, tennis, volleyball and handball — place the shoulder under repetitive, high-velocity loads that make it the most commonly injured joint in these athletes. Screening is the structured, pre-season or periodic evaluation of the shoulder to identify modifiable deficits (range of motion, strength, scapular control and load tolerance) that predispose to injury, and to guide prevention and rehabilitation.

Its purpose is not simply to predict who will get hurt, but to find and correct impairments before they become an injury. Screening is therefore part of primary prevention and a bridge to a targeted prehabilitation programme.

2Physiology

The glenohumeral joint is inherently unstable, relying on a fine balance between static restraints (glenoid labrum, capsule, glenohumeral ligaments) and dynamic restraints (rotator cuff, deltoid and scapular stabilisers). The overhead motion occurs in phases — wind-up, cocking, acceleration, deceleration and follow-through — during which the arm is taken into extreme external rotation and abduction, generating very high forces across the anterior capsule and the posterior cuff.

Normal screening values are anchored to this physiology: scapulohumeral rhythm of roughly 2:1 (glenohumeral to scapulothoracic), an external-to-internal rotation strength ratio of about 0.66–0.75, and near-symmetric total rotational range. Deviation from these norms is what screening detects.

3Pathophysiology

Repeated overhead loading produces adaptive and maladaptive changes: glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD), total rotational range deficit, scapular dyskinesis, and eccentric rotator-cuff weakness (especially the external rotators). These lead to pathology such as rotator-cuff tendinopathy and partial tears, subacromial impingement, internal impingement, labral (SLAP) injury and instability.

In throwers, loss of at least 5° of external rotation in the dominant arm relative to the non-dominant arm has been associated with roughly double the risk of in-season shoulder and elbow injury — the empirical basis for screening these deficits.

4Answer

A shoulder screening battery for the overhead athlete should include:

  • History and load: sport, position, throwing volume, pain phase, previous injury, training load and spikes.
  • Observation and posture: forward head, rounded shoulders, scapular position and winging.
  • Range of motion: external rotation, internal rotation, total rotational motion, horizontal adduction and GIRD, using goniometry or inclinometry.
  • Strength: isometric external and internal rotation (handheld dynamometry), the ER/IR ratio, and scapular muscle strength (serratus anterior, lower trapezius).
  • Scapular control: lateral scapular slide test and dynamic scapular-dyskinesis observation.
  • Special tests: Neer and Hawkins–Kennedy (impingement), empty can and drop arm (supraspinatus), external-rotation lag and belly-press (subscapularis), apprehension/relocation and anterior release (instability), and O'Brien (SLAP).
  • Functional screen: Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test (CKCUEST) and sport-specific throwing mechanics.
DomainTestPositive finding
ImpingementHawkins–KennedyPain with internal rotation in 90° flexion
Cuff (external)External rotation lagInability to hold externally rotated position
Cuff (subscapularis)Belly-pressElbow drops or wrist flexes
InstabilityApprehensionApprehension reproduced, relieved by relocation
ScapulaLateral scapular slideSide-to-side difference > 1.5 cm

Findings are interpreted together and linked to a prevention programme that targets mobility, eccentric external-rotation strength, scapular control and the kinetic chain.

Conclusion

Screening the shoulder in the overhead athlete means systematically measuring the modifiable deficits — GIRD and rotational range, ER/IR strength ratio, scapular control and load tolerance — so that injury risk is reduced by correcting impairments before they become pathology.

5Recent advances

  • Schwank et al. (2022) — the 2022 Bern Consensus Statement gives best-practice, principle-based guidance on shoulder injury prevention, rehabilitation and return to sport, and cautions that no single screening test reliably predicts injury.
  • Asker et al. (2022) — this three-armed cluster randomised trial showed the Shoulder Control warm-up programme cut shoulder injury rates by 56% in elite adolescent handball players, confirming that structured preventive exercise works.
  • Pozzi et al. (2020) — this systematic review and meta-analysis found that pre-season external-rotation range-of-motion screening can identify professional baseball pitchers and swimmers at risk, but is less useful in handball, volleyball, softball and tennis players.
  • Andersson et al. (2017) — a cluster-randomised trial in elite handball showed that a short warm-up prevention programme reduced shoulder and elbow injury rates.
  • Moiroux-Sahraoui et al. (2024) — this systematic review emphasised kinetic-chain and trunk-control assessment, moving the focus beyond the shoulder alone.

Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Explain the screening techniques of forearm region in diagnosis of tennis elbow.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit III — Screening of the elbow and forearm

★ Memory hook — Tennis elbow is a load problem at the common extensor origin — test the tendon, then screen the neck and radial nerve.

1Introduction

Tennis elbow, or lateral elbow tendinopathy (lateral epicondylalgia), is the most common cause of lateral elbow pain in adults. It is a degenerative, load-related tendinopathy of the common extensor origin, chiefly the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB). Screening the forearm region means systematically reproducing the patient's pain, localising it to the extensor tendon, grading its severity, and excluding other sources such as the cervical spine, the radial nerve and the elbow joint itself.

It is a clinical diagnosis: screening is designed to reproduce the tendon's pain on load and to exclude the mimics, so that treatment targets the right tissue.

2Physiology

The common extensor tendon arises from the lateral epicondyle and includes ECRB, extensor digitorum communis, extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor digiti minimi. These muscles extend and stabilise the wrist during gripping and lifting. The radial nerve and its posterior interosseous branch pass close to the lateral elbow, and the extensor–supinator muscle mass is the prime mover for wrist extension and forearm supination.

Grip strength depends heavily on the wrist extensors, which is why pain-free grip is such a useful clinical measure: the ECRB contracts strongly to stabilise the wrist whenever the hand grips, so gripping reproduces the tendon's pain and its strength reflects function.

3Pathophysiology

Histologically, lateral elbow tendinopathy shows angiofibroblastic degeneration — disorganised collagen, increased ground substance and neovessels — rather than true acute inflammation, which is why the term tendinopathy is preferred to tendinitis. Pain is provoked by resisted wrist and middle-finger extension and by gripping.

In a proportion of cases, radial-nerve mechanosensitivity and cervical or thoracic spine dysfunction contribute, so a purely local view can be misleading. The lesion is an overload-driven failure of tendon healing, not a single inflammatory event.

4Answer

Screening sequence for the forearm and lateral elbow:

  • History: gradual onset of lateral elbow pain, pain on gripping, lifting or using tools; occupational and sporting load; dominant arm.
  • Palpation: tenderness over the common extensor origin, just anterior to the lateral epicondyle.
  • Resisted tests: resisted wrist extension (Cozen's test) — pain at the lateral epicondyle; resisted middle-finger extension (Maudsley's test) — pain from ECRB.
  • Mill's test: passive wrist flexion with pronation and elbow extension stretches the extensor origin and provokes pain.
  • Chair-lift test: lifting a chair with the forearm pronated reproduces pain.
  • Grip strength: pain-free grip strength measured with a dynamometer is reduced and is a sensitive outcome measure.
  • Neural screen: upper limb neurodynamic test for the radial nerve (ULNT 2b) to detect mechanosensitivity.
  • Adjacent-joint screen: cervical spine, thoracic spine, shoulder and wrist to exclude referred pain.
  • Outcome measure: Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation (PRTEE).
TestMethodPositive sign
Cozen'sResisted wrist extensionPain at lateral epicondyle
Maudsley'sResisted middle-finger extensionPain at ECRB origin
Mill'sPassive wrist flexion, pronation, elbow extensionPain over extensor origin
Pain-free gripDynamometer, symptomatic armReduced vs. unaffected side
Conclusion

Screening the forearm in tennis elbow reproduces pain in the common extensor origin with resisted extension, Mill's, chair-lift and grip tests, quantifies it with pain-free grip and the PRTEE, and excludes the cervical spine and radial nerve — confirming the tendon as the source before treatment.

5Recent advances

  • Lucado et al. (2022) — the JOSPT clinical practice guideline on lateral elbow pain and muscle function impairments provides current, evidence-based guidance on tests and measures for lateral elbow tendinopathy.
  • Bisset et al. (2006) — this landmark randomised trial showed that elbow mobilisation with movement plus exercise beat corticosteroid injection in the long term (52 weeks), with far fewer recurrences.
  • Coombes et al. (2013) — this JAMA factorial randomised trial found corticosteroid injection produced worse 1-year outcomes and higher recurrence than placebo, reinforcing exercise-based physiotherapy over injection.
  • Karanasios et al. (2021) — this systematic review and meta-analysis found that exercise produces better outcomes than passive interventions, though the effect size is small.
  • Clifford et al. (2020) — this meta-analysis of isometric exercise in tendinopathy supported isometric and eccentric loading programmes as central to management, whether supervised or self-performed.

Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Explain the importance of primary care in physiotherapy for degenerative conditions.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit IV — Primary care and degenerative musculoskeletal conditions

★ Memory hook — In degenerative disease, primary care physiotherapy is not about cure — it is about education, load and keeping people moving.

1Introduction

Degenerative musculoskeletal conditions — chiefly osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee, hip, hand and spine — are the leading cause of chronic pain and disability in older adults. Because they are chronic, non-curable and strongly influenced by lifestyle, they are ideally managed in primary care, where physiotherapists provide first-contact assessment, education, exercise prescription and self-management support.

Primary care physiotherapy reduces the burden on specialist services and gives patients early, conservative, evidence-based care — the care that actually alters the long-term trajectory of these conditions.

2Physiology

Healthy synovial joints maintain themselves through intermittent loading: movement circulates synovial fluid, nourishes avascular cartilage and maintains muscle strength and proprioception. Subchondral bone remodels continuously in response to load, and strong quadriceps and gluteal muscles reduce joint reaction forces and improve shock absorption.

Physical activity is therefore protective for a joint, provided it is appropriate in type and dose. This physiology is the scientific basis of the reassurance that "movement is medicine" for the arthritic joint.

3Pathophysiology

OA involves focal loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone sclerosis, osteophyte formation and low-grade synovitis. It is now understood as a whole-joint disease, with muscle weakness, arthrogenic muscle inhibition, altered gait and central sensitisation contributing to pain.

Patients typically become less active, which worsens weakness, stiffness and cardiovascular risk — a downward spiral that primary care physiotherapy aims to reverse. Inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis) adds systemic inflammation and joint destruction, requiring close medical co-management.

4Answer

The importance of primary care physiotherapy in degenerative conditions lies in:

  • Early access and triage: first-contact assessment to distinguish OA from inflammatory, red-flag or referred conditions and to refer appropriately.
  • Education and self-management: explaining that pain does not equal damage and that exercise is safe, using tools such as the OARSI implementation recommendations.
  • Exercise prescription: individualised, progressive, multicomponent programmes (strength, aerobic, flexibility, neuromotor) at adequate dose, tailored to function and preference.
  • Weight and lifestyle management: supporting healthy weight, physical activity and behaviour change.
  • Pain management: manual therapy, heat and coping strategies as adjuncts, not stand-alone treatments.
  • Function and participation: aids, footwear, work advice and falls prevention.
  • Continuity and monitoring: regular review using outcome measures to keep patients engaged long-term.
  • Red-flag screening and referral: for joint replacement, rheumatology or imaging when indicated.
DomainPrimary care physiotherapy action
AssessmentFirst-contact diagnosis, red-flag screen
EducationReassurance, self-management plan
ExerciseProgressive, multicomponent, tailored
LifestyleWeight, activity, behaviour change
MonitoringOutcome measures, long-term adherence

In Indian practice, where specialist access is uneven and out-of-pocket costs are high, this first-contact, education-led model is especially valuable.

Conclusion

In degenerative conditions primary care physiotherapy matters because it delivers early, non-surgical, education- and exercise-based care that reduces pain, maintains function and slows the spiral of inactivity — reducing dependence on specialists and drugs.

5Recent advances

  • Moseng et al. (2023) — the 2023 EULAR recommendations for the non-pharmacological core management of hip and knee OA place individualised, multicomponent management, education and exercise with tailored dosage at the centre of care.
  • Bannuru et al. (2019) and Holden et al. (2022) — the 2019 OARSI guidelines and the 2022 OARSI Rehabilitation Discussion Group consensus provide practical, evidence-informed guidance for delivering therapeutic exercise in OA.
  • Abuhl et al. (2025) — this systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials found first-contact physiotherapy in primary care reduced imaging and prescription-medication rates with clinical outcomes equal or superior to usual GP-led care.
  • Nelligan et al. (2021) — a randomised trial showed that behaviour-change text messages and web-based delivery improve long-term exercise adherence in knee OA, supporting digital and telerehabilitation approaches.
  • Niemeijer et al. (2020) — this meta-analysis of 180 Cochrane reviews found exercise therapy did not increase serious adverse events, confirming it is a safe, low-cost core treatment for degenerative joint disease.

6References

Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Explain the special tests of knee complex used in musculoskeletal system.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit III — Screening of the knee complex

★ Memory hook — Lachman for the ACL, McMurray for the meniscus, valgus and varus for the collaterals — name the test, position, force and positive sign.

1Introduction

Special tests of the knee are the standardised manual procedures used to confirm which structure is injured or dysfunctional after the history and general examination have narrowed the field. They form part of the objective assessment of the knee complex — ligaments, menisci, patellofemoral joint and capsule.

Each test applies a specific force in a specific position to a specific structure, and its result is interpreted together with other findings rather than in isolation, because no single test is perfectly accurate.

2Physiology

The knee is a modified hinge joint stabilised by four main ligaments: the anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments (ACL, PCL) controlling antero-posterior translation and rotation, and the medial and lateral collateral ligaments (MCL, LCL) controlling varus and valgus stress. The medial and lateral menisci distribute load, improve congruence and aid rotational stability.

The patellofemoral joint depends on balanced quadriceps and VMO activity and on the Q-angle for normal tracking. The screw-home mechanism and normal proprioception complete the functional picture, and each of these structures has a corresponding test that loads it selectively.

3Pathophysiology

Injury patterns include ligament sprains (ACL rupture from a non-contact pivot, PCL from a dashboard injury, collateral sprains from valgus/varus stress), meniscal tears from twisting under load, and patellofemoral pain or instability from maltracking or overload. Combined injuries and associated instability are common.

The special tests are designed to reproduce the specific mechanical fault — abnormal translation, rotation or pain — and to associate it with the structure responsible, so that the examination points to the correct diagnosis.

4Answer

Knee special tests — position, force and positive sign:

TestPosition & forcePositive sign
LachmanSupine, knee 20–30° flexion; anterior tibial translationSoft/lax endpoint, increased translation
Anterior drawerSupine, knee 90° flexion; anterior pullExcess anterior glide of tibia
Pivot shiftExtension, valgus and internal rotation then flexionVisible clunk/reduction of subluxation
Lever signFist under calf; downward force on femurHeel does not rise (positive)
Posterior drawer / sag signKnee 90°; posterior push / observationExcess posterior translation, sagging tibia
Valgus stressKnee 20–30° flexion; medial forceMedial laxity/pain (MCL)
Varus stressKnee 20–30° flexion; lateral forceLateral laxity/pain (LCL)
McMurraySupine, full flexion; rotation and extensionClick/pain over joint line
ThessalyStanding, 20° flexion, rotate bodyJoint-line pain/discomfort
ApleyProne, knee 90°; compression and rotationPain or clicking (meniscus)
Patellar apprehensionSupine, quadriceps relaxed; lateral glideApprehension/fear of dislocation
Clarke'sSupine; quadriceps contraction with patellar pressurePain at patella

Meniscal and ligament tests should be clustered, because no single test is perfectly accurate. The diagnostic accuracy of the ACL tests is comparable, and the pivot shift is the most specific for ruling in a tear.

Conclusion

The special tests of the knee complex are structure-specific provocation and laxity manoeuvres — Lachman and pivot shift for the ACL, posterior drawer and sag sign for the PCL, valgus/varus stress for the collaterals, McMurray/Thessaly/Apley for the menisci and apprehension/Clarke's for the patellofemoral joint — interpreted as a cluster, not singly.

5Recent advances

  • Sokal et al. (2022) — this bivariate meta-analysis found the Lachman test's accuracy had been previously overestimated and that the pivot shift and lever sign are best for ruling in and ruling out ACL tears respectively.
  • Hu et al. (2024) — this diagnostic meta-analysis of the lever sign reported pooled sensitivity of about 0.81 and specificity of about 0.78, supporting it as an adjunct rather than a stand-alone test.
  • Smith et al. (2015) — this systematic review and meta-analysis found McMurray's, joint-line tenderness and the Thessaly test have only modest accuracy for meniscal tears, cautioning against relying on any single special test.
  • Vaidya et al. (2020) — showed that a smartphone accelerometer can quantify the pivot shift reliably, part of a move to objective laxity devices that reduce examiner variability.
  • Karachalios et al. (2005) — introduced and validated the Thessaly test, a weight-bearing meniscal test with good diagnostic performance.

6References

Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Exercise testing and prescription in arthritis patient.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit V — Exercise testing and prescription in arthritis

★ Memory hook — Test safely, prescribe FITT-VP, and remember low-impact, land or water — movement is medicine for the arthritic joint.

1Introduction

Exercise is the cornerstone of non-pharmacological management of arthritis, both osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Exercise testing establishes the patient's baseline capacity and safety, and exercise prescription translates that into a specific, individualised programme.

In arthritis the goal is to improve pain, function and quality of life while protecting the joint, so both testing and prescription must be adapted to the disease, its activity and the patient's comorbidities.

2Physiology

Regular exercise improves aerobic capacity, muscle strength, joint stability and proprioception, and helps control weight and cardiovascular risk — all of which reduce load on arthritic joints. Cartilage nutrition depends on intermittent loading, so appropriate movement is beneficial rather than harmful.

In RA, exercise must be balanced against systemic inflammation and fatigue, but the muscle weakness and deconditioning of inflammatory arthritis respond well to supervised, moderate-intensity training. The physiological target is to build strength and aerobic capacity without provoking a disease flare.

3Pathophysiology

In OA, cartilage loss, synovitis and muscle weakness produce pain and reduced function; arthrogenic muscle inhibition further weakens the quadriceps. In RA, chronic synovitis erodes cartilage and bone, and systemic inflammation causes muscle wasting (rheumatoid cachexia) and fatigue.

Both conditions are associated with sedentary behaviour and increased cardiovascular risk, so exercise testing must also screen for cardiac limitation. This pathophysiology dictates that testing be graded and that prescription be modified during flares.

4Answer

Exercise testing. Begin with pre-participation screening (ACSM algorithm / PAR-Q+): current activity level, signs or symptoms, known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and desired intensity. Then measure:

  • Aerobic capacity — 6-minute walk test, submaximal cycle or treadmill test, or a symptom-limited test where indicated.
  • Muscular strength — handheld dynamometry, grip strength, 1-RM or estimated 1-RM.
  • Range of motion — goniometry of the affected joints.
  • Function and pain — WOMAC or KOOS for OA, HAQ or DAS-28 for RA, and a numerical pain rating scale.
  • Perceived exertion — Borg RPE to monitor intensity.

Exercise prescription (FITT-VP):

ComponentRecommendation in arthritis
FrequencyAerobic 3–5 days/week; strengthening 2–3 days/week
IntensityModerate (RPE 11–14); start low if joints are inflamed
TimeBuild towards 150–300 min/week aerobic, in bouts
TypeLow-impact: walking, cycling, swimming, aquatic therapy, resistance
Volume/ProgressionProgress gradually; avoid overloading acutely inflamed joints

Include flexibility and neuromotor/balance work. Educate the patient about expected soreness versus a flare, and modify the programme during disease flares. Re-test periodically to document change.

Conclusion

Exercise testing in arthritis establishes safe baseline capacity and screens for cardiac risk, while prescription follows the FITT-VP principle with low-impact, progressive, individualised exercise — adapting dose to disease activity so that movement improves pain and function without provoking a flare.

5Recent advances

  • Moseng et al. (2023) — the 2023 EULAR recommendations emphasise exercise of adequate dosage with progression tailored to physical function, preferences and services, and support varied delivery modes including digital technology and aquatic exercise.
  • Bannuru et al. (2019) and Holden et al. (2022) — the 2019 OARSI guidelines and 2022 OARSI Rehabilitation Discussion Group consensus give detailed, practical guidance on dose, progression and adherence in hip and knee OA.
  • de Jong et al. (2003) — the RAPIT multicentre randomised trial showed a 2-year high-intensity exercise programme improved functional ability in rheumatoid arthritis without increasing radiographic joint damage, establishing that intensive exercise is safe in RA.
  • Bartels et al. (2016) — this Cochrane review found aquatic and land-based exercise have comparable benefits in knee and hip OA, with aquatic exercise useful when land exercise is painful.
  • Rodriguez-Sanchez-Laulhe et al. (2022) — a randomised trial of a smartphone app (CareHand) showed app-supported exercise and self-management improve hand function in rheumatoid arthritis, supporting telerehabilitation in chronic arthritis.

Q7. Describe in detail about the post operative assessment in Head of femur fracture in 58 year old female. Add note on its complications.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit VI — Post-operative assessment in hip fracture

★ Memory hook — After a femoral neck fracture, assess the surgery, the wound, the weight-bearing status and the function — and hunt for the classic complications.

1Introduction

Fracture of the head/neck of the femur is a common fragility fracture in older adults and a major cause of morbidity and mortality. In a 58-year-old female, the fracture is usually treated by internal fixation or by arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement), depending on displacement and bone quality.

Post-operative physiotherapy assessment determines what the patient can safely do and guides progressive rehabilitation. In this age group the goal is not merely survival but return to work and community function.

2Physiology

The femoral head receives its blood supply mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery via the retinacular vessels and the artery of the ligamentum teres. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that transmits body weight from the pelvis to the femur; the abductor muscles (gluteus medius and minimus) stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance.

Normal hip function requires an intact capsule, good muscle strength and a stable, congruent joint. Arthroplasty replaces the joint surfaces, so the rehabilitation focus shifts to protecting the prosthesis and restoring function.

3Pathophysiology

Intracapsular femoral neck fractures disrupt the retinacular blood supply, risking avascular necrosis and non-union; displaced fractures are therefore often treated with arthroplasty in older patients. Extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures heal more reliably with fixation.

After surgery, muscle atrophy from disuse, post-operative pain, and the risk of dislocation (after arthroplasty) shape the clinical picture. In a 58-year-old, the goal is return to work and community function, not just survival.

4Answer

Post-operative assessment should cover:

  • History: fracture type, surgery performed (fixation, hemiarthroplasty, THR), approach, weight-bearing status, surgeon's precautions, comorbidities and pre-fracture function.
  • Observation: wound and dressing, swelling, limb position, leg-length discrepancy, deformity, skin condition.
  • Pain and wound: pain score, signs of infection, drain sites.
  • Range of motion: active and passive hip ROM, respecting precautions after arthroplasty (avoid flexion beyond 90°, adduction and internal rotation).
  • Strength: hip abductors, extensors, quadriceps, using MMT or dynamometry.
  • Gait and mobility: transfer ability, weight-bearing status, use of aids, gait pattern, balance (Berg Balance Scale, Timed Up and Go).
  • Function and outcome: Harris Hip Score or HOOS, Barthel Index, 6-minute walk test.
  • Circulation and neurology: distal pulses, sensation, signs of deep vein thrombosis.

Complications to watch for:

ComplicationClinical clue
Deep vein thrombosis / PECalf pain, swelling, breathlessness
Dislocation (arthroplasty)Sudden pain, deformity, leg shortening
Avascular necrosisPersistent pain, collapse on imaging
Non-union / fixation failureContinued pain, inability to weight-bear
InfectionWound discharge, fever, raised CRP
Pressure sores, pneumoniaImmobility-related
DeliriumAcute confusion, common post-operatively
Conclusion

Post-operative assessment after a femoral neck fracture in a 58-year-old combines history, wound and neurovascular checks, ROM, strength, gait and function against a background of surgical precautions — with vigilant screening for the classic complications (DVT, dislocation, AVN, non-union, infection, delirium) that determine recovery.

5Recent advances

  • Min et al. (2021) — this clinical practice guideline for post-operative rehabilitation in older patients with hip fractures strongly recommends multidisciplinary care, progressive resistance exercise and balance training, and supports early ambulation.
  • NICE (2023) — NICE guideline CG124 (updated 2023) requires rehabilitation to start no later than the day after surgery, at least once a day.
  • Diong et al. (2016) — this systematic review and meta-analysis found structured exercise improves mobility after hip fracture, with progressive resistance training and non-hospital settings giving the largest effects.
  • Kimmel et al. (2016) — the HIP4Hips randomised trial found intensive hospital physiotherapy is safe and shortens length of stay after an isolated hip fracture.
  • AAOS (2021) — the AAOS Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults guideline recommends surgery within 24-48 hours and immediate full weight-bearing as tolerated after surgical treatment.

Q8. Write in detail about the musculoskeletal assessment method and screening in congenital dislocation of hip.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit VI — Paediatric musculoskeletal screening

★ Memory hook — Ortolani reduces, Barlow dislocates, Galeazzi reveals the shortening — screen the newborn hip early.

1Introduction

Congenital dislocation of the hip, now called developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), is a spectrum of abnormal development ranging from a mildly dysplastic acetabulum to frank dislocation of the femoral head. Early detection is critical because treatment in the first months of life is simple and effective, whereas late diagnosis requires major surgery.

The physiotherapist's role is in clinical screening, in supporting surveillance, and in post-treatment rehabilitation.

2Physiology

At birth the acetabulum is shallow and the femoral head is largely cartilaginous, so the hip is developmentally immature. Normal development requires the femoral head to remain concentrically reduced within the acetabulum, providing the stimulus for acetabular deepening.

Ligamentous laxity is normal in the newborn and usually resolves; the hip must be kept in a position that maintains concentric reduction for normal growth. This is why positioning (avoiding extended-hip swaddling) and early harness treatment are effective. On ultrasound the normal acetabular alpha angle is greater than 60°; values below this define the Graf type II–IV dysplasia that screening aims to detect.

3Pathophysiology

In DDH, capsular laxity, a shallow acetabulum and abnormal femoral head position produce instability, subluxation or dislocation. Risk factors include breech presentation, female sex, first-born status, family history, oligohydramnios and swaddling with the hips extended.

Left untreated, DDH leads to limping, leg-length discrepancy, early osteoarthritis and disability. Most mild dysplasia detected at birth resolves spontaneously, which complicates screening and is why universal ultrasound remains controversial.

4Answer

Clinical screening tests (newborn):

TestMethodPositive sign
OrtolaniHips flexed and abducted, femoral head lifted into socketA palpable clunk of reduction
BarlowHips flexed and adducted, gentle posterior pressureA palpable clunk of dislocation
GaleazziHips and knees flexed, compare knee heightsLower knee on the affected side
Abduction rangePassive abductionLimited or asymmetrical abduction
Skin creasesInspect thigh/gluteal creasesAsymmetry

Imaging: ultrasound is the investigation of choice before ossification (Graf method, using the alpha angle to classify types I–IV); plain radiography is used after about 4–6 months of age.

Older-child assessment: gait (Trendelenburg, limping), leg-length measurement, hip range of motion and the Trendelenburg test.

Screening strategy: every newborn has a clinical hip examination within the first days of life and again at 6–8 weeks. Infants with risk factors or an abnormal examination undergo targeted hip ultrasound; universal ultrasound screening remains controversial because most detected abnormalities resolve. Confirmed DDH is treated with a Pavlik harness in early infancy, and the physiotherapist reinforces safe hip positioning (avoiding tight swaddling with the hips extended) and monitors harness wear.

Indian context: in settings where routine newborn ultrasound is not universal, repeated clinical examination at the immunisation visits (6, 10 and 14 weeks) is the practical safety net, and delayed presentation with a limping toddler remains common — so the physiotherapist must keep DDH on the differential in any child with a limp or leg-length discrepancy.

Conclusion

Screening for DDH is a clinical examination — Ortolani and Barlow for instability, Galeazzi and crease/asymmetry checks — supported by targeted ultrasound (Graf) and repeated at 6–8 weeks, so that dysplasia is caught early, when a Pavlik harness can restore normal hip development.

5Recent advances

  • Marletta et al. (2025) — this systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed that early Pavlik-harness treatment, ideally in the first months of life, gives the best outcomes for Graf IIb-IV hips.
  • Bewick et al. (2025) — this multicentre UK study showed physiotherapy-led DDH clinics achieve high Pavlik-harness success (96%) and low residual dysplasia, matching medically-led clinics.
  • Sharma et al. (2022) — this scoping review found early, structured, individualised physiotherapy improves hip function and reduces complications in children with developmental dysplasia of the hip.
  • Ho et al. (2025) — this case report highlights the physiotherapist's role in detecting delayed DDH and in post-casting rehabilitation, restoring movement, strength and age-appropriate function.

6References

Q9. Explain the uses of ICF in diagnosis of musculoskeletal disorders.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit II — ICF framework in musculoskeletal diagnosis

★ Memory hook — ICF turns a diagnosis into a profile: what is impaired, what the patient cannot do, and what the environment allows.

1Introduction

The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF), published by the WHO in 2001, provides a standard language and framework for describing health and health-related states. In musculoskeletal practice it moves the clinician beyond a purely tissue-based diagnosis towards a biopsychosocial profile of the patient's functioning.

It is used in assessment, goal setting, outcome measurement and communication across disciplines, and it underpins modern physiotherapy diagnosis.

2Physiology

The ICF describes functioning across two parts. The first is Functioning and Disability, comprising Body Functions and Structures (physiological and anatomical status) and Activities and Participation (execution of tasks and involvement in life situations). The second is Contextual Factors, comprising Environmental Factors and Personal Factors.

These components interact dynamically with the health condition, so that a musculoskeletal disorder is understood as the result of the interaction between the pathology and the person's context, not the pathology alone.

3Pathophysiology

A musculoskeletal disorder — for example, knee osteoarthritis — produces impairment at the level of body function and structure (pain, reduced joint mobility, muscle weakness), activity limitation (difficulty walking or climbing stairs) and participation restriction (unable to work or socialise).

Environmental factors (stairs at home, workplace demands) and personal factors (age, coping, beliefs) modulate the impact. Recognising all these domains prevents the common error of treating only the tissue and ignoring the person.

4Answer

Uses of the ICF in musculoskeletal diagnosis and management:

  • Comprehensive assessment: it provides a checklist of domains to examine — body functions and structures, activities, participation and contextual factors — so nothing important is missed.
  • Core Sets: condition-specific ICF Core Sets (low back pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, post-acute musculoskeletal conditions) define the categories most relevant to each condition and make the framework practical.
  • Qualifiers: each category is graded from 0 (no problem) to 4 (complete problem), giving a quantitative profile that can be tracked over time.
  • Goal setting: goals can be set at impairment, activity and participation levels, aligning treatment with what matters to the patient.
  • Outcome measurement: the profile serves as a baseline and a measure of change.
  • Interdisciplinary communication: it provides a common language across physiotherapy, medicine, occupational therapy and social services.
  • Rehabilitation planning: it links identified problems to interventions and to the responsible professional.
ICF componentExample in low back pain
Body functionsb280 Sensation of pain
Body structuress760 Structure of trunk
Activities & participationd430 Lifting and carrying objects
Environmental factorse580 Health services, systems and policies
Conclusion

The ICF turns a musculoskeletal diagnosis into a biopsychosocial profile across body function, activity, participation and context — making assessment comprehensive, goals meaningful, outcomes measurable and communication shared across the rehabilitation team.

5Recent advances

  • Hernandez-Lazaro et al. (2023) — this multicentre study confirmed the content validity of the comprehensive ICF Core Set for post-acute musculoskeletal conditions in primary care physiotherapy services.
  • Selb et al. (2022) — developed an ICF-based assessment schedule to facilitate assessment and reporting of functioning in manual medicine, using low back pain as a model.
  • Cieza et al. (2004) — produced the ICF Core Sets for low back pain, which are now used as starting points for examination and outcome measurement in musculoskeletal conditions.
  • Bickenbach et al. (2020) — published the ICF Core Sets Manual for Clinical Practice (2nd edition), giving clinicians a step-by-step method and documentation tool for applying ICF Core Sets.
  • WHO (2001) — published the ICF framework, which is now increasingly embedded in national rehabilitation policies and primary care musculoskeletal pathways.

6References
