Q10. What are the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults?

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit V — Fitness evaluation and exercise prescription

★ Memory hook — Screen before you test: check activity level, symptoms, known disease and intended intensity, then measure the five components of fitness.

1Introduction

Fitness evaluation in adults is the structured assessment of health status and physical fitness before an exercise programme is prescribed. Its purposes are to detect individuals at risk of exercise-related cardiovascular events, to establish a baseline, and to guide safe, effective prescription.

The evaluation has two parts: pre-participation health screening and the measurement of the components of fitness.

2Physiology

Physical fitness is the ability to perform daily tasks with vigour and without undue fatigue. It has five health-related components: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition; balance is an important additional component in older adults.

Regular exercise improves all of these and reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and all-cause mortality. The body's acute response to exercise — heart rate, blood pressure, ventilation and oxygen uptake — is the basis of the tests used to assess capacity.

3Pathophysiology

The main risk of exercise testing is an exercise-related cardiovascular event, particularly sudden cardiac death or myocardial infarction, which is more likely in people with known or occult cardiovascular disease who undertake unaccustomed vigorous exercise.

Sedentary lifestyle, obesity, hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia increase this risk. Screening therefore aims to identify who needs medical clearance, while avoiding excessive referral that discourages physical activity.

4Answer

Criteria for fitness evaluation in adults:

  • Pre-participation health screening — using the ACSM algorithm based on (a) current level of structured physical activity, (b) presence of major signs or symptoms or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and (c) the desired exercise intensity. The PAR-Q+ may be used as a self-administered tool. The outcome is whether medical clearance is needed before starting.
  • Resting measures — heart rate, blood pressure, body mass index, waist circumference and resting ECG where indicated.
  • Cardiorespiratory fitness — a submaximal or maximal test (cycle or treadmill, or a field test such as the 6-minute walk) to estimate VO2max.
  • Muscular fitness — grip strength, push-up or sit-up tests, and 1-RM or estimated 1-RM.
  • Flexibility — sit-and-reach or goniometric measures.
  • Body composition — BMI, waist girth and, where available, body-fat percentage.
  • Balance and functional capacity — relevant in older adults (Berg Balance Scale, Timed Up and Go).

Indications to stop a test include chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness, pallor, a drop in systolic blood pressure, or a hypertensive response. Interpretation compares results with age- and sex-based norms and forms the basis of the FITT-VP prescription.

ComponentTest example
CardiorespiratorySubmaximal cycle, 6-minute walk
Muscular strengthGrip dynamometry, 1-RM
FlexibilitySit-and-reach
Body compositionBMI, waist girth
Conclusion

The criteria for fitness evaluation in adults are: pre-participation screening (ACSM algorithm / PAR-Q+) to decide on medical clearance, resting measures, and measurement of the five health-related components of fitness (plus balance in the elderly) — interpreted against age- and sex-based norms to prescribe exercise safely.

5Recent advances

  • Bull et al. (2020) — the WHO 2020 guidelines recommend 150-300 minutes of moderate or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity per week for adults, plus muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days.
  • Piercy et al. (2018) — the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans (2nd edition) formalised the 150-300 minute aerobic target and, for the first time, recommended balance training alongside aerobic and strengthening activity in older adults.
  • Riebe et al. (2015) — the ACSM pre-participation screening model removed routine cardiovascular risk-factor profiling and now bases medical clearance on activity level, symptoms/disease and intended intensity, reducing unnecessary physician referrals.
  • Ross et al. (2016) — showed that cardiorespiratory fitness is a clinical vital sign that predicts cardiovascular and all-cause mortality independent of traditional risk factors.
  • Sherrington et al. (2019) — this Cochrane review found that balance and strength training reduces falls in older adults, so multicomponent training is now specifically recommended for them.

6References

Question 1 · 10 marks

Q1. Describe the role of investigations in assessment.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 1 – Principles of clinical assessment, medical screening and diagnostic investigations

★ Memory hook — "History tells the story, examination writes the chapter, and investigations only confirm the plot."

1Introduction

Investigations are structured diagnostic procedures — laboratory tests, imaging and electrophysiology — that a clinician orders to confirm or exclude a working diagnosis, screen for serious pathology, grade severity, guide treatment and monitor progress. In musculoskeletal physiotherapy assessment they form the third pillar of clinical reasoning, standing alongside the subjective history and the physical examination. Their single most important role is to reduce diagnostic uncertainty: they convert a probability statement ("this looks like a lateral epicondylalgia") into a defensible diagnosis. Equally important is what they are not: an investigation never replaces the clinical examination, because imaging findings frequently exist in asymptomatic people (a large proportion of pain-free adults show disc degeneration or meniscal tears on MRI), so a report must always be read against the clinical picture. In autonomous or direct-access practice the physiotherapist must therefore know which test answers which question, when it is indicated, and how to integrate the result.

2Physiology

Normal tissues have characteristic signatures that make abnormality recognisable. Cortical bone appears dense and white on plain radiography because it attenuates X-rays strongly; cancellous bone shows a fine trabecular pattern; hyaline cartilage is radiolucent on plain film (visualised only indirectly as joint-space width) but returns a smooth, uniform low signal on MRI. Muscle, tendon and ligament return intermediate-to-low signal, while fat is bright on T1. Blood markers have defined reference ranges: ESR is typically under 20 mm/hr and CRP under 5–10 mg/L, and their normal values reflect the absence of systemic inflammation. Nerve conduction velocities and electromyographic recruitment patterns are also stable in health, so deviation from these norms signals disease. Understanding normal appearances and values is the physiological baseline against which every investigation is judged.

3Pathophysiology

Investigations detect the structural and biochemical footprints of disease. A fracture shows as a cortical breach with displacement or angulation; osteoporosis as reduced bone density; osteoarthritis as joint-space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis; and infection or tumour as bone destruction or periosteal reaction. On MRI, bone-marrow oedema (bright on fluid-sensitive STIR or fat-suppressed T2 sequences) signals active inflammation, stress injury or infection. Nerve-root compression shows as disc protrusion or foraminal narrowing, and inflammatory arthropathy raises ESR and CRP while showing erosions and marrow oedema. Each pathology thus leaves a signature that a correctly chosen investigation can reveal — but the same finding may occur without symptoms, which is precisely why the clinical context governs interpretation.

4Answer

Investigations may be grouped as follows:

CategoryExamplesChief role in assessment
Laboratory (blood/urine)ESR, CRP, HLA-B27, RF, anti-CCP, vitamin D, uric acidScreen inflammatory, metabolic and systemic disease
Plain imagingX-ray (radiograph), DEXAFracture, alignment, joint-space narrowing, bone density
Cross-sectionalCT, MRISoft tissue, marrow, disc, cord and nerve-root detail
Dynamic / functionalDiagnostic ultrasound, fluoroscopy, stress viewsReal-time tendon, effusion and stability assessment
Nuclear / metabolicBone scan, PET, SPECTOccult fracture, infection, metastasis, active bone turnover
ElectrophysiologyNerve conduction studies, EMGLocalise and grade nerve injury or radiculopathy
Invasive / specialArthroscopy, biopsy, arthrocentesisTissue diagnosis and direct visualisation

Their roles in assessment are: (i) diagnostic confirmation or exclusion of the working hypothesis; (ii) screening for red flags — fracture, infection, malignancy, inflammatory arthritis and cauda equina syndrome; (iii) grading and staging severity (e.g. Schatzker classification, sacroiliitis grade); (iv) guiding and monitoring treatment (e.g. weight-bearing progression after fracture fixation); (v) prognosis; and (vi) documentation and medico-legal defensibility. The physiotherapist's role is to gather the clinical data (age, trauma, mechanism, weight-bearing ability, tenderness, red-flag features) that determine whether a test is indicated, to request imaging only where it will change management, and to interpret the report in context rather than treating the image alone.

5Recent advances

  • Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) — increasingly used by musculoskeletal physiotherapists at the bedside to assess effusion, tendon integrity and tissue glide in real time, supplementing rather than replacing formal imaging.
  • IFOMPT (2020) — the International Federation of Orthopaedic Manipulative Physical Therapists international framework reframed red flags as a clinical-reasoning pathway rather than a simple checklist, guiding when investigation is genuinely warranted in suspected serious spinal pathology.
  • Cuff et al. (2020) — a scoping review of 31 clinical practice guidelines found that routine imaging for non-traumatic low back, knee and shoulder pain is not justified and should be reserved for suspected serious pathology or failure to respond to care.
  • Crowell et al. (2016) — in a direct-access sports physical therapy clinic, radiologists judged more than 80% of physical therapist-ordered MRI/MRA examinations appropriate against American College of Radiology criteria, and advanced imaging was ordered in only about 8% of evaluations, supporting physiotherapist imaging referral privileges.
  • Rundell et al. (2021) — a survey showed that physical therapists frequently recommend diagnostic imaging but rarely refer patients directly for it, highlighting how under-used imaging referral authority is even where direct-access rights exist.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St Louis: Elsevier; 2021.

Question 2 · 10 marks

Q2. Describe screening of the wrist following Colles fracture.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 2 – Assessment and screening of the wrist and hand

★ Memory hook — "After a Colles, check the Nerve, the Tendon, the Deformity and the Function — N-T-D-F."

1Introduction

A Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement and dorsal angulation of the distal fragment, usually the result of a fall on the outstretched hand in an older, osteoporotic patient. Because the wrist is a compact region packed with the median nerve, flexor and extensor tendons, the triangular fibrocartilage complex and the distal radio-ulnar joint, the fracture and its cast treatment can leave several secondary problems. Screening of the wrist after a Colles fracture is therefore not merely about checking that the bone has united; it is a systematic search for the complications that limit hand function — median nerve compression (carpal tunnel syndrome), extensor pollicis longus rupture, complex regional pain syndrome, malunion, distal radio-ulnar joint instability and scapholunate injury. Early, structured screening allows the physiotherapist to refer promptly and to design rehabilitation that restores range, strength and function.

2Physiology

Normal wrist function depends on a mobile radiocarpal and midcarpal joint, a congruent distal radio-ulnar joint and a carpal tunnel that transmits the median nerve and nine flexor tendons beneath the transverse carpal ligament. Normal values used in screening include about 70–80 degrees of wrist flexion and extension, 80–90 degrees of pronation and supination, and grip strength on the affected side that is normally within 10–15 per cent of the uninjured side. On plain radiography the healed distal radius normally shows a radial inclination of about 22 degrees, radial height of about 11–12 mm, and a volar tilt of about 11 degrees; ulnar variance is neutral to slightly negative. These norms are the reference against which the post-fracture wrist is compared.

3Pathophysiology

Malunion with residual dorsal angulation, radial shortening or loss of radial inclination alters the load distribution across the radiocarpal joint and predisposes to pain and post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Dorsal displacement and swelling raise pressure within the carpal tunnel, compressing the median nerve and producing carpal tunnel syndrome. Attrition of the extensor pollicis longus tendon over the fracture callus can cause it to rupture, presenting as loss of thumb interphalangeal extension. Prolonged immobilisation and pain can trigger complex regional pain syndrome with vasomotor, sudomotor and trophic changes. Injury to the triangular fibrocartilage complex or the scapholunate ligament may coexist and cause ulnar-sided pain or instability. Screening targets each of these mechanisms.

4Answer

Screening proceeds in a logical sequence:

  1. History: mechanism, dominant hand, occupation, prior fractures, pain pattern, numbness or night pain in the hand, loss of thumb movement, stiffness.
  2. Observation: swelling, deformity (dinner-fork if unreduced), surgical scar, skin colour, temperature, hair growth and sweating (for complex regional pain syndrome), and willingness to move the hand.
  3. Palpation: tenderness over the distal radius, the carpal tunnel, the anatomical snuffbox (scaphoid), the triangular fibrocartilage complex fovea and the distal radio-ulnar joint.
  4. Range of motion: active and passive wrist flexion, extension, radial and ulnar deviation, plus pronation and supination compared with the other side.
  5. Strength: grip and pinch strength (grip fraction = affected/unaffected), and resisted thumb extension for extensor pollicis longus.
  6. Neurological screen: median, ulnar and radial nerve sensation and power; Tinel sign and Phalen test for the median nerve.
  7. Special tests: Watson (scaphoid shift) test for scapholunate instability; fovea sign for triangular fibrocartilage complex; piano-key and ulnar grind tests for distal radio-ulnar joint; Froment sign for ulnar nerve.
  8. Function: ability to grasp, pinch, pour and perform activities of daily living.
  9. Outcome measures and investigations: Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation and QuickDASH questionnaires, grip fraction and flexion-extension arc; radiographs for radial inclination, radial height, volar tilt and ulnar variance.

Each special test is recorded as position–force–positive sign: for example, in the Watson test the examiner holds the wrist in ulnar deviation and volar pressure on the scaphoid tubercle while moving the wrist from ulnar to radial deviation; a positive sign is a painful clunk as the scaphoid subluxes, indicating scapholunate instability.

5Recent advances

  • Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) and QuickDASH — responsiveness studies show these wrist-specific measures are more sensitive than generic measures in the first 6–12 months after distal radius fracture, supporting their routine use.
  • Chung et al. (2021) — the multicentre WRIST (Wrist and Radius Injury Surgical Trial) in adults over 60 showed surgical and non-surgical treatment yield broadly similar 12- and 24-month functional outcomes, reframing rehabilitation goals around function rather than radiographic perfection.
  • Reid et al. (2020) — a multicentre randomised trial found that adding supination and wrist-extension mobilisation-with-movement to exercise and advice after cast immobilisation produced faster, greater gains in supination, range of motion and function (PRWE, QuickDASH), although the benefit faded by 12 months.
  • Gutiérrez-Espinoza et al. (2022) — a systematic review and meta-analysis found that adding mobilisation-with-movement and manual lymphatic drainage improved wrist and upper-limb function and reduced hand oedema after distal radius fracture.
  • Soares et al. (2023) — an updated meta-analysis of 15 trials found no clear difference between supervised and non-supervised exercise after distal radius fracture, but all evidence was of very low quality, so therapist-supervised programmes cannot yet be assumed superior.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St Louis: Elsevier; 2021.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  3. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2018.
  4. Chung KC, Kim HM, Malay S, Shauver MJ. The Wrist and Radius Injury Surgical Trial (WRIST): a multicenter randomized clinical trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2020;3(1):e1918910.
  5. Measuring outcomes over time in distal radius fractures: responsiveness of the SF-36, DASH and PRWE. J Hand Surg Am. 2020;45(11):1064–1071.
  6. Adding mobilisation with movement to exercise and advice after cast immobilisation for distal radius fracture: a multicentre randomised trial. J Physiother. 2020;66(4):227–235.
Question 3 · 10 marks

Q3. Describe screening of the lower back following lumbar canal stenosis at L2-L3 level.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 3 – Assessment and screening of the lumbar spine and neural claudication

★ Memory hook — "Stenosis loves to walk and stand, and hates to sit and stoop — extension provokes, flexion relieves."

1Introduction

Lumbar canal stenosis is a narrowing of the central spinal canal, lateral recess or intervertebral foramen that compresses the cauda equina and lumbosacral nerve roots, producing the characteristic syndrome of neurogenic claudication — leg and buttock pain, heaviness or numbness brought on by walking or standing and relieved by sitting or bending forward. Stenosis at the L2-L3 level is comparatively uncommon but important, because it affects the upper lumbar roots (L2 and L3) and can mimic hip or femoral pathology. Screening the lower back at this level means systematically confirming the clinical syndrome, localising the level, excluding mimics (especially vascular claudication) and identifying red flags that mandate imaging or surgical referral.

2Physiology

The lumbar canal contains the cauda equina and, at each level, the exiting nerve roots. At L2-L3 the relevant roots are L2 and L3, whose myotomes include hip flexion and knee extension (quadriceps), whose dermatomes cover the anterior and medial thigh and the anterior knee, and whose reflex is the knee jerk (mainly L3-L4). In the healthy spine the canal has ample reserve, and walking is limited only by cardiovascular fitness. Lumbar flexion increases canal and foraminal dimensions, whereas extension and standing reduce them — the physiological basis of the posture-dependent symptoms of stenosis.

3Pathophysiology

Degenerative changes — facet hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum thickening, disc bulging and osteophyte formation — narrow the canal and compress the neural and vascular elements of the cauda equina. Compression is dynamic: extension and standing further reduce canal dimensions and venous return, causing nerve-root ischaemia and the claudication symptoms, while flexion restores space and relieves them. Compression of the L2 and L3 roots produces anterior thigh pain, quadriceps weakness and a diminished knee jerk. Because radiological narrowing is common in asymptomatic older adults, the diagnosis must rest on the clinical syndrome, with imaging used as an auxiliary rather than a stand-alone test.

4Answer

Screening follows a structured sequence:

  1. History: age over 60, leg or buttock pain brought on by walking and standing, relief on sitting or leaning forward, the "shopping-cart sign" (relief when leaning on a trolley), motor or sensory disturbance while walking, and normal symmetric foot pulses. The International Society for the Study of the Lumbar Spine taskforce identified these as the key items for clinical diagnosis.
  2. Observation and gait: stooped or flexed posture, flattened lumbar lordosis, reduced walking distance; assess balance.
  3. Provocative tests: sustained lumbar extension reproduces leg symptoms; a walking-tolerance test in upright versus stooped posture, or treadmill walking versus stationary cycling, distinguishes neurogenic from vascular claudication.
  4. Neurological examination: dermatomal sensation of the anterior and medial thigh (L2, L3), myotomes — hip flexion (L2) and knee extension (L3, L4) — and the knee reflex; femoral nerve stretch test.
  5. Differential diagnosis: exclude vascular claudication (absent or diminished pedal pulses, low ankle-brachial index, symptoms provoked by cycling), hip osteoarthritis, greater trochanteric pain syndrome, peripheral neuropathy and disc herniation.
  6. Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index, Zurich Claudication Questionnaire, and walking tests (self-paced walk test, 6-minute walk test).
  7. Investigations: MRI is the imaging of choice to define the level and degree of stenosis; CT or CT myelography where MRI is contraindicated. Electrophysiology and, in selected cases, three-dimensional MRI or diffusion-tensor imaging help with foraminal stenosis.

Red flags requiring urgent referral include saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, rapidly progressive weakness and bilateral severe deficits, which suggest cauda equina compression.

5Recent advances

  • Tomkins-Lane et al. (2016) — an ISSLS international Delphi consensus defined seven history items that give clinicians about 80 per cent certainty of the clinical diagnosis of lumbar spinal stenosis within six questions.
  • Konno et al. (2007) — developed and validated a self-administered, self-reported history questionnaire (SSHQ) as a screening tool for lumbar spinal stenosis (sensitivity about 84 per cent, specificity about 78 per cent), though its specificity remains limited for excluding other causes of leg pain.
  • Bussières et al. (2021) — a clinical practice guideline on non-surgical management of lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication recommends multimodal non-pharmacological care (education, exercise, manual therapy) and advises against routine NSAIDs, gabapentin and epidural steroid injections.
  • Minetama et al. (2021) — a randomised trial found supervised physical therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks gave greater improvement in symptom severity and physical function than unsupervised home exercise at 1 year, and roughly halved the likelihood of receiving surgery (7% vs 23%).
  • Ammendolia et al. (2018) — a randomised trial showed a 6-week comprehensive nonsurgical programme combining manual therapy, supervised exercise and a cognitive-behavioural approach produced large, sustained improvements in walking ability compared with self-directed care in neurogenic claudication.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St Louis: Elsevier; 2021.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  3. Ammendolia C, Stuber KJ, Rok E, et al. Consensus on the clinical diagnosis of lumbar spinal stenosis: results of an international Delphi study. Spine. 2016;41(15):1239–1246.
  4. Ammendolia C, Hofkirchner C, Plener J, et al. Non-surgical interventions for lumbar spinal stenosis leading to neurogenic claudication: a clinical practice guideline. J Pain. 2021;22(9):1015–1039.
  5. Anderson DB, Mathieson S, Eyles J, et al. Measurement properties of walking outcome measures for neurogenic claudication: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Spine J. 2021;21(9):1378–1396.
  6. De Schepper EIT, Overdevest GM, Suri P, et al. Diagnosis of lumbar spinal stenosis: a systematic review of the accuracy of diagnostic tests. Spine. 2013;38(8):E469–E481.
Question 4 · 10 marks

Q4. Challenges faced by Physiotherapists in autonomous practice.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 4 – Professional issues, direct access and autonomous practice

★ Memory hook — "Autonomy means you own the decision — and the L-E-G-A-L load that comes with it: Legal, Ethical, Gatekeeping, Accountability, Liability."

1Introduction

Autonomous practice means that a physiotherapist examines, diagnoses within the physiotherapy scope, plans and delivers treatment, and decides on discharge or referral without needing a physician's authorisation for each step. Its fullest form is direct access or self-referral, in which patients consult a physiotherapist first.

Autonomy raises the professional standing of physiotherapy and improves access, timeliness and cost-effectiveness of musculoskeletal care, but it also transfers clinical, legal and ethical responsibility onto the physiotherapist. Many of the challenges physiotherapists face in autonomous practice arise from this transfer of responsibility, from legal and reimbursement systems that lag behind the profession, and from interprofessional relationships that must be renegotiated.

2Physiology

Framed professionally, the “normal function” of an autonomous practitioner is a set of competencies: competent subjective and physical examination, sound clinical reasoning, confident diagnostic triage, recognition and management of red flags, appropriate referral, evidence-based intervention, and reflective, ethical decision-making. These are the competencies that entry-level education is expected to develop for a graduate to function autonomously.

In a healthy autonomous system these competencies operate within a clear legal scope of practice, a defined referral pathway and a supportive interprofessional environment — the professional analogue of a body in homeostasis.

3Pathophysiology

When any of these supports is missing, autonomous practice becomes dysfunctional. Restrictive or ambiguous legislation narrows the scope of practice and forces dependence on medical referral. Inconsistent reimbursement policies make direct access financially unattractive. Uncertainty about screening and diagnostic skills breeds defensive practice. Territorial resistance from other professions creates friction and referral barriers. Each of these is a “lesion” in the professional system that limits the practitioner's ability to function autonomously and safely.

4Answer

The principal challenges can be grouped by domain, each with its consequence and the remedy that addresses it:

DomainChallengeConsequenceRemedy
Legal & regulatoryIn much of India direct access is not expressly permitted and scope-of-practice law still subordinates physiotherapy to medicine; the Clinical Establishments Act (2010) and the NCAHP Act (2021) leave the scope loosely definedPractising beyond scope risks disciplinary action; therapists depend on medical referralClear scope-of-practice legislation and regulation under the National Commission for Allied and Healthcare Professions
Reimbursement & insuranceInsurers and schemes (e.g. ESIC) may not cover self-referred episodes or pay less for a direct-access assessmentDirect access is financially unattractive; out-of-pocket cost falls on the patientUniform, transparent insurer policies recognising autonomous physiotherapy
Medico-legal liabilityWith autonomy comes responsibility for missed diagnoses (fracture, infection, malignancy, cauda equina)The physiotherapist carries liability that was once shared with the referrerIndemnity insurance, rigorous red-flag screening, meticulous documentation
Competency & education gapsTherapists trained before autonomy entered the curriculum may lack confidence in diagnostic reasoning, screening and requesting investigationsDefensive or unsafe practice; under-use of direct-access rightsPostgraduate education in diagnostic reasoning and continuing professional development
Gatekeeping responsibilityThe therapist is the first-contact gatekeeper deciding what lies within scope and when to referAnxiety about missing serious pathology; variable referral thresholdsClear protocols and validated red-flag frameworks (e.g. IFOMPT)
Interprofessional conflictSome medical bodies and physicians resist direct access, citing safety and diagnostic competenceReferral and communication barriersInterprofessional collaboration, shared protocols, evidence of safety
Public awareness & demandPatients often do not know they can consult a physiotherapist directlyDemand and utilisation remain lowPublic and community education
Evidence, audit & CPDAutonomous practitioners must justify interventions with evidence and avoid unnecessary treatment or investigationRisk of over-treatment or unsupported practiceOutcome measurement, audit and lifelong learning

Meeting these challenges requires clear scope-of-practice legislation, uniform reimbursement, postgraduate education in diagnostic reasoning, interprofessional collaboration and public education — in short, the systems that let a competent therapist use autonomy safely.

Conclusion

Autonomous practice is limited less by the therapist's skill than by the surrounding legal, financial and interprofessional systems; the challenges are therefore best met by pairing individual competence (screening, reasoning, documentation) with structural reform (scope-of-practice law, insurer policy and public awareness).

5Recent advances

  • ENPHE/World Physiotherapy (2022) — competencies for autonomous practice provide an educational framework so that entry-level graduates and experienced therapists can develop the competencies needed for direct access.
  • Cattrysse et al. (2024) — a scoping review of the impact of direct access found physiotherapy direct access improved provider decision-making and treatment compliance and, from a societal view, reduced waiting times, medication use and imaging, with no evidence of harm.
  • Alnaqbi et al. (2021) — a UAE survey of 264 physiotherapists documented recurring barriers (limited physician and policymaker support, limited autonomy and scope, and patient-safety concerns); a complementary 2026 Hong Kong implementation study reported similar barriers alongside facilitators such as competency assurance and public education.
  • Reviews of direct-access implementation — show that uniform, transparent insurer policies and clinician training are decisive for success.
  • IFOMPT (2020) — the international red-flag framework now underpins safe autonomous screening, giving therapists a defensible clinical-reasoning pathway for suspected serious pathology.

6References

  1. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  2. European Network of Physiotherapy in Higher Education (ENPHE). Physiotherapy Competencies for Autonomous Practice. 2022.
  3. Impact of direct access on the quality of primary care musculoskeletal physiotherapy: a scoping review. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2024;25:544.
  4. Physiotherapists' perspectives on barriers to implementation of direct access of physiotherapy services in the United Arab Emirates. PLoS One. 2021;16(6):e0253155.
  5. Barriers and facilitators of direct access model to physiotherapy. Arch Public Health. 2026;84:1.
  6. Finucane LM, Downie A, Mercer C, et al. International framework for red flags for potential serious spinal pathologies. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2020;50(7):350–372.
Question 5 · 10 marks

Q5. Describe the various special tests for screening the neck.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 5 – Special tests and screening of the cervical spine

★ Memory hook — "Screen the neck for the 4 M-V-F-I: Myelopathy, Vascular, Facet and nerve-root (Instability too)."

1Introduction

The cervical spine is a highly mobile region that houses the spinal cord, the vertebral arteries and the cervical nerve roots, so a neck complaint may represent anything from simple mechanical pain to a compressive myelopathy, a vascular insufficiency or an unstable upper-cervical joint. Special tests for the neck are the structured provocative and positional manoeuvres used during physical examination to reproduce a patient's symptoms or to reveal a specific underlying dysfunction. Their purpose is not to replace the neurological examination or history, but to sharpen the clinical hypothesis, to help distinguish nerve-root from cord or vascular involvement, and to guide referral. Because no single test is highly accurate on its own, tests are best interpreted as clusters within a consistent clinical picture.

2Physiology

Normal cervical function depends on the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints for most rotation, the mid- and lower-cervical facet joints for flexion, extension and side-flexion, and an intact disc and ligamentous complex for stability. The cervical nerve roots exit through the intervertebral foramina, which are narrowed by extension, side-flexion and rotation. The vertebral arteries pass through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 and are mechanically stressed by rotation and extension. The transverse and alar ligaments stabilise the atlanto-axial joint. These normal relationships explain why particular positions provoke particular symptoms.

3Pathophysiology

Degenerative disc disease, osteophytes and facet hypertrophy narrow the foramina and compress a nerve root, causing cervical radiculopathy with dermatomal arm pain, paraesthesia and myotomal weakness. Cord compression from a large disc, osteophyte or canal stenosis produces myelopathy with upper motor neurone signs. Rotational or extension stress on a compromised vertebral artery may produce vertebrobasilar insufficiency with dizziness, diplopia or drop attacks. Laxity of the transverse or alar ligaments from trauma or inflammatory disease produces upper-cervical instability. Facet-joint dysfunction produces localised, movement-related pain. Special tests are designed to reproduce each of these mechanisms.

4Answer

The special tests can be grouped by the structure being screened:

GroupTestsPosition, force and positive sign
Nerve-root (radiculopathy)Spurling test (foraminal compression)Neck side-flexed and extended toward the painful side with axial compression; positive if familiar arm pain is reproduced
Nerve-rootDistraction (traction) testGentle axial traction applied; positive if arm pain is relieved
Nerve-rootShoulder abduction (relief) signPatient raises the hand onto the head; positive if arm pain eases
Nerve-rootValsalva manoeuvrePatient bears down; positive if arm pain is reproduced
Nerve-rootUpper limb neurodynamic tests (ULNT 1, 2a, 2b, 3)Sequenced arm positions loading the neural tissue with structural differentiation; positive if familiar symptoms are reproduced and change with neck side-flexion
MyelopathyHoffmann sign, Babinski sign, clonus, Lhermitte signPassive flick of the middle finger (Hoffmann) or neck flexion (Lhermitte); positive sign is reflex finger flexion or an electric shock down the spine
VascularVertebrobasilar insufficiency tests (Hautant, De Kleyn, sustained rotation-extension)Sustained neck rotation and extension; positive if dizziness, nystagmus, diplopia or nausea appear
InstabilitySharp-Purser test, alar ligament testSharp-Purser: head flexion with posterior glide of the atlas; positive if the atlas slides and symptoms ease, indicating atlanto-axial instability
Facet / jointCervical flexion-rotation test, cervical rotation lateral-flexion (Bragard) test, quadrant testFull passive flexion with rotation to each side; positive if rotation is restricted and pain reproduced, suggesting upper-cervical facet dysfunction
Muscle controlCraniocervical flexion testPatient performs craniocervical nodding with a pressure sensor; positive if deep flexor activation is weak or the superficial muscles dominate

Interpretation rules: a positive Spurling, distraction and Valsalva test (each highly specific) supports radiculopathy, whereas a negative upper-limb neurodynamic test helps rule it out; a cluster of three or more positive neurodynamic tests raises the likelihood of radiculopathy. Myelopathy signs or vascular symptoms require urgent medical referral, and vertebral-artery testing must precede any cervical manipulation.

5Recent advances

  • Grondin et al. (2021) — a diagnostic-accuracy study of upper-limb neurodynamic tests found single tests are poor, but three or more positive tests (LR+ about 12.9) can rule in cervical radiculopathy, while all-negative tests can rule it out.
  • Thoomes et al. (2026) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of physical tests for cervical radiculopathy confirmed Spurling test has high specificity and that combinations of four neurodynamic tests are the most useful, though the certainty of evidence remains low.
  • Jinright et al. (2020) — documented inconsistencies in how the Spurling test is performed and interpreted across clinical practice, prompting standardisation of the manoeuvre and its interpretation.
  • Hariharan et al. (2021) — an inter-examiner reliability study showed the cervical flexion-rotation test has excellent reliability (kappa about 0.88–0.96) when asymmetry of motion is used as the positive criterion.
  • de Best et al. (2021) — advanced understanding of the reliability and validity of cervical examination procedures, supporting test clusters over single tests.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St Louis: Elsevier; 2021.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  3. Grondin F, Cook C, Hall T, et al. Diagnostic accuracy of upper limb neurodynamic tests in the diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy. Musculoskelet Sci Pract. 2021;55:102427.
  4. Rubinstein SM, Pool JJM, van Tulder MW, et al. A systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of provocative tests of the neck for diagnosing cervical radiculopathy. Eur Spine J. 2007;16(3):307–319.
  5. Thoomes EJ, van Geest S, van der Windt DA, et al. Value of physical tests in diagnosing cervical radiculopathy: a systematic review. Spine J. 2018;18(1):179–189.
  6. Jinright H, Kassoff N, Williams CP, Hazle CR. Spurling's test – inconsistencies in clinical practice. J Man Manip Ther. 2020;29(1):23–32.
Question 6 · 10 marks

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for ankylosing spondylitis.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 6 – Investigations in inflammatory spinal disease

★ Memory hook — "Ankylosing spondylitis: Blood, X-ray, MRI, Measures — B-X-M-M."

1Introduction

Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the prototypical axial spondyloarthritis: a chronic inflammatory disease that begins at the sacroiliac joints and entheses and may progress to spinal fusion. Because early inflammatory back pain is easily mistaken for mechanical back pain, and because structural damage on plain radiographs appears only after months to years, investigations play a central role in diagnosis, classification, monitoring and prognosis. The investigation of AS combines laboratory markers of inflammation and genetic susceptibility, imaging of the sacroiliac joints and spine, and validated clinical scoring tools. No single test is diagnostic on its own; the diagnosis is built by combining the clinical picture of inflammatory back pain with the appropriate investigations.

2Physiology

The sacroiliac joint and the vertebral entheses are the primary targets of AS. The normal sacroiliac joint has a narrow, well-defined joint space with smooth subchondral bone, and the normal spine has square vertebral bodies, intact discovertebral junctions and flexible motion. Normal inflammatory markers are low (ESR under about 20 mm/hr, CRP under about 5–10 mg/L), and HLA-B27, though present in a minority of the healthy population, is the strongest genetic marker of the disease. These normal baselines make the inflammatory and structural changes of AS recognisable.

3Pathophysiology

AS begins with inflammation at the enthesis — the insertion of ligament or capsule into bone. At the sacroiliac joints this produces sacroiliitis with subchondral bone-marrow oedema (osteitis), which appears on MRI as a bright signal on fluid-sensitive sequences months to years before radiographic change. Ongoing inflammation leads to erosion, sclerosis, joint-space narrowing and eventually ankylosis of the sacroiliac joints. In the spine, inflammation at the discovertebral junction and annulus produces syndesmophytes, ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament and the classic "bamboo spine", with squaring of vertebral bodies and a rigid, kyphotic spine. The inflammatory process also raises ESR and CRP, though these may be normal in early or mild disease.

4Answer

(a) Laboratory investigations

  • HLA-B27 — a genetic marker positive in about 90 per cent of patients with AS, but also present in a small proportion of healthy people; useful mainly in the clinical arm of classification, not as a stand-alone diagnostic test.
  • ESR and CRP — non-specific markers of inflammation; often raised during active disease but may be normal.
  • Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP — typically negative, helping to distinguish AS from rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Full blood count and other tests — to assess anaemia of chronic disease and to exclude other causes of back pain.

(b) Imaging

  • Plain radiography of the sacroiliac joints — the first-line investigation; graded by the modified New York criteria (grade 0 normal to grade 4 ankylosis). Definite radiographic sacroiliitis is bilateral grade 2 or unilateral grade 3–4; its specificity is high but sensitivity is low in early disease.
  • Plain radiography of the spine — shows squaring of vertebral bodies, syndesmophytes, ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament and the bamboo-spine appearance.
  • MRI of the sacroiliac joints — the most sensitive test for early disease. An "ASAS-positive MRI" requires bone-marrow oedema (osteitis) clearly present in the subchondral bone on a fluid-sensitive (STIR or fat-suppressed T2) sequence, highly suggestive of spondyloarthritis.
  • CT — useful for detailed structural change where radiography is equivocal.
  • Ultrasound — can detect peripheral enthesitis and synovitis.

(c) Classification and clinical measures

  • ASAS classification criteria for axial spondyloarthritis combine inflammatory back pain of more than three months beginning before age 45 with either an imaging arm (radiographic or MRI sacroiliitis plus one clinical feature) or a clinical arm (HLA-B27 plus two clinical features).
  • BASDAI (disease activity), BASFI (function), BASMI (metrology/spinal mobility) and ASDAS (a composite disease-activity score) are the validated measures used to monitor the disease and response to treatment.

(d) Differential diagnosis — mechanical back pain, disc herniation, osteitis condensans ilii, and other spondyloarthritides (psoriatic, reactive, enteropathic).

5Recent advances

  • Rudwaleit et al. (2009) — the ASAS classification criteria, together with the ASAS MRI definition of active sacroiliitis (updated 2016 by the ASAS MRI working group), established the concept of non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis and made early diagnosis possible, and remains the major international classification framework.
  • Dagfinrud et al. (2008) — a Cochrane review of physiotherapy for ankylosing spondylitis found an individualised home-based or supervised exercise programme is better than no intervention, supervised group physiotherapy is better than home exercise, and combined inpatient spa-exercise followed by group physiotherapy is best.
  • Gravaldi et al. (2022) — a systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials showed supervised physiotherapy improved disease activity (BASDAI) and functional capacity (BASFI) versus usual care in ankylosing spondylitis, though it was not superior to home exercise.
  • Zhang et al. (2024) — a meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials showed exercise therapy improved BASFI, BASMI, BASDAI, ASDAS, 6-minute walk distance, pain and fatigue in axial spondyloarthritis, confirming exercise as a core, measurable physiotherapy outcome domain.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St Louis: Elsevier; 2021.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.

Question 7 · 10 marks

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative management following fracture of the tibial plateau.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 7 – Postoperative assessment and rehabilitation of the knee

★ Memory hook — "Protect the plateau, then Move, then Load, then Strengthen, then Function."

1Introduction

Tibial plateau fractures are intra-articular fractures of the proximal tibia, most often caused by a high-energy axial or valgus force in road-traffic accidents or a low-energy fall in older patients. They are classified by the Schatzker (I–VI) and AO/OTA systems. Because the fracture involves the weight-bearing articular surface, treatment aims to restore joint congruity, alignment and stability, usually by open reduction and internal fixation. Postoperative physiotherapy is decisive for the final outcome: the goals are to protect the fixation while preventing the complications of immobilisation — stiffness, muscle atrophy, venous thromboembolism and loss of function — and to restore range, strength, proprioception and gait.

2Physiology

The knee is a modified hinge joint whose stability depends on the tibial plateau, menisci, cruciate and collateral ligaments and the quadriceps mechanism. The articular hyaline cartilage tolerates compression only within normal joint congruity; even small step-offs increase local contact stresses. The menisci distribute load and the quadriceps and hamstrings control the joint. Normal knee range is 0 degrees of extension to about 135 degrees of flexion. The patellofemoral and tibiofemoral joints must glide freely for normal movement. Preserving these relationships after fracture is the physiological aim of rehabilitation.

3Pathophysiology

An intra-articular fracture disrupts the articular surface, and depressed or comminuted fragments cause joint incongruity and malalignment. If this is not corrected, abnormal contact stresses lead to post-traumatic osteoarthritis. Surgery restores congruity but the fixation must be protected while bone heals, because early excessive loading risks loss of reduction and implant failure. Immobilisation, in turn, causes joint stiffness, capsular contracture, muscle atrophy, cartilage degeneration and venous stasis. The postoperative period is therefore a balance between protecting the repair and mobilising the joint — the central tension in rehabilitation after tibial plateau fracture.

4Answer

Postoperative management is staged and guided by the surgeon's weight-bearing prescription and fracture type:

  1. Phase 1 – Protection (week 0–2): control pain and swelling (elevation, cryotherapy), prevent venous thromboembolism (ankle pumps, anticoagulation, early mobility), maintain patellar mobility, and begin isometric quadriceps and hamstring exercises. The limb is often protected in a brace; weight-bearing is usually toe-touch or non-weight-bearing. Continuous passive motion or assisted range exercises may be used as permitted.
  2. Phase 2 – Early motion (week 2–6): progressive active-assisted and active range of motion of the knee, aiming to restore full extension and improve flexion; continue quadriceps and hamstring strengthening; begin closed-chain exercises within the prescribed weight-bearing limit. Immobilisation appears to offer no benefit over early protected motion.
  3. Phase 3 – Weight-bearing progression (week 6–12): advance weight-bearing as directed — often partial weight-bearing from about 6–8 weeks and full weight-bearing by about 9–12 weeks, later for high-energy or comminuted (Schatzker IV–VI) fractures. Gait re-education, balance and proprioceptive training are introduced.
  4. Phase 4 – Strengthening and function (week 12 onwards): progressive resistance training, eccentric quadriceps work, closed-chain and functional exercises, stair and hill training, and return to work and sport. Ongoing rehabilitation with emphasis on quadriceps strength and proprioception is recommended.
  5. Monitoring: assess pain, swelling, range of motion, muscle power, gait and function with tools such as the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score or the Oxford Knee Score, and monitor radiographs for loss of reduction, delayed union or osteoarthritis.

Complications to watch: knee stiffness, loss of reduction, infection, deep vein thrombosis, delayed or non-union, and post-traumatic osteoarthritis.

5Recent advances

  • Iliopoulos & Galanis (2020) — a systematic review of physiotherapy after tibial plateau fracture fixation concluded that early range-of-motion exercise and early weight-bearing should be encouraged, that immobilisation confers no benefit, and that ongoing quadriceps and proprioceptive rehabilitation is important.
  • Canton et al. (2022) — a systematic review found that early weight-bearing after internal fixation showed comparable complication rates (loss of reduction, mechanical failure, delayed healing) to restricted weight-bearing, with possible benefits in faster recovery.
  • Arnold et al. (2017) — a scoping review of 124 studies found that postoperative care most commonly involved 4–6 weeks of non-weight-bearing followed by partial weight-bearing, with full weight-bearing typically at 9–12 weeks, later for complex (Schatzker IV–VI) fractures.
  • Mohamed et al. (2019) — a randomised trial found that adding early weight-bearing from postoperative day 3 to conventional physiotherapy for Schatzker type II tibial plateau fractures was as safe as delayed weight-bearing (no difference in fracture stability or range of motion) and avoided the complications of prolonged immobilisation.
  • Ibrahim et al. (2025) — a randomised trial of 45 patients found immediate weight-bearing as tolerated after ORIF (Schatzker I–IV) gave better 6-month clinical outcomes (pain, walking capacity, knee range of motion) with no difference in radiological measures, supporting accelerated rehabilitation.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2018.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  3. Arnold JB, Tu CG, Phan TM, et al. Characteristics of postoperative weight bearing and management protocols for tibial plateau fractures: findings from a scoping review. Injury. 2017;48(12):2634–2642.
  4. Physiotherapy after tibial plateau fracture fixation: a systematic review of the literature. SAGE Open Med. 2020;8:2050312120969318.
  5. Early weight bearing in tibial plateau fractures treated with ORIF: a review of the literature. J Orthop Surg Res. 2022;17:278.
  6. Williamson MJ, Iliopoulos E, Jain A, et al. Immediate weight bearing after plate fixation of fractures of the tibial plateau. Injury. 2018;49(10):1886–1890.
Question 8 · 10 marks

Q8. Describe in detail the assessment following above knee amputation.

Read this answer in plain English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 8 – Assessment and prosthetic screening of the amputee

★ Memory hook — "Assess the L-I-M-B-S: Limb (residual), Impairments, Mobility, Balance, Skin/socket."

1Introduction

Above-knee (transfemoral) amputation removes the limb above the knee, most often for peripheral vascular disease or diabetes in older patients and for trauma or tumour in younger patients. Assessment after transfemoral amputation is a comprehensive process that characterises the residual limb, the whole person's impairments and functional capacity, and the suitability for and fit of a prosthesis. It is not a single examination but a structured evaluation that determines rehabilitation goals, prosthetic prescription (including the Medicare functional K-level) and outcome measurement. A thorough baseline assessment allows realistic goal-setting, safe prosthetic fitting and objective monitoring of progress.

2Physiology

After transfemoral amputation the residual limb retains the hip joint and the hip musculature, but the knee and ankle are lost. Normal residual-limb function depends on good hip abductor and extensor strength to control the pelvis and the prosthesis, a well-healed, conical, non-oedematous limb of adequate length, an intact and pain-free skin envelope, and maintained hip range of motion. The hip abductors and extensors are the principal motors of a transfemoral prosthetic gait, and the sound limb bears most of the load, so its health is critical. Normal socket function depends on a stable, comfortable interface that transmits load without shear or pressure injury.

3Pathophysiology

Amputation produces several predictable impairments. The residual limb may be oedematous, tender, scarred or adherent, and may have neuromas or heterotopic ossification. Postoperative immobilisation and pain predispose to a hip flexion and abduction contracture, which compromises prosthetic alignment and gait. Phantom limb sensation and phantom limb pain are common. The sound limb, the spine and the upper limbs are subjected to increased load, risking osteoarthritis, back pain and overuse injury. Vascular or diabetic disease may compromise wound healing and skin integrity. Reduced balance and cardiopulmonary reserve limit walking distance. Each of these must be identified during assessment because each influences prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation.

4Answer

The assessment covers the following domains:

  1. History: cause and date of amputation, surgical technique, comorbidities (diabetes, vascular disease, cardiac disease), medications, smoking, occupation, home environment and goals.
  2. Residual limb inspection: length and shape (conical/cylindrical), scars, skin condition, oedema, volume stability, adhesions, neuromas, heterotopic ossification and any wound.
  3. Range of motion: hip flexion, extension, abduction and rotation — specifically look for flexion and abduction contractures.
  4. Muscle strength: hip abductors, extensors, flexors and knee (sound limb) power, using manual muscle testing or dynamometry.
  5. Sensation and pain: residual-limb sensation, phantom sensation and phantom limb pain, using a visual analogue scale or the Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire.
  6. Balance and mobility: static and dynamic balance, transfers, and gait with or without a prosthesis; assess the ability to walk and to use assistive devices.
  7. Functional level: assign the Medicare functional classification level (K-level 0–4), which guides prosthetic prescription.
  8. Prosthetic fit: socket comfort and fit (Socket Comfort Score), suspension, alignment and skin response to wearing the prosthesis.
  9. Outcome measures: Amputee Mobility Predictor, Timed Up and Go, Two-Minute Walk Test, Six-Minute Walk Test, Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire, Prosthetic Limb Users Survey of Mobility, Trinity Amputation and Prosthesis Experience Scales–Revised, and a generic quality-of-life measure.
  10. Psychosocial and cardiopulmonary: mood, adjustment, motivation, and exercise tolerance for prosthetic ambulation.

5Recent advances

  • ISPO COMPASS (2023) — the Consensus Outcome Measures for Prosthetic and Amputation Services recommends a standard set (Amputee Mobility Predictor, Timed Up and Go, Two-Minute Walk Test, and the Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire utility and residual-limb-health subscales, plus the Trinity scales) for routine use before and after prosthetic care.
  • COMPASS+ — adds the Comprehensive High-Level Activity Mobility Predictor and the Six-Minute Walk Test for highly active individuals.
  • Hanspal et al. (2003) — developed and validated the Socket Comfort Score, while Gailey et al. (2019) developed the Comprehensive Lower-limb Amputee Socket Survey (CLASS); both are increasingly used to quantify socket fit and comfort objectively.
  • Gailey et al. (2020) — a pilot randomised controlled trial showed the Evidence-Based Amputee Rehabilitation (EBAR) programme significantly improved functional mobility (Amputee Mobility Predictor with and without prosthesis and 6-minute walk distance) in people with transtibial amputation who had already completed standard rehabilitation.
  • Kurtaran & Çelik (2024) — a randomised controlled trial found telerehabilitation-based structured exercise was superior to home exercise alone for gait, muscle strength, balance confidence, prosthesis satisfaction and quality of life in unilateral transtibial amputation.

6References

  1. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2019.
  2. Dutton M. Dutton's Orthopaedic Examination, Evaluation, and Intervention. 5th ed. New York: McGraw-Hill; 2020.
  3. International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics. Lower-limb COMPASS: Consensus Outcome Measures for Prosthetic and Amputation Services. 2023.
  4. Gailey RS, Roach KE, Applegate EB, et al. The Amputee Mobility Predictor: an instrument to assess determinants of the lower-limb amputee's ability to ambulate. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 2002;83(5):613–627.
  5. Selecting, administering, and interpreting outcome measures among adults with lower-limb loss: an update. J Prosthet Orthot. 2020;32(4):252–262.
  6. Legro MW, Reiber GE, Smith DG, et al. Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire for persons with lower limb amputations. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. 1998;79(8):931–938.
Question 9 · 10 marks

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for low back pain.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 9 – Outcome measurement in spinal pain

★ Memory hook — "Measure low back pain across P-D-P-Q-G: Pain, Disability, Psychosocial, Quality of life, Global change."

1Introduction

Low back pain (LBP) is the leading cause of years lived with disability worldwide and is a biopsychosocial condition in which pain, physical limitation and psychological factors interact. Outcome measures are the standardised tools used to quantify the patient's status at baseline and to detect change after intervention. Because LBP is multidimensional, a single measure is never sufficient: a comprehensive evaluation combines pain intensity, condition-specific disability, psychosocial risk, quality of life and a global rating of change, supplemented where appropriate by performance-based tests. Choosing measures with known reliability, validity and responsiveness, and knowing their minimal clinically important difference, allows the physiotherapist to justify treatment, monitor progress and make defensible discharge decisions.

2Physiology

The normal lumbar spine transmits load between the trunk and pelvis, protects the neural elements and provides a balance between stability and mobility through the coordinated action of the deep and superficial trunk muscles, the discs, the facet joints and the ligaments. Normal function is characterised by pain-free, symmetrical movement, normal endurance of the trunk stabilisers and the capacity to tolerate the physical demands of daily life and work. Outcome measures of pain and disability are anchored to this normal baseline, with lower scores denoting better function.

3Pathophysiology

LBP arises from nociceptive, neuropathic and central mechanisms. Nociceptive pain comes from discs, facets, muscles or ligaments; neuropathic pain from nerve-root compression or irritation; and central sensitisation amplifies pain in chronic states. Psychological factors — catastrophising, fear-avoidance, distress and low self-efficacy — strongly predict chronicity and are as important to measure as the physical impairment. This multidimensional pathophysiology is why outcome measurement in LBP must span pain, function and psychosocial domains.

4Answer

Outcome measures for LBP fall into several categories:

  • Pain intensity: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Numerical Rating Scale (NRS); the McGill Pain Questionnaire for pain quality.
  • Condition-specific disability/function: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI, 0–100 per cent), Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ, 0–24), and the Quebec Back Pain Disability Scale.
  • Psychosocial risk and beliefs: STarT Back Screening Tool (prognostic stratification), Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire, Pain Catastrophising Scale, Orebro Musculoskeletal Pain Questionnaire, and measures of depression/anxiety (PHQ-9, GAD-7).
  • Health-related quality of life: Short Form-36 or SF-12, EuroQol EQ-5D.
  • Global change: Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC).
  • Performance-based: lumbar range of motion, trunk endurance (Biering-Sorensen, plank tests), walking distance and the 6-minute walk test, and sit-to-stand tests.

A useful comparison of the two most common disability measures:

FeatureOswestry Disability IndexRoland-Morris Disability Questionnaire
Items / scoring10 sections; score 0–100 per cent24 yes/no items; score 0–24
FocusActivities of daily living and severityPhysical function/activity limitation
Best suited toModerate–severe and chronic LBPMild–moderate LBP
MCID (approx.)10 points or 30 per cent2–3 points or 30 per cent

Recommended minimum set for routine practice: an NRS/VAS for pain, the ODI or RMDQ for disability, the STarT Back Tool for prognosis, and the PGIC for global change, with the choice guided by the patient's presentation and the purpose of measurement. The STarT Back Tool stratifies patients into low, medium and high risk and matches them to appropriate care; the ODI and RMDQ should not be used interchangeably.

5Recent advances

  • Hill et al. (2011) — reviews of stratified care using the STarT Back Tool show that benefits depend heavily on faithful implementation (matching patients to the recommended treatment), and that many later trials failed to replicate the original positive results of the STarT Back trial.
  • Lemmers et al. (2024) — a prospective cohort study found a medium or high STarT Back risk score predicted higher baseline disability, a different recovery trajectory and poorer 12-month disability on the ODI.
  • Kersten et al. (2021) — confirmed the ODI and RMDQ are not interchangeable and cannot be converted into one another, so a service should standardise on one.
  • Ostelo et al. (2008) — an international consensus emphasised the minimal clinically important change (about 30 per cent improvement from baseline) as the benchmark for interpreting change.
  • Psychologically informed physiotherapy — guided by psychosocial screening tools, is now recommended for high-risk LBP to prevent chronicity.

6References

  1. Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 7th ed. St Louis: Elsevier; 2021.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2019.
  3. Hill JC, Dunn KM, Lewis M, et al. A primary care back pain screening tool: identifying patient subgroups for initial treatment (STarT Back). Arthritis Rheum. 2008;59(5):632–641.
  4. Hill JC, Whitehurst DGT, Lewis M, et al. Comparison of stratified primary care management for low back pain with current best practice (STarT Back): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2011;378(9802):1560–1571.
  5. Chiarotto A, Maxwell LJ, Terwee CB, et al. Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire and Oswestry Disability Index: which has better measurement properties for measuring physical functioning in nonspecific low back pain? Phys Ther. 2016;96(10):1620–1637.
  6. Evaluating the STarT Back stratified treatment approach for low back pain: a literature review. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2024;25:511.
Question 10 · 10 marks

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total knee replacement.

Read this answer in simple English →

SYLLABUSPaper III, Unit 10 – Pre- and postoperative evaluation and screening for arthroplasty

★ Memory hook — "Fitness for TKR is H-E-A-R-T-S: History, Exercise capacity, Anaemia, Risk (cardiac), Thrombosis risk, Screening & function."

1Introduction

Total knee replacement (TKR) is offered to adults with advanced knee arthritis when pain and disability are no longer controlled by conservative care. Fitness evaluation around TKR has two complementary purposes. The first is preoperative fitness assessment — determining whether the patient is medically and functionally fit to undergo anaesthesia and surgery, and optimising modifiable risk factors to reduce complications. The second is postoperative evaluation of fitness — judging whether the patient is fit to progress through rehabilitation, to bear weight, to be discharged and to return to activity. Both are structured, criteria-based processes that combine medical risk assessment with functional and psychological evaluation, and both rely on objective, validated tools rather than impression alone.

2Physiology

Undergoing and recovering from TKR demands physiological reserve. The heart must tolerate the stress of surgery and of early mobilisation, the lungs must maintain oxygenation, the blood must carry sufficient oxygen (adequate haemoglobin), and the renal, endocrine and coagulation systems must remain stable. Functionally, the patient needs adequate quadriceps and hip strength, a stable and balanced gait, sufficient range of knee motion for walking and transfers, and enough aerobic capacity to walk and exercise. Normal knee function after TKR approximates 0 degrees of extension to about 110–120 degrees of flexion, with good quadriceps control. These physiological requirements define the targets of fitness evaluation.

3Pathophysiology

Adults awaiting TKR often carry comorbidities — ischaemic heart disease, hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, obesity, chronic lung disease and venous thromboembolism risk — that increase the chance of perioperative complications such as myocardial infarction, stroke, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, infection and delayed wound healing. Reduced preoperative fitness and functional capacity are independently associated with slower recovery, longer hospital stay and poorer outcomes. Postoperatively, stiffness, quadriceps weakness, poor balance and cardiopulmonary deconditioning limit the ability to mobilise safely. Fitness evaluation targets these mechanisms so that risk can be quantified and modified before surgery and progress can be judged safely afterwards.

4Answer

(a) Preoperative fitness evaluation

  1. Cardiovascular risk assessment: structured evaluation of venous thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk factors (history of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia and stroke) within 30 days of surgery. For patients aged 65 or older, those aged 45–64 with significant cardiovascular disease, or those with a Revised Cardiac Risk Index of one or more, measurement of BNP or NT-proBNP is recommended to refine risk.
  2. Functional capacity screening: screen all patients with a validated tool such as the Duke Activity Status Index, Godin-Shephard questionnaire or International Physical Activity Questionnaire. Reduced capacity warrants objective assessment — cardiopulmonary exercise testing is the gold standard, with simpler alternatives (incremental shuttle walk test, 6-minute walk test, one-minute sit-to-stand, Timed Up and Go) where it is unavailable.
  3. Comorbidity optimisation: control of diabetes, hypertension, anaemia, heart failure, lung disease, renal and liver impairment, and sleep-disordered breathing; review of opioids and dependency-forming drugs; and referral of complex chronic-pain patients to a pain team.
  4. Thrombosis and infection risk: assess venous thromboembolism risk and screen for active infection or colonisation (including dental and skin sources) before implantation.
  5. Nutrition, obesity and smoking: identify modifiable factors; a body mass index threshold is often used to prompt referral to weight management, and smoking cessation is advised.
  6. Psychological and educational assessment: screen for anxiety and depression and provide pre-operative education and prehabilitation to set realistic expectations and improve outcomes.

(b) Postoperative fitness evaluation for progression and discharge

  1. Medical stability: stable vital signs, controlled pain, no signs of infection, DVT or pulmonary embolism, adequate wound healing and haemoglobin.
  2. Functional criteria: ability to perform safe transfers and to mobilise with the prescribed aid, independent or assisted ambulation, and adequate knee extension and flexion for function.
  3. Strength and balance: sufficient quadriceps control and standing balance for safe walking and stair use.
  4. Wound and skin: clean, dry, healing wound and no skin breakdown.
  5. Outcome measures: Oxford Knee Score or Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score, knee range of motion, quadriceps strength, Timed Up and Go and 6-minute walk test to document function.
  6. Education and self-management: competence with home exercises, precautions and recognition of warning signs.

5Recent advances

  • UK Centre for Perioperative Care (2021) — guidance established that all surgical candidates should be screened for reduced functional capacity with a validated tool such as the Duke Activity Status Index, and that improving fitness before surgery (prehabilitation) reduces complications and length of stay.
  • Anderson et al. (2021) — a UK modified Delphi consensus produced recommendations for pre-operative TKR education and prehabilitation, including exercise, weight management and psychological support.
  • Nguyen et al. (2022) — a landmark multicentre randomised trial (EDEX, 262 patients) found that multidisciplinary prehabilitation before TKR did not improve short-term functional independence or midterm activity limitations versus usual care, tempering claims for routine prehabilitation although uptake of the intervention was low.
  • Konnyu et al. (2022) — a systematic review of 13 TKA trials found prehabilitation may increase strength and reduce length of stay (low certainty) without added harms, but has little effect on pain, range of motion or activities of daily living.
  • Wu et al. (2026) — a network meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials found prehabilitation effects are outcome-specific: resistance training best improved functional reserve (Timed Up and Go, quadriceps strength), neuromuscular and aerobic training best reduced pain, and multimodal exercise best improved knee flexion range of motion.

6References

  1. Kisner C, Colby LA. Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2018.
  2. O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ, Fulk GD. Physical Rehabilitation. 7th ed. Philadelphia: FA Davis; 2019.
  3. Centre for Perioperative Care. Preoperative Assessment and Optimisation for Adult Surgery. London: CPOC; 2021.
  4. Halvorsen S, Mehilli J, Cassese S, et al. 2022 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular assessment and management of patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery. Eur Heart J. 2022;43(39):3826–3924.
  5. Consensus on pre-operative total knee replacement education and prehabilitation recommendations: a UK-based modified Delphi study. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2021;22:352.
  6. Duceppe E, Parlow J, MacDonald P, et al. Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines on perioperative cardiac risk assessment and management for patients who undergo noncardiac surgery. Can J Cardiol. 2017;33(1):17–32.

Quantitative claims across all papers were re-verified against published sources (PubMed, WHO/ACSM/Cochrane, JOSPT) in a dedicated fact-check pass, and fifteen errors found were corrected in this version — then re-checked line-by-line against the prescribed textbooks themselves: Nordin & Frankel (Basic Biomechanics), Levangie & Norkin (Joint Structure and Function, 6th ed.) and Mulligan (Manual Therapy: NAGS, SNAGS, MWMS).

Exam mode: a 3-hour timed simulation per paper with autosaved notes and self-marking against the evaluator's scheme; scores stay on your device.

Study tools (this edition): Attempt-first (paper view jump bar) hides every model answer until you tap “reveal” — read the question and its marking scheme, attempt it on paper, then compare. The ★ button on each question stars it for the Revise starred questions list — a personal weak-list for spaced revision, saved on this device. Memory-hook boxes flag mnemonics and must-remember numbers on the highest-yield answers. Viva rapid-fire drills 67 one-liner facts drawn from the last-hour sheets and glossary — answer aloud, then flip. Quantitative claims were re-verified in this edition against published sources (PubMed/PMC, ACR criteria papers, WHO/ACSM). Shared and maintained by @fysio.in on Instagram (DM for access). The official RGUHS topic-weightage blueprint (2021-22 batch onwards) is built in — home screen “RGUHS blueprint” — showing expected questions per topic for all four papers. All 62 case-form answers now follow the institution’s Orthopedic Physiotherapy Evaluation Form exactly — subjective examination; objective examination with observation, palpation, motor, sensory, functional (FIM), gait, balance, hand-function and coordination sub-parts; investigations; special tests with explicit positive/negative results; a three-part problem list (impairment / functional limitation / disability); functional diagnosis; short- and long-term goals; treatment plan; and home programme — after a word-by-word multi-agent review of every answer.
