110 marks

Q1. Describe the role of assessment in diagnosis.

Full answer →

Show assessment as a reasoning process (history, hypotheses, tests, diagnosis, reassessment), not a list of tests.

  • What earns marks: Present the answer as a process — history, then hypotheses, then tests, then diagnosis, then reassessment · Use the words 'hypothesis' and 'differential' and actually apply them · Link every finding to the ICF (body function, activity, participation).
  • Definition: Assessment is the systematic collection of data about a patient's status.
  • Definition: Diagnosis is the label you reach after interpreting that data.
  • PT diagnosis: In physiotherapy, assessment ends in a physiotherapy (movement-system) diagnosis — a cluster of signs and symptoms naming the dysfunction the therapist is trained to treat.
  • Example: e.g. 'subacromial impingement with scapular dyskinesis'.
  • Link to medical diagnosis: The PT diagnosis is separate from, but always linked to, the medical diagnosis.
  • Subjective (history): demographic data, chief complaint (onset, location, duration, aggravating/easing factors), pain behaviour (24-hour pattern), functional limits, past history, medications, and red/yellow-flag screening.
  • Key fact: The history alone steers about 80% of the hypothesis list.
  • Objective examination: observation (posture, deformity, gait), palpation, active/passive and accessory ROM (PPIVMs, PAIVMs), strength (MMT), joint mobility and special tests, neuro screening (dermatomes, myotomes, DTRs), and functional measures.
  • Hypothesis-oriented process: Good assessment is not a checklist but a hypothetico-deductive cycle.
  • Steps: generate competing hypotheses from the history, design tests to confirm or refute each, commit to a working diagnosis, and reassess after each treatment.
  • Reference: This is Jones & Rivett's clinical-reasoning model.
  • ICF mapping: findings map to body structure/function (e.g. restricted flexion, weak abductors), activity (can't squat) and participation (can't work as a farmer).
  • Purpose of mapping: it defines both the treatment targets and the outcome measures used for reassessment.
  • Assessment does five things: (i) establishes a baseline, (ii) enables differential diagnosis and red-flag screening for referral, (iii) guides treatment selection, (iv) measures change, and (v) gives the legal/professional documentation of autonomous practice.
  • Safety: red flags are screened at EVERY step.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 1 & 6.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (syllabus reference 4).
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function. (reference 2)
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. (standard clinical-reasoning text)
210 marks

Q2. Describe the screening of neck following C3-C4 disc prolapse.

Full answer →

Anchor every neurological line to C3/C4 — the high-collar dermatome, the shrug myotome, and 'no C4 reflex, test C5/C6'.

  • What earns marks: Anchor every neurological finding to C3/C4 — a generic neck exam loses marks · Draw the C3-C4 'high-collar' dermatome map with the myotome, reflex and special tests beside it · Name the red flags and finish with a clear conclusion.
  • Core idea: A C3-C4 prolapse usually compresses the C4 nerve root.
  • Pain pattern: pain in the suboccipital/neck region radiating to the shoulder cap and clavicular area (C4 dermatome — a 'high-collar' distribution).
  • C3 referral: C3 gives occipital/sub-occipital referral.
  • History: ask about onset, trauma, posture/occupation (e.g. prolonged laptop flexion), and night pain.
  • Red flags: myelopathy signs (gait change, hand clumsiness, bowel/bladder), fever, weight loss, trauma.
  • Observation: forward head posture, loss of cervical lordosis, antalgic tilt.
  • Palpation: paraspinal muscle spasm/guarding, segmental tenderness at the C3-C4 level, upper trapezius trigger points.
  • ROM: flexion/extension, side-flexion, rotation — look for painful arcs and a capsular vs non-capsular pattern.
  • Provocation: extension combined with ipsilateral rotation reproduces radicular symptoms in the affected dermatome.
  • Segmental mobility: central and unilateral posterior-anterior glides (PAIVMs) at C3-C4 for stiffness vs pain; intersegmental movement testing (PPIVMs).
  • Myotome C4: scapular elevation (shoulder shrug) and diaphragm (C3-C5) — 'C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive'; test the resisted shrug.
  • Reflex: there is no pure C4 DTR — test the biceps jerk (C5) and brachioradialis (C6) to exclude adjacent-root involvement.
  • Sensation: pinprick/light touch over the neck, clavicle and upper shoulder cap.
  • Also: complete the upper-limb screen for a broader deficit pattern.
  • Special tests: Spurling's test (extension + ipsilateral rotation + axial compression — radicular reproduction).
  • Special tests: cervical distraction (relief is confirmatory), shoulder-abduction (bakery) relief sign, and ULNT/neurodynamic testing for mechanosensitivity.
  • Special tests: Hoffman's test for myelopathy; quadriceps/Babinski if cord signs are suspected.
  • Close: integrate findings into a working PT diagnosis and baseline (NDI — Neck Disability Index).
  • Close: refer urgently for MRI if myelopathy or red flags appear.

Myotome ladder: C5 abduct, C6 wrist extend, C7 elbow extend, C8 finger flex, T1 finger abduct; Spurling (compression) pairs with distraction (relief).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2a.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. Elsevier (reference 4) — cervical spine chapter.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1)
310 marks

Q3. Describe the screening of upper back for fibromyalgia.

Full answer →

State both criteria sets (ACR 1990 tender-point count and ACR 2010 WPI + SSS) and quote the 4 kg thumb pressure.

  • What earns marks: Quote BOTH criteria sets — the ACR 1990 tender-point count AND the ACR 2010/2016 WPI + SSS · Give the exact numbers — 18 sites, about 4 kg thumb pressure, 11 or more positive · Contrast a myofascial trigger point with a fibromyalgia tender point.
  • Definition: Fibromyalgia is chronic widespread pain (axial + bilateral, above and below the waist) for more than 3 months, with fatigue, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive symptoms.
  • ACR 1990: 11 or more of 18 tender points on about 4 kg thumb pressure.
  • ACR 2010/2016 revision: Widespread Pain Index (0-19) + Symptom Severity Scale — usable without a tender-point count.
  • History: female predominance (7:1), ages 30-50.
  • History: pain 'all over' and migrating; sleep disturbance, morning stiffness over 30 min, irritable bowel/bladder, mood symptoms; and no mechanical relieving postures.
  • Observation: often normal posture but 'hurting everywhere' on light touch; guarded, protective posturing.
  • Palpation — 9 paired sites (4 in/around the upper trunk): suboccipital muscle insertions, low-cervical (C5-C7) interspinous ligaments, mid-upper trapezius, and supraspinatus at the medial scapular border.
  • Complete the set with: 2nd rib costochondral junctions, lateral epicondyles, gluteal and greater-trochanteric sites — 18 sites in total.
  • Technique: thumb pressure of about 4 kg; positive when the patient winces (the 'jump sign').
  • ROM & chest: thoracic mobility, chest expansion (normal 5 cm or more — markedly restricted suggests ankylosing spondylitis, not fibromyalgia), and scapulothoracic rhythm.
  • Differential: myofascial trigger points are local, with a taut band and reproducible referral — fibromyalgia points are systemic tender points with no taut band.
  • Differential: also rule out hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica (age over 50, raised ESR), inflammatory arthritis, and cervical/thoracic spondylosis.
  • Central sensitisation: screen for allodynia to light touch.
  • Quantify: use the FIQR (Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire) and a pain diagram.
  • Conclusion: document a body map of positive sites and score the FIQR for baseline.
  • Conclusion: coordinate a multidisciplinary plan — education, graded aerobic exercise, and sleep and stress management; physiotherapy is a cornerstone of fibromyalgia management.

Fibromyalgia numbers: ACR 1990 — 18 sites, 4 kg pressure, 11 or more needed; ACR 2016 — WPI + SSS, no palpation. Trigger point = taut band (local); tender point = systemic (central sensitisation).

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 2.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4).
  • Wolfe F et al. The American College of Rheumatology 1990 / 2010/2016 criteria for fibromyalgia. Arthritis Rheum / Semin Arthritis Rheum. (primary)
  • McCarty DJ, Koopman WJ. Arthritis and Allied Conditions. (syllabus reference 11).
410 marks

Q4. Describe the importance of direct access in Physiotherapy.

Full answer →

Balance importance across patient, profession and system, then add the safeguards — never celebrate autonomy without red-flag screening.

  • What earns marks: Cover three angles — importance for the patient, the profession and the health system · Always add the safeguard paragraph (red-flag screening and referral criteria) — autonomy alone reads as naive · Mention both the global and the Indian scenario.
  • Definition: Direct access means patients may seek physiotherapy assessment and treatment without a physician's referral.
  • Role: the physiotherapist acts as a first-contact, autonomous practitioner in a primary-care musculoskeletal service.
  • Self-referral: patient self-referral is the operational form of direct access.
  • Importance — earlier treatment: no waiting for referral; early intervention in acute LBP/ankle sprain improves outcomes and prevents chronicity.
  • Importance — cost-effectiveness: studies (US military, UK NHS self-referral pilots) show fewer physician visits, imaging and medication without worse outcomes.
  • Importance — professional autonomy: recognises the physiotherapist's competence to diagnose within scope, screen for red flags and refer appropriately.
  • Autonomy detail: it is the foundation of the 'doctor of physiotherapy' and primary-spine-care models.
  • Importance — patient choice & satisfaction: shorter care pathways, fewer consultations, and better access in underserved areas.
  • Importance — system decongestion: frees physician time for complex disease; in India, it addresses the specialist-burden crisis.
  • Global scenario: direct access is legal in 50+ US states, the UK, Australia, the Netherlands and much of the EU.
  • Indian scenario: it remains partial — some states' practice and the IAP support autonomous practice, but referral culture, insurance rules and Clinical Establishments Act implementation vary.
  • Indian view: it is an evolving frontier for the profession.
  • Responsibility — competence: first-contact practitioners must be competent in differential diagnosis and red-flag screening (cancer, fracture, infection, visceral referral).
  • Responsibility — safeguards: maintain strict referral criteria, indemnity insurance, meticulous documentation and continuing competency.
  • Key line: autonomy is earned by clinical rigour, not demanded.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 3 (a-d).
  • World Physiotherapy (2011/2019) policy statement — Description of physiotherapy / direct access and patient self-referral.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
510 marks

Q5. A 30-year-old female comes with a history of ankle injury. Describe the various special tests for the ankle.

Full answer →

Cluster the tests by structure (lateral ligaments, syndesmosis, medial, tendon/fracture) and keep the exact angles and translation values.

  • What earns marks: Cluster the tests by structure — lateral ligaments, then syndesmosis, then medial, then tendon/fracture screen · Give the exact positions — drawer in 10-15 degrees plantarflexion for ATFL, and 90 degrees for CFL in talar tilt · Say that acute-day testing is unreliable; tests are more reliable at day 4-5.
  • Background: a 30-year-old woman with an inversion injury most likely sprains the lateral ligament complex.
  • Order of injury: anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) first, then calcaneofibular (CFL), rarely posterior talofibular (PTFL).
  • Grades: Grade I (stretch), II (partial), III (complete).
  • Timing: acutely, effusion and pain limit testing — examinations are more reliable at day 4-5.
  • Anterior drawer (ATFL): patient prone/supine, foot relaxed in about 10-15 degrees plantarflexion.
  • Anterior drawer technique: one hand stabilises the tibia while the other draws the talus forward on the fibula.
  • Anterior drawer positive: more than 4-5 mm anterior translation (or a clunk/soft end-feel) suggests ATFL rupture.
  • Talar-tilt (inversion stress) for CFL: foot at 90 degrees, invert the talus in the mortise; compare sides.
  • Talar-tilt positive: more than 5-10 degrees asymmetry or a soft end-feel indicates CFL injury.
  • Squeeze test: squeeze at the mid-calf; cross-over pain helps localise ligament territory.
  • Syndesmosis — calf/squeeze test: compress the fibula against the tibia at mid-calf; distal syndesmotic pain is positive.
  • Syndesmosis — external rotation (Kleiger) test: stabilise the leg, dorsiflex + externally rotate the foot — gives syndesmotic and deltoid pain.
  • Syndesmosis — Cotton (fibular translation) test: anteroposterior fibular glide; plus the point-toe (plantarflex-external rotation) test.
  • Deltoid ligament (eversion stress): medial pain/valgus laxity; implies possible syndesmosis/fracture.
  • Ottawa ankle rules (fracture triage, not laxity): X-ray if pain over the malleolar zone plus bone tenderness over the posterior edge/tip, or inability to bear weight 4 steps.
  • Also: Thompson/Simmonds test for an intact Achilles, anterior impingement test, and a peroneal-tendon subluxation screen.
  • Conclusion: grade the sprain and baseline the patient with the FAAM/Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool.

Ankle ligament tests: plantarflexion, then ATFL (drawer); 90 degrees, then CFL (talar tilt); syndesmosis trio = Squeeze, Kleiger, Cotton.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4b.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — ankle & foot chapter.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. (reference 1) — ankle biomechanics.
  • Stiell IG et al. Ottawa ankle rules. JAMA. 1993 (primary, for triage).
610 marks

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for osteoporosis.

Full answer →

Cover DEXA (with sites L1-L4 + hip), FRAX, other imaging and labs — and keep the -1 / -2.5 cutoffs exact.

  • What earns marks: Name the DEXA sites — lumbar spine L1-L4 plus proximal femur (hip) · Quote the WHO T-score cutoffs exactly: -1 or above normal; -1 to -2.4 osteopenia; -2.5 or below osteoporosis; a fragility fracture upgrades to severe · Explain that BMD is only a risk factor — FRAX converts it into a 10-year fracture probability.
  • Gold standard: DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) measures areal bone mineral density (g/cm2) at the lumbar spine (L1-L4) and proximal femur.
  • DEXA radiation: minimal — about 1/10 of a chest X-ray.
  • T-score: compares with the young-adult mean; WHO cutoffs in postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or more: -1 or above normal; -1 to -2.4 osteopenia; -2.5 or below osteoporosis; with a fragility fracture = severe osteoporosis.
  • Z-score: age-matched; -2 or below = 'below expected for age' (used in premenopausal women and younger men).
  • FRAX: computes the 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic and hip fracture from BMD plus clinical risk factors.
  • FRAX risk factors: age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parent hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, rheumatoid arthritis, alcohol, and secondary causes.
  • FRAX thresholds: treatment is FRAX-based, not BMD alone (e.g. hip-probability 3% or more in Indian guidelines, adapting WHO/NOF cut-points).
  • Plain radiographs: show complications (vertebral compression, cortical thinning, trabecular rarefaction) only after 30-40% bone loss; also used for vertebral fracture assessment morphometry.
  • Quantitative CT: true volumetric BMD, sensitive but a higher dose; pQCT for peripheral sites.
  • Quantitative ultrasound (heel): radiation-free screening (SOS/BUA) — not for diagnosis.
  • MRI/bone scan: for occult fracture and malignancy differentiation.
  • Labs (to exclude secondary causes): serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D, PTH, TSH, renal/liver profile; in men, testosterone.
  • Turnover markers: resorption (serum/urine CTx) and formation (P1NP) — mainly used to monitor therapy.

T-score ladder: above -1 normal, -1 to -2.4 osteopenia, -2.5 or below osteoporosis; a fragility fracture upgrades to severe. DEXA sites: L1-L4 + hip.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 4d.
  • McKinnis LN. Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging. FA Davis (reference 8).
  • Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach. (reference 9).
  • WHO Technical Report / Kanis JA. FRAX — Assessment of osteoporotic fracture risk (primary).
710 marks

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative assessment following supracondylar fracture of elbow.

Full answer →

Put neurovascular and compartment screening first, then ROM and radiology, and always warn: never force passive extension.

  • What earns marks: Put the neurovascular and compartment check FIRST — it is the safety half of the answer · State clearly — NEVER force passive extension in a post-supracondylar elbow (myositis ossificans risk) · Keep the exact angles — carrying angle about 11 degrees valgus in men, Baumann's angle about 75-80 degrees.
  • Context: supracondylar humerus fracture (Gartland I-III) is the commonest elbow fracture of children (fall on an outstretched hand).
  • Treatment: displaced types are treated by closed/open reduction and K-wire fixation, with a cast for 3-4 weeks.
  • Timing: post-op assessment begins the day after surgery.
  • Vascular: check radial pulse, capillary refill, and colour/temperature of the hand — brachial-artery injury/kinking threatens the limb.
  • Watch for Volkmann's ischaemic contracture — the 5 Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis), especially pain on passive finger extension.
  • Neural: test anterior interosseous (median — OK sign), main median, radial (wrist/thumb extension) and ulnar nerves — all are at risk from both injury and K-wires.
  • Compartment syndrome screen: tense forearm, pain out of proportion.
  • Local: wound/pin sites — check for discharge and infection; check the cast/splint condition.
  • ROM: elbow flexion-extension and pronation-supination once the cast is off (expect stiffness; grade objectively by goniometer).
  • Carrying angle: normal valgus about 11 degrees in men, about 13 degrees in women (Dutton: 11-14 / 13-16 degrees); loss = cubitus varus ('gunstock', the classic malunion).
  • Radiology: Baumann's angle (humeral capitellar angle, about 75-80 degrees; a falling value warns of varus) plus callus formation define union progression.
  • Strength: MMT of elbow/forearm/wrist musculature once pain allows; circumference for atrophy.
  • Function: functional tasks (writing, feeding); outcome instruments (QuickDASH, pediatric PROMIS).
  • Complications to hunt for: pin-tract infection, myositis ossificans (calcification anteriorly — avoid forceful passive stretching), stiffness, malunion (varus), nerve palsy, growth disturbance.
  • Conclusion: findings set the rehabilitation stage — early gentle active motion, no forced passive stretching, progressive strengthening — re-assessed every visit against a documented baseline.

Supracondylar alarm: the 5 Ps + pain on passive finger extension = compartment syndrome — the earliest sign. NEVER force extension (myositis ossificans); Baumann angle about 75-80 degrees.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 5a.
  • Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. (reference 16).
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4) — elbow chapter.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13).
810 marks

Q8. Describe in detail the assessment following below-knee amputation.

Full answer →

Follow the structure — residual limb, proximal joints, prosthesis, gait, scales, psychosocial — and name AMP/LCI-5 with their purpose.

  • What earns marks: Follow the structure — residual limb, then proximal joints, then prosthesis, then gait, then functional scales, then psychosocial · Name at least one standardised scale (AMP or LCI-5) with its one-line purpose · Differentiate phantom-limb pain from residual-limb pain — the viva's pet question.
  • Residual-limb shape: ideal is firm — cylindrical for total-surface-bearing sockets, conical for traditional patellar-tendon-bearing; matured by 3-6 months post-op.
  • Residual-limb skin: scars, grafts, moisture, breakdown over bony points; check wound healing and whether the scar is adherent or mobile.
  • Sensation: check for hyper-sensitivity and neuroma (Tinel's sign).
  • Volume: oedema/volume fluctuation (circumferential measurements; test socks); limb length and soft-tissue padding over the bone end.
  • Musculoskeletal: hip and knee ROM — a knee flexion contracture is the enemy of prosthetic gait (even 10 degrees matters).
  • Strength: hip flexors/extensors, abductors, quadriceps and hamstrings (MMT); knee stability.
  • Also: upper-limb strength (crutch/transfer readiness) and trunk control/balance.
  • Pain: differentiate phantom-limb pain (painful sensations in the absent foot) from residual-limb pain (neuroma, bone spur, socket pressure) and back pain.
  • Prosthesis: socket fit (pistoning, pressure marks, redness that doesn't fade in 10-15 min), suspension, and alignment in standing and walking; component condition (foot category, SACH etc.).
  • Gait: observe for vaulting, circumduction, lateral trunk bending, knee instability and unequal step length — each names a fitting or weakness problem.
  • Functional instruments: Amputee Mobility Predictor (AMP) (with/without prosthesis), Locomotor Capabilities Index-5, and Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire.
  • Also: 2-minute/6-minute walk test, TUG, and the SIGAM mobility grades; K-levels (0-4) classify mobility potential.
  • Energy: the O2 cost of amputee gait is higher — relevant to rehab planning.
  • Psychosocial: body image, depression screening, motivation, family support, occupation and financial access to prosthetic services — decisive in the Indian setting for prosthetic success.

Ideal stump: gently cylindrical, firm, healed, volume-stable by 3-6 months, scar mobile, soft-tissue pad over bone. Assess with AMP / LCI-5 for mobility prediction.

Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 5d & 6.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10) — amputation chapters.
  • Chui KC et al. Orthotics and Prosthetics in Rehabilitation. (reference 18).
  • Gailey RS et al. Amputee Mobility Predictor. Arch Phys Med Rehabil. (primary)
910 marks

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for shoulder pain.

Full answer →

Give each scale's item count and best use, pair one measure per ICF level, and never call VAS a function measure.

  • What earns marks: Pair one measure per ICF level — body function plus activity/participation · Give each scale's item count and best use — one line each beats a paragraph on any one scale · Never write 'VAS is the gold standard for shoulder function' — VAS measures pain intensity, not function.
  • Selection principles: choose by ICF level (impairment / activity / participation), region vs condition specificity, psychometric quality in the target population, and responsiveness with a known MCID.
  • Body function — ROM: goniometry of flexion, abduction and rotations (pain arc 60-120 degrees); inclinometer/smartphone apps.
  • Body function — strength: handheld dynamometry / MMT of rotator cuff and scapular muscles.
  • Body function — pain: VAS/NRS at rest and with provocation; a pain diary.
  • SPADI: 13 items (5 pain, 8 disability), 0-100 — best for general shoulder pathology; sensitive in frozen shoulder.
  • DASH / QuickDASH: 30 / 11 items, 0-100 — upper-limb-wide disability; good for multiple joints.
  • ASES: 13 items, 0-100 — rotator-cuff pathology; physician- plus self-rated.
  • Constant-Murley: 100 points (35 subjective + 65 objective) — European standard including ROM and strength.
  • UCLA: best for arthritis & arthroplasty.
  • SST: 12 yes-no single-answer questions.
  • Penn: general shoulder pathology.
  • WORC: rotator-cuff disease.
  • WOSI: instability.
  • PSFS: 3 patient-chosen activities (0-10) — individualised and very responsive.
  • Interpretation: report baseline to discharge change against the MCID of the chosen scale (SPADI about 8-10 points; DASH about 10-15 points).
  • Interpretation: use two complementary levels (an impairment measure plus a self-report scale) for a defensible ICF-rounded evaluation.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Unit 6.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. (reference 10).
  • Roach KE et al. SPADI. Arthritis Care Res. 1991 (primary).
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. (reference 4).
1010 marks

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total hip replacement.

Full answer →

Answer as a decision chain — impairments, gait/balance, functional tests, fit or continue — and keep the exact numbers (TUG 12 s or less, gait speed 1 m/s or more).

  • What earns marks: Answer as a chain — impairments, then gait/balance, then functional tests, then fit or continue rehab · Keep the numbers exact — TUG 12 s or less, gait speed 1.0 m/s or more, abductors 4/5 or more, single-leg stance 10 s or more · Name one patient-reported scale (Harris/Oxford/HOOS) to complete the ICF triangle.
  • Surgical & safety screening: confirm radiological implant position and stability, a healed wound, and absence of infection/heterotopic ossification (HO).
  • Note the surgical approach — posterior precautions vs direct-anterior (fewer restrictions).
  • Pain level: 3/10 or less on activity; medical clearance if there is cardiac comorbidity.
  • ROM criteria: hip flexion 110 degrees or more, abduction 30 degrees or more, ER in abduction; documented risk-relevant limits per approach.
  • Strength criteria: abductors grade 4/5 or more (no Trendelenburg sign in single-leg stance for 10-30 s), extensors and flexors 4/5 or more; no pain on resisted tests.
  • Leg-length equality within 1-1.5 cm; no fixed contracture.
  • Gait: independent gait without an assistive device, symmetrical cadence and step length, no limp/Trendelenburg lurch.
  • Balance: single-limb balance 10 s or more (eyes open), Stork/functional reach within norms.
  • Stairs: ascending and descending reciprocally with a rail.
  • Timed Up-and-Go: community ambulation benchmark 12-14 s or less; 8-10 s or less for near-normal.
  • Six-minute walk test: compare with age norms (roughly 400-600 m for healthy adults; a post-THR patient should exceed about 70% predicted).
  • 10-metre walk: gait speed 1.0 m/s or more = community standard; also the stair test and sit-to-stand x5.
  • Fitness verdict: the adult is declared fit for independent community ambulation/work when — painless independent gait, abductor strength 4/5 or more, negative Trendelenburg, functional ROM, TUG 12 s or less, safe stairs, and stable 6MWT performance.
  • Reassessment: the criteria are graded on reassessment at 3, 6 and 12 months.
Sources
  • RGUHS MPT 2020 Syllabus (MSK), Paper III Units 4f & 6.
  • Maxey L, Magnusson J. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. (reference 13) — THR criteria.
  • Wilk KE et al. Clinical Orthopaedic Rehabilitation. (reference 14).
  • ACSM. Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription. (reference 12).
110 marks

Describe the various special tests used for pain around the elbow.

Full answer →

Show the special tests that localise and confirm the source of elbow pain — lateral and medial epicondylalgia, the ligaments, and the nerves — giving the position, the force, the positive sign and the structure loaded.

  • What earns marks: write every test as position + force + positive finding + structure loaded. Four tests written that way score more than ten names alone · localise by palpation first, then confirm with resisted tests that load the tendon, stress tests that load the ligament, and provocation tests that load the nerve.
  • Elbow pain has four possible sources: lateral epicondylalgia (wrist extensor common origin), medial epicondylalgia (wrist flexor origin), the collateral ligaments, and the three nerves that wrap the joint (ulnar, radial, median).
  • Cozen's test: the patient makes a fist with the forearm pronated; the examiner stabilises the elbow, palpates the lateral epicondyle with one thumb and resists wrist extension with radial deviation (Dutton lists the elbow extended; flexed about 90° is the common Indian convention).
  • Cozen's positive: sharp pain over the lateral epicondyle — the extensor carpi radialis brevis origin is loaded under resistance.
  • Mill's test: the arm is held with the elbow extended and forearm pronated; the examiner passively flexes the wrist (some add slight ulnar deviation). Positive: pain at the lateral epicondyle because the common extensor origin is stretched, not contracted.
  • Chair (lift) test: the patient lifts a chair gripping its back, elbow extended, forearm pronated; reproduction of lateral elbow pain is positive.
  • Maudsley's test: resist extension of the middle finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint; pain at the lateral elbow suggests extensor origin involvement or radial tunnel irritation.
  • Resisted-grip test: grip strength measured with the elbow extended versus flexed drops notably in tennis elbow.
  • Medial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow): reverse the logic. Resisted wrist flexion with the elbow extended and forearm supinated, palpating the medial epicondyle, reproduces pain at the common flexor origin (reverse Cozen's).
  • Reverse Mill's: passive wrist extension with the elbow extended stretches the flexor origin; always compare grip strength.
  • Medial symptoms also raise the ulnar nerve and the medial collateral ligament in the differential — which is why the ligament and nerve tests follow.
  • Valgus stress with the elbow flexed to about 25° and the humerus in external rotation tests the medial (ulnar) collateral ligament; varus stress in the same position tests the lateral collateral / lateral ulnar collateral ligament and may produce posterolateral rotatory instability.
  • Moving valgus stress test: applying a valgus load while the elbow moves from flexion toward extension reproduces the patient's medial pain in the arc of about 120° to 70°.
  • For posterolateral rotatory instability use the push-up or chair-rise test with the forearm supinated, and the lateral pivot-shift apprehension test. Mentioning the 30° position (isolating the anterior band, relaxing the capsule) converts a list into an answer.
  • Tinel's sign: percuss at the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle — tingling radiating into the ulnar two fingers suggests ulnar nerve irritation.
  • A positive Tinel over the radial tunnel region (3–4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle) with a positive Maudsley's test points to radial tunnel syndrome rather than tennis elbow — the classic examiner trap.
  • Elbow flexion test: sustained maximal flexion, forearms supinated and wrists extended, for three to five minutes provokes ulnar symptoms; the upper limb tension test biases the nerve bed.
  • Interpretation: no single elbow test is definitive, so interpret a cluster — palpation point plus two concordant resisted or stretch tests plus functional provocation (gripping a jar, lifting a bucket).
  • Lateral pain with a normal neck screening but positive Cozen's and Mill's supports local epicondylalgia; add sensory testing and cervical screening to exclude C6–C7 referral.
  • Conclusion: localise by palpation, confirm by loading the tissue, clear the joints above and below, and screen the nerves.

Cozen's = same pain with resistance (contraction); Mill's = same pain with passive stretch. The pain must land exactly on the lateral epicondyle.

Sources
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  • Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
210 marks

Describe the various steps involved in the decision-making process in physiotherapy.

Full answer →

Explain the structured patient-management decision cycle from examination to outcome, plus the modes of reasoning and the factors and biases that influence decisions.

  • What earns marks: marks sit in the verbs — collect, evaluate, diagnose, prioritise, prognose, select, re-examine, modify. Seven verbs, seven sentences, full marks · present the structured cycle as the backbone, and remember that under direct access every step must also ask: treat, or refer?
  • Decision making in physiotherapy is the deliberate process of collecting and weighting clinical information to answer four questions: what is wrong (diagnosis), what can physiotherapy change (prognosis), which intervention is most likely to change it (selection), and is it actually changing (re-examination).
  • Under direct access the physiotherapist is the first contact, so the process must also decide when to treat and when to refer.
  • Analytic (hypothetico-deductive) mode: slow, conscious and hypothesis-testing — the novice's route and the route for complex patients.
  • Intuitive or pattern-recognition mode: fast, built on experience, efficient but prone to bias.
  • Narrative reasoning: listens to the patient's illness story and goals. Experts blend all three, but the written answer must present the structured cycle as the backbone.
  • Step 1 — Examination: gather demographic data, history and systems review, then select tests and measures.
  • Step 2 — Evaluation: interpret the data — cluster findings, compare sides, weigh the findings against hypotheses.
  • Step 3 — Physiotherapy diagnosis and problem list: label the movement or functional impairment (for example, painful resisted wrist extension with grip weakness), and prioritise problems that matter to this patient.
  • Step 4 — Prognosis: estimate achievable improvement and time frame, and set SMART goals with the patient.
  • Step 5 — Intervention selection: choose techniques that match the impairments, the stage of healing, the evidence and the patient's preferences, in agreed doses.
  • Step 6 — Re-examination: measure immediate effects (pain relief after a trial technique, range change after mobilisation) and progress at each visit.
  • Step 7 — Modify or progress, and decide discharge when goals are met or a plateau is reached. The loop closes: re-examination feeds new examination data.
  • Factors that influence the decision: patient factors (age, comorbidity, occupation, expectations, finances), clinician factors (knowledge, skill, experience), environmental factors (equipment, caseload, time, referral access) and research evidence.
  • Biases to name: anchoring on the first impression, confirmation bias and availability bias.
  • In Indian settings, travel distance, payment out of pocket and family involvement shape follow-up and goal decisions.
  • Application example: a 45-year-old teacher with subacromial pain — history suggests stage 2 impingement, tests confirm a painful arc and positive empty-can; goals are overhead writing and sleeping; intervention is scapular and rotator cuff loading; re-examination at two weeks uses the SPADI score and the painful arc.
  • Shared decision making means the patient chooses between options with the clinician's guidance — and documentation of each step protects the autonomous practitioner.

Seven verbs, seven sentences: examine, evaluate, diagnose, prioritise, prognose (SMART), intervene, re-examine — then modify. The cycle is a loop, not a list.

Sources
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
310 marks

Write in detail about the postoperative management following both-bone fracture of the upper limb (radius-ulna fracture).

Full answer →

Give the phased rehabilitation after ORIF of a both-bone forearm fracture, with what is allowed and forbidden in each phase, the complications to monitor, and the discharge criteria.

  • What earns marks: the phrase "guided by radiological union and surgeon protocol" plus the six Ps of compartment syndrome earns the safety marks most candidates miss · give the three phase boundaries with what is allowed and what is forbidden in each.
  • A both-bone forearm fracture disrupts the ring formed by the radius, ulna and interosseous membrane — the hinge that lets us pronate and supinate.
  • Open reduction and internal fixation with plates and screws (dynamic compression plating) restores anatomy and is usually rigid enough to permit early controlled motion.
  • The single most important sentence: rehabilitation after ORIF of the forearm is motion-first, because crossed synostosis and stiffness are the enemies.
  • Phase 1 (days 0–14) — assess first: neurovascular status (radial and ulnar pulses; median, radial and ulnar nerve territories), wound condition, pain by VAS, oedema by circumference or figure-of-eight.
  • Phase 1 — watch the six Ps of compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pallor, paraesthesia, pulselessness, paralysis, pressure.
  • Phase 1 treatment: elevation above heart level, cryotherapy, active finger and thumb exercises every waking hour, tendon glides.
  • Phase 1 also: shoulder and elbow active range within the surgeon's protocol, gentle pain-free wrist motion if allowed, and education on sling use and sleeping position.
  • Phase 1 rule: no loading, no resistance, no passive stretching of the incision.
  • Phase 2 (weeks 2–6) — with the wound healed and callus beginning, progress active elbow flexion-extension, wrist flexion-extension, and the functional gold of the forearm: pronation and supination.
  • Pronation-supination: first gravity-eliminated (elbow at side, doing doorknob turns), then against gravity.
  • Add scar mobilisation once suture lines are mature, heat before sessions, and graded grip work with putty only if the fracture pattern and surgeon permit.
  • Re-measure every visit: goniometric arcs, oedema, pain with the patient-rated scales. Expect roughly half to two-thirds of full arcs by six weeks; document why if not.
  • Phase 3 (weeks 6–12 and beyond) — once radiological union signs appear (usually 8–12 weeks), begin progressive resisted exercise: theraband wrist and elbow work, weighted pronation-supination with a hammer or wiper bar, isometric gripping, then eccentric wrist extensor loading.
  • Functional retraining mirrors the Indian patient's life: carrying a water bucket, wringing a mop, riding a two-wheeler, lifting a child, keyboard or field work. Athletes follow plyometric and return-to-sport stages; heavy manual workers may need 4–6 months.
  • Complications to monitor: compartment syndrome (most dangerous early), re-fracture after plate removal, and radioulnar synostosis (especially proximal-third and head-injury patients).
  • Also: malunion with loss of the interosseous space (and therefore loss of supination), non-union, superficial or deep infection, nerve injury (posterior interosseous), complex regional pain syndrome, and distal radioulnar joint instability.
  • Each complication changes the plan — synostosis needs prolonged motion work or surgical excision; CRPS needs desensitisation and graded exposure, not force.
  • Discharge criteria: pronation-supination and wrist arcs functional for the patient's tasks (about 50° each way of pro-sup covers most daily activity), grip within about 80% of the other side, and independence in a home programme — progress is always paired with radiological union, never ahead of it.

Motion first — stiffness and synostosis are the enemies; assess every visit with the 6 Ps, arcs, oedema, pain and X-ray union; compartment syndrome is a refer-now emergency.

Sources
  • Hoppenfeld S, Murthy VL. Treatment and Rehabilitation of Fractures. Lippincott.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.
410 marks

Write in detail about various investigations used for spinal cord injuries.

Full answer →

Describe the ASIA/ISNCSCI clinical exam and classification, then imaging (MRI, X-ray, CT, myelography), electrophysiology, and urodynamics — showing what each investigation adds.

  • What earns marks: write out the ten key muscles and the AIS A–E definitions verbatim — these are the two lists this question is really set for · close with each investigation answering a question the others cannot — imaging grades structure, ASIA grades function, electrophysiology gives conduction and prognosis, urodynamics protects the kidneys.
  • The ASIA / ISNCSCI exam is the bedrock. Sensory testing: light touch and pin prick graded 0–2 over 28 dermatomes each side, plus deep anal pressure.
  • Motor testing: the 10 key myotomes (C5 elbow flexors, C6 wrist extensors, C7 elbow extensors, C8 finger flexors, T1 finger abductors; L2 hip flexors, L3 knee extensors, L4 ankle dorsiflexors, L5 long toe extensors, S1 ankle plantarflexors) graded 0–5, plus voluntary anal contraction.
  • From these derive the neurological level of injury, and the AIS grade.
  • AIS grades: A complete (no sacral sparing S4–5); B sensory incomplete; C motor incomplete with less than half of key muscles below the level grade 3 or more; D motor incomplete with at least half grade 3 or more; E normal.
  • The 2019 revision refined the zone of partial preservation — it can now be recorded for incomplete injuries lacking sacral motor or sensory function — and introduced a star-tagging system for non-SCI-related deficits.
  • Spinal shock is tracked clinically; return of the bulbocavernosus reflex signals its end and makes the exam reliable.
  • MRI is the investigation of choice for cord parenchyma: it shows cord contusion, oedema, haemorrhage, compression by disc, bone fragment or haematoma, and ligamentous injury.
  • Length of haemorrhage and length of oedema on T2 carry prognostic weight — haemorrhage predicts poorer motor recovery. MRI also picks up underlying pathology such as tumour, syrinx or demyelination.
  • MRI contraindications: pacemakers and ferromagnetic implants.
  • Plain films in the trauma series (lateral cervical spine first) screen alignment and fractures; CT with reformats is superior for fracture morphology, canal encroachment and surgical planning, and is now the primary screening modality in most trauma protocols.
  • Together: MRI tells you about the cord, CT tells you about the column.
  • Myelography: contrast injected into the thecal sac outlines the cord and nerve roots on X-ray/CT; it is reserved for patients in whom MRI is contraindicated or unavailable — still relevant in Indian district practice where MRI access may be limited.
  • Myelography shows canal obstruction, root avulsion and arachnoiditis; complications include post-lumbar-puncture headache and, rarely, seizure.
  • Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEP) stimulate a peripheral nerve (typically tibial or median) and record cortical responses, testing the dorsal column pathways — useful in spinal shock, intra-operatively to monitor the cord, and prognostically (a preserved SSEP early on favours motor recovery).
  • Motor evoked potentials (MEP) test the corticospinal tract, complementing SSEPs; needle EMG and nerve conduction distinguish a superimposed peripheral nerve or root injury from cord pathology and detect neurogenic bladder candidates for intervention.
  • Urodynamics (cystometry with uroflowmetry and leak point pressures) characterises the neurogenic bladder (areflexic versus hyperreflexive, dyssynergic), guides clean intermittent catheterisation and guards the upper tracts from high-pressure storage.
  • Digital rectal examination assesses anal tone and the bulbocavernosus reflex; the ASIA autonomic standards record sudomotor and cardiovascular function; bone mineral density scans surveil disuse osteoporosis, and blood work (creatinine for renal surveillance, vitamin D, haemoglobin) completes the picture.
  • Conclusion: imaging grades the injury structurally, the ASIA exam grades it functionally, electrophysiology gives conduction and prognosis, and urodynamics protects the kidneys.

Every number in the classification comes from the clinical exam, not the scanner — MRI for the cord, CT for the bone, evoked potentials for conduction.

Sources
  • American Spinal Injury Association. International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury (ISNCSCI), 2019 revision.
  • McKinnis LN. Fundamentals of Musculoskeletal Imaging. FA Davis.
  • Greenspan A, Beltran J. Orthopaedic Imaging: A Practical Approach. Lippincott.
510 marks

Describe screening of the knee following posterior cruciate ligament injury.

Full answer →

Explain the screening of a PCL injury — mechanism, the posterior drawer with its grading, the sag sign and quadriceps active test, how to spot combined injuries, and the referral rule.

  • What earns marks: the three word-pictures for the drawer grades — anterior (grade I), flush (grade II), behind (grade III) — and never forget "compare with the other knee" · end with the referral line — isolated grade I–II injuries do well with quadriceps-focused rehabilitation; grade III or combined injuries need orthopaedic referral.
  • The PCL is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation at 90° of flexion — the strongest ligament in the knee.
  • It tears either by a direct blow to the anterior tibia (dashboard injury, or falling onto a flexed knee with the foot plantarflexed) or by hyperextension.
  • Classic presentation: vague posterior aching, swelling that is mild compared with ACL tears, and difficulty with descending stairs and deceleration — the quadriceps works harder to hold the tibia forward.
  • Posterior drawer — the gold standard: patient supine, hip flexed 45°, knee flexed 90°, foot stabilised on the plinth (the examiner may sit lightly on the foot); hamstrings must be relaxed — palpate them.
  • Thumbs sit on the joint line feeling the step-off between the medial tibial plateau and the medial femoral condyle; the normal plateau sits about 1 cm anterior to the condyle.
  • A posteriorly directed force is applied to the proximal tibia. Grade I = 0–5 mm translation, plateau still anterior to the condyle; grade II = 5–10 mm, plateau flush with the condyle; grade III = more than 10 mm, plateau drops behind the condyle, and suspect an associated posterolateral corner injury.
  • The posterior drawer is the most accurate test for PCL diagnosis, with reported sensitivity near 90% and specificity near 99%; always compare with the other knee because congenital laxity exists.
  • Repeat in internal and external rotation: increased laxity in external rotation points to the posterolateral corner.
  • Posterior sag sign (Godfrey test): with the hips and knees flexed to 90° and legs supported at the heels, look from the side — gravity makes the tibia visibly drop backwards on the affected side, flattening the normal step-off contour.
  • It can be reinforced by a gentle anterior push that reduces the tibia with a visible shift. Around 79% sensitivity and essentially 100% specificity are reported — a highly specific screening sign that is simply observation, so always look before you touch.
  • Quadriceps active test: knee at 90°, foot flat; ask the patient to slide the foot gently down the plinth (or isometrically extend the knee against the examiner's hand).
  • In a PCL-deficient knee the quadriceps contraction pulls the posteriorly subluxed tibia visibly anterior — the relocation is the positive. Sensitivity is modest (about half of proven tears) but specificity is high (about 97%), and it demonstrates the dynamic compensatory role of the quadriceps, the rationale for quadriceps-dominant rehabilitation.
  • Screening for combined injuries: a grade III drawer is rarely isolated. The dial test at 30° and 90° — more than about 10° of excess external rotation at 30° only suggests an isolated posterolateral corner; at both 30° and 90° suggests PCL plus posterolateral corner.
  • Varus stress and reverse pivot shift, gait observation for varus thrust, and hyperextension recurvatum complete the screen.
  • Remember the trap: a posteriorly subluxed tibia makes a routine anterior drawer look falsely positive — reduce the sag first, then test the ACL.
  • Interpretation: cluster the posterior drawer, sag sign and quadriceps active test with the mechanism and functional history.
  • Screen quadriceps and hamstring strength, step-down control, and use the knee outcome scales from Paper III Unit 6.
  • Conclude: isolated grade I–II injuries do well with quadriceps-focused rehabilitation; grade III or combined injuries need orthopaedic referral.

Grades read off the step-off at the medial joint line: I anterior, II flush, III behind (over 10 mm = suspect posterolateral corner).

Sources
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  • Rubinstein RA Jr et al. The accuracy of clinical examination in PCL injuries. Am J Sports Med. 1994.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott.
610 marks

Describe in detail the assessment following Symes amputation.

Full answer →

Describe the Symes amputation and its advantages, then the residual-limb, proximal-segment and whole-patient assessment, the prosthetic logic, gait analysis and complications.

  • What earns marks: the five advantages — end bearing, long lever, self-suspension, near-normal energy, bare-stump standing — is a guaranteed marks list · assess the residual limb in the examiner's order — look, feel, measure, move.
  • A Symes amputation is a disarticulation at the ankle joint with removal of the malleoli; the heel pad is sutured over the end of the tibia to create a durable, end-bearing stump.
  • Advantages: virtually full end bearing (the heel pad is made for load); an intact long tibial lever arm with preserved knee and good muscle control.
  • Also: self-suspension from the bulbous distal end; a shorter but fully end-bearing limb (a leg-length discrepancy is expected); and lower energy cost of walking than transtibial amputation.
  • Uniquely, the patient can hobble short distances on the bare stump (a real advantage for night bathroom use in Indian homes).
  • Disadvantages to mention: the bulbous end is cosmetically bulky in a prosthesis, and heel pad migration can occur.
  • Residual limb — shape: the classical Symes stump is bulbous with a narrow shaft above; note any dog-ears or prominences that the socket must accommodate.
  • Skin and heel pad: intact plantar skin, no breakdown or wart-like cysts on the end; check whether the pad is stable over the tibia or migrates on weight bearing (pinch and glide it distally).
  • Scars: posterior heel-flap scar placement and maturity. Circulation and sensation: palpable pulses proximal and at the flap margins, and protective sensation of the pad — critical for an end-bearing limb.
  • Measurements: residual length from medial tibial plateau to end, circumference at defined levels, and comparison with the sound side; the bulbous diameter determines prosthetic design. Palpate the bony end for tenderness and heterotopic bone.
  • Volume stability: oedema versus mature stump — sockets are prescribed on mature volume.
  • Proximal segment: because the knee is intact, the big wins are hip and quadriceps power, full knee range, and absence of hip flexion contracture; assess manually and functionally (sit-to-stand).
  • Whole patient: balance, upper limb strength for aids, cardiovascular endurance, vision, and the systemic disease that caused the amputation (diabetes control, Hansen's disease status) frame the prognosis. Document the pre-prosthetic stage: stump conditioning, shrinker socks, walking with crutches.
  • Prosthetic considerations: the bulbous end must pass through a narrow shank, so socket designs manage this — posterior-opening or medial-window sockets (Canadian type), expandable-wall closed sockets, or bivalve designs. The socket gives total contact, distributes load between the end-bearing pad and the proximal tibia, and the bulbous flare provides suspension; a suprapatellar strap is added when the flare is insufficient.
  • Because the space between stump end and floor is small, a thin SACH or solid-ankle cushioned foot is standard — few modern Symes prostheses use articulated ankles.
  • Gait with the prosthesis: near-normal gait is expected because limb length is preserved and the knee is intact; look for shortened stance phase, reduced push-off, vaulting on the sound side, and early knee flexion issues.
  • Check socket pistoning (pad migration or volume loss), pressure areas over the malleolar remnants, and stairs, slopes and floor sitting — cross-legged sitting and squatting matter to the Indian patient. Without the prosthesis, assess skin tolerance for short-distance bare-stump walking.
  • Complications: heel pad migration, skin breakdown and cysts, stump overgrowth in children, and wound failure in dysvascular or diabetic patients.
  • Reported outcomes are strong: roughly four in five adults walk with their prosthesis, energy cost is close to normal, and most need minimal therapy. Conclusion: the assessment revolves around the end-bearing pad and the intact knee — protect the first and strengthen the second.

Five advantages: end bearing, long lever, self-suspension, near-normal energy cost, bare-stump standing. The whole prosthesis is built around the heel pad.

Sources
  • Maxey L, Magnusson M. Rehabilitation for the Postsurgical Orthopedic Patient. Mosby.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation. 5th ed. FA Davis.
  • Kanas JL, Stevens PM. Syme ankle disarticulation: prosthetic management. Atlas of Amputations and Limb Deficiencies. AAOS.
  • Chui J et al. Syme amputation: a systematic review. Foot Ankle Int. 2018.
710 marks

Describe the role of demographic data and history taking in assessment.

Full answer →

Show how demographic data and the history guide the working diagnosis and plan — what each variable rules in or out — plus the pain analysis, past/social history, red flags and documentation.

  • What earns marks: do not just list "age, sex, occupation" — state what each one rules in or out. Value, not vocabulary · remember that about 80% of the diagnosis is reached before you touch the patient, and the history decides WHICH tests you run — not the other way round.
  • Age tells you the probability of pathology — osteochondritis in the young, osteoarthritis after fifty, osteoporotic fracture in the postmenopausal woman, tendon degeneration in mid-life.
  • Sex modifies probabilities again: osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis and fibromyalgia in women; ankylosing spondylitis in young men.
  • Occupation predicts the tissue: a farmer's knee, a tailor's shoulder, a software engineer's cervical pain, a construction worker's low back with a flexion-loading history.
  • Hand dominance localises the symptomatic limb and sets functional expectations.
  • Residence and socioeconomic status shape diagnosis (brucellosis and tuberculosis of the spine in endemic areas — spinal tuberculosis is still India's commonest spine pathology) and modify the plan (travel distance, ability to attend, home help).
  • Religion, habits like tobacco and alcohol, marital status and family structure inform support and consent; marital status, literacy and language also decide how the plan will be explained.
  • Chief complaint: begin with the patient's own words for the main complaint and its duration.
  • History of present illness — dissect each symptom along the standard ladder: onset (sudden or gradual, trauma), character and distribution, aggravating and relieving factors, timing and diurnal pattern, associated features like stiffness, swelling, paraesthesia, and the effect of treatment so far.
  • Pain is analysed by site, character, severity on a VAS, radiation, temporal pattern and behaviour with posture and activity; night pain and rest pain are flagged immediately.
  • The pattern is a diagnostic shortcut: inflammatory pain is worse at rest and in the second half of the night with morning stiffness over an hour; mechanical pain worsens with load and eases with rest.
  • Past medical history (diabetes, tuberculosis, malignancy, previous surgery), past physiotherapy and its result.
  • Drugs: steroids and osteoporosis, anticoagulants and bleeding risk, analgesic dependence.
  • Family history: rheumatological disease, ankylosing spondylitis, haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell in central India.
  • Social and occupational history: workload, posture, sports, sleep surface — a thin cotton mattress on the floor versus a hard cot changes spine advice.
  • Red flags inside the history: unexplained weight loss, night pain unrelieved by position, fever, loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, history of carcinoma, and trauma in the osteoporotic or anticoagulated patient.
  • A positive red flag changes the whole day — stop, document, refer. In the Indian context, chronic low back pain with evening fever and weight loss must raise spinal tuberculosis.
  • Documentation and reasoning: the history is where shared goals are set — ask what the patient expects and what function they must recover (fetching water, sitting cross-legged for meals, riding a scooter).
  • Record in standard formats (SOAP or the departmental assessment sheet) so the data can steer hypothesis testing: the history chooses the tests, the tests confirm or reject, and both together set the treatment. A well-taken history shortens examination, avoids unnecessary investigations, and is the single cheapest diagnostic instrument available.

The history funnel: demographics in, working hypothesis out — with the red-flag gate before any hands-on testing.

Sources
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function: A Comprehensive Analysis. FA Davis.
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
810 marks

Describe various outcome measures used for knee pain.

Full answer →

Describe the main knee outcome measures — WOMAC, KOOS, Lysholm, Tegner, Kujala, VAS and Knee Society Score — with their item counts, scoring direction and when to choose each.

  • What earns marks: score direction and item counts are the discriminating marks — WOMAC 24, KOOS 42, Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — with opposite directions of "better" · map each tool to the ICF level (impairment, activity, participation) and finish with a selection rule.
  • An outcome measure converts the patient's knee into a number we can track across visits and report to surgeons, insurers and researchers.
  • A usable instrument needs reliability (same score on repeat testing), validity (measures what it claims), responsiveness (detects real change) and interpretability — the minimal clinically important difference, which for KOOS subscales is roughly 8 to 10 points.
  • ICF mapping: impairment-level measures like VAS, activity-level measures like WOMAC and KOOS, participation-level measures like the Tegner activity scale.
  • WOMAC — the osteoarthritis classic: 24 items in three domains — pain (5 items), stiffness (2 items) and physical function (17 items) — scored 0–100 where higher means worse.
  • WOMAC is validated in knee osteoarthritis, available in translated Indian-language versions, and responsive to change. Limits: no sport or quality-of-life domain, ceiling effects in younger or higher-function patients, and poor performance in patellofemoral problems.
  • KOOS — the expanded successor: 42 items across five subscales — symptoms, pain, activities of daily living, function in sport and recreation, and knee-related quality of life.
  • Each KOOS subscale is scored 0–100 where higher means better (note the reversal from WOMAC; examiners love this trap). It captures the young athletic patient where WOMAC ceilings out, making it the preferred measure after ACL reconstruction and for sports injuries.
  • Lysholm knee scoring scale: a knee-specific 8-item questionnaire — limp, support, locking, instability, pain, swelling, stair climbing, squatting — scored 0–100, higher is better. It is short, so it suits busy Indian OPDs, but it has a ceiling in high-functioning athletes.
  • Tegner activity level scale: grades current and pre-injury activity from 0 (sick leave, desk work) to 10 (competitive sports at national level). Together with Lysholm it answers two different questions — how the knee feels and what the patient can do.
  • Kujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale: 13 items covering limp, walking, stairs, squatting, running, jumping, prolonged sitting, pain and swelling, all weighted to patellofemoral complaints, scored 0–100 with higher being better.
  • Kujala is the instrument of choice for patellofemoral pain and patellar instability studies.
  • Visual Analogue Scale (0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable) or its numeric cousin is the universal impairment measure — quick, repeatable, but one-dimensional.
  • Knee Society Score (Insall, 1989): combines a knee score (pain, range, stability, alignment — clinician-rated) with a functional score (walking, stairs), originally built for total knee arthroplasty follow-up.
  • Selection logic: osteoarthritis or post-arthroplasty means WOMAC or KSS; sports injury or young active knee means KOOS with Lysholm–Tegner; patellofemoral pain means Kujala.
  • Every patient gets a pain scale plus objective measures (goniometry, manual muscle testing, timed walk or stair tests) — because patient-reported and performance-based numbers together tell the whole story.

WOMAC 24, KOOS 42, Lysholm 8, Kujala 13 — and remember WOMAC high is BAD, while KOOS and Lysholm high is GOOD.

Sources
  • Bellamy N et al. Validation study of WOMAC. J Rheumatol. 1988.

Describe screening of the ankle following ankle subluxation.

Full answer →

Describe the screening of an ankle after subluxation — ligament anatomy and mechanism, history and observation, the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests, clearing the syndesmosis and medial side, and functional screening.

  • What earns marks: say "compare with the other ankle" after each stress test, and never forget the pulses — the viva question hiding at the end of this paper · give the order of ligament failure, and close with the grading — mechanical laxity plus functional instability means rehabilitation; bony avulsion, syndesmosis injury or neurovascular deficit means immediate referral.
  • An ankle subluxation — a momentary partial dislocation, almost always the talus shifting under the tibiofibular mortise during an inversion or eversion episode — means the restraining ligaments failed.
  • The three lateral ligaments: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL — weakest, fails first in inversion), the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL — next, crosses both the tibiotalar and subtalar joints), and the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL — last).
  • Repeated subluxation equals chronic instability, so screening asks three questions: which ligaments are loose, what else is injured, and can the dynamic stabilisers compensate.
  • History: mechanism (inversion-plantarflexion for lateral), previous episodes — the single strongest predictor of chronic instability — inability to bear weight, swelling and bruising pattern, and functional giving way on uneven ground or stairs.
  • Observe swelling, ecchymosis over the lateral ligaments, hindfoot alignment, arch posture, and gait (antalgic, avoidant push-off).
  • Palpate systematically: distal fibula, ATFL and CFL course, base of the fifth metatarsal (avulsion), anterior syndesmosis, deltoid, and the proximal fibula — a Maisonneuve pattern referred up the leg.
  • Anterior drawer test (the ATFL test): patient sitting with leg hanging, ankle relaxed in about 10° to 20° of plantarflexion; the examiner stabilises the tibia with one hand and grips the calcaneus with the other, drawing the hindfoot forward while the talus is distracted from the mortise.
  • Positive: excessive anterior translation with a soft end-feel compared with the other side indicates ATFL insufficiency. Best done after five to seven days, once acute spasm has settled.
  • A side-to-side difference of about 3 mm or more on stress imaging is the laboratory counterpart, and manual grading is subjective — hence always compare with the uninjured ankle.
  • Talar tilt (inversion stress) test: stabilise the tibia and calcaneus together, then invert (adduct) the talus in the mortise — a comparison test for the CFL and subtalar restraint.
  • Positive: increased tilt with a soft end-feel against the other side indicates lateral ligament laxity; pure talar tilt also loads the subtalar joint, so attribute carefully.
  • Both tests can be done with an arthrometer or stress ultrasound/radiographs for objectivity when surgery is contemplated.
  • Clearing the rest of the ring: the squeeze test (compress the calf mid-shaft; pain distally at the syndesmosis is positive) and external rotation test (dorsiflex the ankle and externally rotate — syndesmotic pain) rule out a high sprain.
  • Deltoid palpation and eversion stress rule out the medial side; the Ottawa ankle rules guide radiography (malleolar or midfoot bone tenderness plus inability to bear four steps).
  • The Thompson test clears the Achilles; the neurovascular check (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulse, sensation) is mandatory after any subluxation episode.
  • Functional screening: test what the instability actually steals — single-leg balance with eyes open and closed, the Star Excursion Balance Test, hopping and figure-of-eight running, and stair descent.
  • Quantify with the Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool or FAAM for outcome tracking.
  • Conclude by grading: mechanical laxity (positive stress tests) plus functional instability (positive balance and giving-way) with muscle weakness means a structured proprioceptive-peroneal rehabilitation programme; bony avulsion, syndesmotic injury or neurovascular deficit means immediate referral.

Inversion order of failure: ATFL first, CFL second, PTFL last — drawer in 10–20° plantarflexion tests ATFL, talar tilt tests CFL; always compare with the other ankle.

  • Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.
  • Nordin M, Frankel VH. Basic Biomechanics of the Musculoskeletal System. Lippincott.

Write in detail about clinical reasoning in manual therapy.

Full answer →

Explain clinical reasoning in manual therapy — dual-process theory, hypothesis-oriented examination, the schools of thought, red-flag screening, re-assessment and expert versus novice reasoning.

  • What earns marks: name Jones, Maitland, McKenzie and Kaltenborn in one paragraph with one reasoning idea each, then close with "immediate re-assessment validates every hypothesis" · put the red-flag gate before any mobilisation.
  • Clinical reasoning is the thinking process that converts patient data into decisions — diagnosis, prognosis and intervention.
  • Modern understanding is dual-process: System 1 is fast, automatic pattern recognition born of experience; System 2 is slow, deliberate, analytic hypothesis testing.
  • The novice must live in System 2 deliberately; the expert runs System 1 and audits it with System 2 when the pattern does not fit.
  • In manual therapy, reasoning decides not only which technique, but whether manual therapy belongs in the plan at all.
  • Hypothesis-oriented examination (Jones model): the examination is structured around hypotheses generated from the very first history sentence.
  • From the referral, demographics and opening complaint the clinician frames candidate hypotheses across categories: the pain source (pathology, tissue), movement impairment, contributing factors (biomechanical, psychosocial), precautions and contraindications, prognosis, and management.
  • Each question and each test then deliberately seeks information that confirms or rejects a hypothesis, and the therapist reweights with every finding.
  • In manual therapy this shows as: does the movement reproduce the pain (a concordant sign), does repeated movement centralise or abolish it, which direction of mobilisation changes it immediately.
  • Schools of thought — Maitland concept (Australian): hypothesis-driven, movement-based, with Maitland's dictum that the therapist needs a hypothesis only until the next piece of data arrives; grades I–IV of oscillation are chosen by irritability and stiffness versus pain.
  • McKenzie method (mechanical diagnosis and therapy): classifies by directional preference — derangement responds to repeated movements in one plane, dysfunction to end-range loading, postural syndrome to education.
  • Kaltenborn-Evjenth/OMPT tradition: reasons by arthrokinematics and grades of translation to restore roll-glide. Paris's reasoning emphasises segmental dysfunction and soft-tissue signs.
  • The modern synthesis (Jones and Rivett) makes reasoning itself explicit: narrative, diagnostic, procedural, interactive, collaborative and predictive reasoning streams run in parallel during one consultation.
  • Red flags before any mobilisation: unexplained weight loss and night pain, fever, history of malignancy, sphincter disturbance or saddle anaesthesia, progressive neurological deficit, trauma in the osteoporotic, anticoagulated or pregnant patient, upper cervical ligament laxity (RA), and vascular claudication.
  • Manual therapy is contraindicated or requires modification in osteoporosis, acute fracture, inflammatory flare, hypermobility and vertebrobasilar insufficiency for cervical techniques.
  • The clinician's reasoning must distinguish nociceptive mechanical pain from systemic or visceral mimicry — in the Indian clinic, spinal tuberculosis and malignancy present late, so vigilance is high.
  • Re-assessment is the manual therapist's stethoscope: immediate re-assessment after a treatment trial is the core skill — the pre-post comparison of the concordant sign (pain on movement, range, or the patient's functional task). Improvement validates the hypothesis and the technique; no change rejects it and redirects the reasoning.
  • Sustained reassessment over visits separates real progress from short-term analgesic effects, and treatment-based classification systems (for example, the Pittsburgh low-back classification) formalise this logic into subgroups: mobilisation responders, specific-exercise responders, centralisation, control-dysfunction groups.
  • Experts reason by organised patterns, tolerate uncertainty, self-monitor for bias, and change course early; novices gather indiscriminately and anchor on first impressions. Conclusion: clinical reasoning in manual therapy is not the decoration of technique selection — it is the safety system that decides who should be mobilised, who should be exercised, and who should be sent to a surgeon today.

One loop per visit — cues, hypothesis, discriminating test, treat and re-assess — with the red-flag gate first; immediate re-assessment of the concordant sign validates or rejects every hypothesis.

Sources
  • Jones MA, Rivett DA. Clinical Reasoning in Musculoskeletal Practice. Elsevier.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment. 4th ed. WB Saunders.
  • Hertling D, Kessler RM. Management of Common Musculoskeletal Disorders. 3rd ed. Lippincott.

Q1. Enumerate basic assessment methods for joint play movements.

Full answer →

List the assessment methods for joint play as a numbered list, after explaining what joint play is.

  • What earns marks: Answer as a numbered list of the methods — the word "enumerate" means list them, not write long paragraphs · First explain the two layers of joint movement, then the methods · Include the five accessory words — roll, spin, glide, traction, compression · Finish with one short clinical example.
  • Every joint moves in two layers.
  • The layer the patient controls is osteokinematics — flexion, abduction, rotation.
  • Underneath is joint play (arthrokinematics) — the accessory roll, spin and glide of the surfaces, plus traction and compression between them.
  • If the voluntary range looks normal but the joint hurts or feels tight, the problem usually sits in the accessory layer.
  • Convex-concave rule: a convex surface moving on a fixed concave one glides opposite to its roll; a concave surface moving on a fixed convex one glides in the same direction as the movement.
  • This rule tells you the direction in which your glide must be tested and treated.
  • The methods: (1) Passive accessory intervertebral and peripheral joint movements (PAIVMs) — central and unilateral glides for the spine, translatoric glides for peripheral joints.
  • (2) Passive physiological movements (PPIVMs) — the therapist moves the joint through its voluntary arc and grades the feel.
  • (3) Assessment of roll, spin and glide in the loose-packed position; (4) long-axis traction and distraction.
  • (5) Compression and joint-springing to reproduce the patient's symptom; (6) end-feel at the physiological limit — bony, capsular or soft-tissue approximation.
  • (7) Maitland's grading of the oscillation — grades I to IV, small-to-large amplitude within or up to the limit; (8) ligamentous stress tests for stability of the accessory restraint system.
  • (9) Hypermobility screening on the other side of the spectrum — the Beighton score.
  • How to test: put the joint near its loose-packed position so the capsule is slack; steady the proximal segment with one hand, glide with the other, take up the slack, then grade the oscillation.
  • Compare with the contralateral side — the patient is their own control; ask two questions of every glide: how far does it travel, and does it reproduce the familiar pain?
  • Interpretation: a firm or hard end-feel with reduced glide = hypomobility (wants mobilisation); a soft, spongy end-feel with excessive travel = hypermobility (wants control, not stretching).
  • Note whether the symptom comes at grade I (pain-dominant, irritable) or only near the limit (stiffness-dominant).
  • Example: knee osteoarthritis that lacks the last 15 degrees of extension — the missing movement is a restricted anterior tibial glide, and graded anterior glides become the treatment.

The five words: roll, spin, glide, traction, compression. "Enumerate" means a numbered list — nine one-line items score better than three paragraphs.

Sources
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — principles chapter and regional chapters.
  • Levangie PK, Norkin CC. Joint Structure and Function — arthrokinematics chapters.
  • Maitland GD. Peripheral Manipulation — grades of movement.

Q2. Explain screening the head and neck in upper cross syndrome.

Full answer →

Describe the upper cross muscle pattern, the screening sequence, the key neck tests, and what the findings lead to.

  • What earns marks: Draw the crossed X — name the tight muscles on top and pair each with its weak opponent below · Give the screening sequence — look first, then test · Name the key tests — craniocervical flexion test, endurance test, length tests · Close with the treatment direction.
  • Upper cross syndrome is Janda's classical muscle-imbalance pattern of the head, neck and shoulder girdle.
  • Two lines cross like an X on the trunk.
  • Tight line (top): upper trapezius, levator scapulae, sternocleidomastoid, suboccipitals, pectoralis major and minor.
  • Weak (inhibited) line (bottom): deep neck flexors, lower and middle trapezius, serratus anterior.
  • Result: forward head, loss of the cervico-thoracic angle, rounded shoulders with protracted and elevated scapulae, and a chin that pokes forward.
  • For the eyes to stay level, the upper cervical spine extends and the lower cervical spine flexes; the suboccipitals shorten while the deep flexors are held long and weak.
  • Step 1 — Observation: stand the patient in profile; the ear should sit over the acromion, but in the syndrome it falls forward.
  • Look at the cervico-thoracic angle, the prominence of the C7 spinous process, scapular position (protracted, elevated, winged), and pectoral prominence.
  • Palpate upper trapezius and levator scapulae for tone and tenderness; take the cervical spine through active range with overpressure to clear the joints.
  • Step 2 — Craniocervical flexion test (the heart of the answer): supine, an inflatable pressure sensor under the neck at a 20 mmHg baseline; the patient nods the head in five graded stages of 2 mmHg; watch for superficial flexor substitution.
  • Step 3 — Deep neck flexor endurance test: chin tuck, lift the head about 2-3 cm off the couch and hold while the quality of the position is timed.
  • Step 4 — Length tests for the tight side: pectoralis minor length in supine (distance of the acromion from the couch); pectoralis major and suboccipital length; upper trapezius and levator length in side-lying.
  • Step 5 — Janda's shoulder abduction test: scapular hitching before 60 degrees of humeral elevation confirms that upper trapezius and levator dominate over the weak lower stabilisers.
  • Interpretation: findings cluster — the chin juts and the sternocleidomastoid tightens during the test; endurance holds fall far short; pectoralis minor measures more than the normal few centimetres; the scapula hikes early in abduction.
  • That cluster — not any single test — is the screen.
  • Where it leads: deep neck flexor retraining with the biofeedback cuff, lengthening the pectorals and suboccipitals, strengthening lower trapezius and serratus anterior, and ergonomic correction of desk and phone posture.

The four words that score: tight, weak, forward, rounded. Pair every tight muscle with its weak opponent.

Sources
  • Janda V. Evaluation of muscular imbalance, in Liebenson C. Rehabilitation of the Spine.
  • Magee DJ. Orthopedic Physical Assessment — cervical spine chapter.
  • O'Sullivan SB, Schmitz TJ. Physical Rehabilitation — posture chapters.
