Q4. Explain the importance of primary care in physiotherapy for degenerative conditions.

Full answer →

Examiners want the specific roles of primary care physiotherapy — early access, education, exercise, lifestyle, monitoring and referral — in chronic degenerative disease.

  • Degenerative conditions (OA) are chronic and cannot be cured, only managed.
  • Primary care physiotherapy gives early, first-contact, conservative care.
  • It reduces the burden on specialist and surgical services.
  • Educate patients that pain does not equal joint damage.
  • Exercise is the core treatment and is safe and cost-effective.
  • Prescribe progressive, multicomponent exercise at adequate dose.
  • Tailor exercise to the patient's function, preferences and services.
  • Support weight loss and healthy lifestyle change.
  • Use manual therapy and heat only as adjuncts.
  • Provide walking aids, footwear advice and falls prevention.
  • Screen for red flags and refer for rheumatology or surgery when needed.
  • Keep patients engaged with regular review and outcome measures.
  • EULAR 2023 and OARSI 2019/2022 guidelines support this approach.
  • Direct-access primary care physiotherapy improves access to care.

In degenerative disease, primary care physiotherapy is not about cure — it is about education, load and keeping people moving.

Q5. Explain the special tests of knee complex used in musculoskeletal system.

Full answer →

Examiners want the named knee special tests with the position, the force applied and the positive sign for each.

  • Special tests confirm which knee structure is at fault.
  • Lachman test: knee 20-30°, anterior translation of tibia — best bedside ACL test.
  • Anterior drawer: knee 90°, anterior pull of the tibia.
  • Pivot shift: valgus and internal rotation — most specific for ACL tear.
  • Lever sign: fist under the calf; heel fails to rise if ACL is torn.
  • Posterior drawer and sag sign test the PCL.
  • Valgus stress tests the MCL; varus stress tests the LCL.
  • McMurray and Apley test the menisci with rotation and compression.
  • Thessaly test is a weight-bearing meniscal test.
  • Patellar apprehension and Clarke's test assess the patellofemoral joint.
  • Interpret tests in clusters — no single test is perfect.
  • The Lachman test's accuracy has been overestimated in older literature.
  • Use MRI or arthrometry if history is suspicious but tests are negative.
  • Record findings with side-to-side comparison.

Lachman for the ACL, McMurray for the meniscus, valgus and varus for the collaterals — name the test, position, force and positive sign.

Q6. Exercise testing and prescription in arthritis patient.

Full answer →

Examiners want the testing tools (aerobic, strength, function, RPE) and the FITT-VP prescription adapted for arthritis.

  • Exercise is the core non-drug treatment for arthritis.
  • Screen first for cardiac and other risk (ACSM / PAR-Q+).
  • Test aerobic capacity with the 6-minute walk test.
  • Measure strength with dynamometry or grip strength.
  • Assess range of motion and function (WOMAC, KOOS, HAQ).
  • Use Borg RPE to monitor exercise intensity.
  • Prescribe with FITT-VP: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type, Volume, Progression.
  • Aerobic: 150-300 min/week, moderate intensity, 3-5 days/week.
  • Strengthening: 2-3 days/week, low-impact.
  • Choose low-impact exercise: walking, cycling, swimming, aquatic therapy.
  • Add flexibility and balance work.
  • Modify the programme during a disease flare.
  • Explain expected soreness versus a flare-up.
  • Re-test to document improvement.

Test safely, prescribe FITT-VP, and remember low-impact, land or water — movement is medicine for the arthritic joint.

  • Confirm the weight-bearing status and any hip precautions.
  • Check the wound, swelling and limb position.
  • Assess pain and watch for infection signs.
  • Measure hip range of motion, respecting arthroplasty precautions.
  • Test hip abductor and quadriceps strength.

Q8. Write in detail about the musculoskeletal assessment method and screening in congenital dislocation of hip.

Full answer →

Examiners want the newborn screening tests (Ortolani, Barlow, Galeazzi), the ultrasound/radiology pathway and the screening strategy.

  • DDH is a spectrum from mild dysplasia to frank dislocation.
  • Early detection allows simple harness treatment.
  • Ortolani test: a clunk as the hip reduces.
  • Barlow test: a clunk as the hip dislocates.
  • Galeazzi sign: unequal knee heights when hips and knees are flexed.
  • Check abduction range and thigh/gluteal crease symmetry.
  • Risk factors: breech, female, first-born, family history, swaddling.
  • Ultrasound (Graf method) is the imaging of choice in early infancy.
  • X-ray is used after about 4-6 months once the femoral head ossifies.
  • Examine every newborn and repeat at 6-8 weeks.
  • Use targeted ultrasound for at-risk or abnormal infants.
  • Universal ultrasound is controversial — most immature hips resolve.
  • Treat confirmed cases with a Pavlik harness in early infancy.
  • In older children assess gait and use the Trendelenburg test.

Ortolani reduces, Barlow dislocates, Galeazzi reveals the shortening — screen the newborn hip early.

Q9. Explain the uses of ICF in diagnosis of musculoskeletal disorders.

Full answer →

Examiners want the ICF components, how the framework is used in assessment, goal setting and outcome measurement, and the role of Core Sets.

  • ICF is the WHO's standard framework for describing functioning.
  • It uses a biopsychosocial, not purely tissue-based, view.
  • Components: Body Functions and Structures, Activities and Participation, Contextual Factors.
  • Environmental and personal factors interact with the health condition.
  • Musculoskeletal pain appears at body function level.
  • Difficulty walking or lifting appears at activity level.
  • Being unable to work appears at participation level.
  • ICF Core Sets list the most relevant categories per condition.
  • Qualifiers grade each problem from 0 to 4.
  • It supports goal setting at impairment, activity and participation levels.
  • It provides a baseline and a measure of change.
  • It gives a common language for the whole team.
  • A 2023 study confirmed the Core Set for post-acute MSK conditions.
  • ICF links problems to interventions and outcomes.

ICF turns a diagnosis into a profile: what is impaired, what the patient cannot do, and what the environment allows.

Q10. What are the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults?

Examiners want the pre-participation screening criteria and the components of fitness that are actually measured.

  • Fitness evaluation has two parts: screening and measurement.
  • Screen using the ACSM algorithm: activity level, symptoms/disease, intended intensity.
  • PAR-Q+ can be used as a self-administered screen.
  • The aim is to decide if medical clearance is needed.
  • Record resting heart rate, blood pressure, BMI and waist circumference.
  • Measure cardiorespiratory fitness (submaximal test or 6-minute walk).
  • Measure muscular strength and endurance (grip, push-ups, 1-RM).
  • Measure flexibility (sit-and-reach).
  • Measure body composition (BMI, waist girth, body fat).

  • Compare results with age- and sex-based norms.

  • Results guide the FITT-VP exercise prescription.

Q1. Describe the role of investigations in assessment.

Full answer →

Examiners want you to say what investigations are, the main types, and exactly what they add to physiotherapy assessment — and the caution that they never replace clinical examination.

  • Investigations = lab tests, imaging and electrical tests ordered to support a diagnosis.
  • They are the third pillar of assessment, after history and physical examination.
  • Main job: confirm or rule out the working diagnosis.
  • Screen for red flags: fracture, infection, cancer, inflammatory disease, cauda equina.
  • Grade or stage severity (e.g. fracture type, sacroiliitis grade).
  • Guide and monitor treatment (e.g. weight-bearing after fracture).
  • Help prognosis and provide medico-legal documentation.
  • Types: blood tests; X-ray; CT; MRI; ultrasound; bone scan; EMG/nerve conduction; biopsy/arthroscopy.
  • Many abnormal findings occur in people with no pain, so the report must fit the clinical picture.
  • Order a test only if the result will change your management (appropriateness).
  • Normal tissue has a known appearance and normal blood ranges, which makes abnormality recognisable.
  • Physiotherapists must know when to request imaging, how to read reports, and when to refer.

Memory hook: History tells the story, examination writes the chapter, investigations only confirm the plot.

Q2. Describe screening of the wrist following Colles fracture.

Full answer →

Examiners want a step-by-step screening sequence that hunts for the classic complications after a Colles fracture, with named special tests and outcome measures.

  • A Colles fracture is a distal radius fracture with the fragment displaced backwards (dorsal).
  • Common after a fall on the outstretched hand in older, osteoporotic patients.
  • Screening looks for the complications, not just the healed bone.
  • Key complications: median nerve compression (carpal tunnel), thumb extensor tendon rupture, complex regional pain syndrome, malunion, wrist instability.
  • Step 1 – History: mechanism, hand dominance, numbness, night pain, stiffness.
  • Step 2 – Observation: swelling, deformity, scar, colour/temperature changes.
  • Step 3 – Palpation: distal radius, carpal tunnel, snuffbox, fovea.
  • Step 4 – ROM: wrist flexion/extension, deviation, pronation/supination vs other side.
  • Step 5 – Strength: grip and pinch; resisted thumb extension.
  • Step 6 – Nerve screen: Tinel and Phalen tests for median nerve.
  • Step 7 – Special tests: Watson (scapholunate), fovea (TFCC), piano-key (DRUJ).
  • Step 8 – Function and outcome measures: PRWE, QuickDASH, grip fraction.
  • Step 9 – X-ray: radial inclination, radial height, volar tilt, ulnar variance.

Memory hook: After a Colles check the Nerve, Tendon, Deformity and Function — N-T-D-F.

Q3. Describe screening of the lower back following lumbar canal stenosis at L2-L3 level.

Full answer →

Examiners want the neurogenic claudication story, the L2-L3 neurological findings, the tests that separate it from vascular claudication, and the red flags.

  • Lumbar canal stenosis = narrowing of the spinal canal that squashes the cauda equina and nerve roots.
  • Classic symptom: neurogenic claudication — leg pain on walking/standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward.
  • L2-L3 affects the L2 and L3 roots.
  • L2/L3 findings: anterior and medial thigh pain/numbness, weak hip flexion and knee extension, reduced knee jerk.
  • History clues: age over 60, shopping-cart sign, relief on sitting, normal foot pulses.
  • Provocation: sustained lumbar extension brings on symptoms; flexion relieves them.
  • Walking test upright vs stooped, or walking vs cycling, separates neurogenic from vascular causes.
  • Exclude vascular claudication: check pedal pulses and ankle-brachial index.
  • Neurological exam: dermatomes, myotomes (hip flexion L2, knee extension L3/L4), knee reflex, femoral nerve stretch test.
  • Outcome measures: Oswestry Disability Index, Zurich Claudication Questionnaire, walking tests.
  • Imaging: MRI is the investigation of choice.
  • Red flags: saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel problems, rapidly worsening weakness — refer urgently (cauda equina).

Memory hook: Stenosis loves to walk and stand, hates to sit and stoop — extension provokes, flexion relieves.

Q4. Challenges faced by Physiotherapists in autonomous practice.

Full answer →

Examiners want you to define autonomous/direct-access practice and then list the legal, financial, clinical, educational and interprofessional challenges clearly.

  • Autonomous practice = examining, diagnosing, treating and discharging without needing a doctor's approval each step.
  • Direct access/self-referral is its fullest form.
  • Benefits: better access, faster care, lower cost, higher professional standing.
  • Challenge 1 – Legal: in many places (including much of India) direct access is not permitted and scope laws still tie physiotherapy to medicine.
  • Challenge 2 – Reimbursement: insurers may not pay, or pay less, for self-referred care.
  • Challenge 3 – Liability: missed diagnoses (fracture, infection, cancer) become the physiotherapist's responsibility.
  • Challenge 4 – Competency: older graduates may lack diagnostic and red-flag skills.
  • Challenge 5 – Gatekeeping: deciding what is in scope and when to refer.
  • Challenge 6 – Interprofessional resistance from some doctors.
  • Challenge 7 – Public awareness: patients may not know they can come directly.
  • Challenge 8 – Evidence-based practice and avoiding over-treatment.
  • Challenge 9 – Documentation, audit and lifelong learning.
  • Solutions: clear laws, uniform insurance rules, postgraduate training, teamwork and public education.

Memory hook: Autonomy means you own the decision — and the L-E-G-A-L load: Legal, Ethical, Gatekeeping, Accountability, Liability.

  • Impact of direct access on primary care MSK physiotherapy: scoping review. BMC. 2024.

Q5. Describe the various special tests for screening the neck.

Full answer →

Examiners want the special tests grouped by what they screen for, each with position, force and the positive sign.

  • Nerve-root (radiculopathy) tests: Spurling (compression), distraction, shoulder abduction relief, Valsalva.
  • Spurling: neck bent sideways and back toward the painful side with downward pressure; positive if arm pain is reproduced.
  • Distraction: gentle pull upward; positive if arm pain eases.
  • Upper limb neurodynamic tests (ULNT 1, 2a, 2b, 3): arm positions that load the nerve; positive if familiar symptoms return and change with neck position.
  • Myelopathy tests: Hoffmann, Babinski, clonus, Lhermitte sign.
  • Vascular tests: Hautant, De Kleyn, sustained rotation-extension — positive if dizziness, nystagmus or nausea.
  • Instability tests: Sharp-Purser and alar ligament tests for upper-cervical instability.
  • Facet/joint tests: cervical flexion-rotation test, rotation-lateral flexion test, quadrant test.
  • Muscle control: craniocervical flexion test.
  • No single test is perfect — use clusters (e.g. 3 or more positive ULNTs suggest radiculopathy).
  • Myelopathy or vascular signs = urgent medical referral; always screen the vertebral artery before manipulation.

Memory hook: Screen the neck for the 4 M-V-F-I — Myelopathy, Vascular, Facet and nerve-root (plus Instability).

Q6. Write in detail about the various investigations used for ankylosing spondylitis.

Full answer →

Examiners want blood tests, imaging and clinical scoring grouped clearly, with MRI highlighted as the key early test.

  • Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory disease starting at the sacroiliac joints and entheses.
  • Blood tests: HLA-B27 (positive in ~90%), ESR and CRP (may be raised), RF and anti-CCP usually negative.
  • Plain X-ray of the sacroiliac joints: first-line; graded 0–4 (modified New York criteria).
  • X-ray of the spine: squaring of vertebrae, syndesmophytes, bamboo spine.
  • MRI of the sacroiliac joints: best for early disease; shows bone-marrow oedema (ASAS-positive MRI).
  • CT: for detailed structural change; ultrasound: for peripheral enthesitis.
  • Clinical measures: BASDAI (activity), BASFI (function), BASMI (mobility), ASDAS (combined score).
  • ASAS criteria combine inflammatory back pain with an imaging arm or a clinical (HLA-B27) arm.
  • MRI oedema can occur in healthy people, so criteria are for classification, not diagnosis.
  • Rule out mechanical back pain and other spondyloarthritides.

Memory hook: Ankylosing spondylitis — Blood, X-ray, MRI, Measures (B-X-M-M).

Q7. Write in detail about the postoperative management following fracture of the tibial plateau.

Full answer →

Examiners want staged rehabilitation — protection, early motion, weight-bearing progression, strengthening — with the weight-bearing timetable and complications.

  • Tibial plateau fracture is an intra-articular break of the top of the shin bone, usually fixed with plates and screws.
  • Goal: protect the fixation while preventing stiffness, wasting and clots.
  • Phase 1 (weeks 0–2): pain and swelling control, ankle pumps, isometric quadriceps/hamstrings, brace, non- or toe-touch weight-bearing.
  • Phase 2 (weeks 2–6): regain knee range of motion, continue strengthening; immobilisation gives no benefit.
  • Phase 3 (weeks 6–12): progress weight-bearing — partial around 6–8 weeks, full around 9–12 weeks (later for complex fractures); gait and balance training.
  • Phase 4 (week 12+): progressive strengthening, proprioception, functional and sport training.
  • Monitor pain, swelling, range, power, gait and function (KOOS/Oxford Knee Score).
  • Complications: stiffness, loss of reduction, infection, DVT, delayed/non-union, osteoarthritis.
  • Early motion and early weight-bearing are now favoured over prolonged immobilisation.

Memory hook: Protect the plateau, then Move, Load, Strengthen, Function.

Q8. Describe in detail the assessment following above knee amputation.

Examiners want a structured assessment of the residual limb, impairments, function, balance and prosthetic fit, with named outcome measures.

  • Above-knee (transfemoral) amputation removes the limb above the knee.
  • History: cause, date, comorbidities (diabetes, vascular, cardiac), goals.
  • Residual limb: length, shape, scars, skin, oedema, volume, neuromas.
  • Range of motion: watch for hip flexion and abduction contracture.
  • Strength: hip abductors and extensors (main muscles for walking with a prosthesis).
  • Sensation and pain: phantom sensation and phantom limb pain.
  • Balance and mobility: transfers, static/dynamic balance, gait.
  • Functional level: assign the K-level (0–4) for prosthetic prescription.
  • Prosthetic fit: socket comfort score, suspension, alignment, skin response.
  • Outcome measures: Amputee Mobility Predictor, Timed Up and Go, 2-minute and 6-minute walk tests, Prosthesis Evaluation Questionnaire, PLUS-M.
  • Also assess mood, motivation and cardiopulmonary fitness.
  • Reassess before and after prosthetic fitting to track change.

Q9. Describe various outcome measures used for low back pain.

Full answer →

Examiners want outcome measures grouped into pain, disability, psychosocial, quality of life and global change, with the ODI vs RMDQ comparison.

  • Low back pain is multidimensional, so one measure is never enough.
  • Pain: Visual Analogue Scale or Numerical Rating Scale.
  • Disability: Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) and Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire (RMDQ).
  • ODI = 10 sections, 0–100%; RMDQ = 24 yes/no items, 0–24. They are not interchangeable.
  • Psychosocial: STarT Back Tool, Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire, Pain Catastrophising Scale, Orebro, PHQ-9.
  • Quality of life: SF-36, EQ-5D.
  • Global change: Patient Global Impression of Change.
  • Performance tests: lumbar range of motion, trunk endurance, walking tests.
  • STarT Back stratifies patients into low/medium/high risk and matches treatment.
  • Use the minimal clinically important difference (~30% improvement) to judge real change.
  • Standardise on one disability measure per service for consistency.

Memory hook: Measure low back pain across P-D-P-Q-G — Pain, Disability, Psychosocial, Quality of life, Global change.

Q10. Explain the criteria for fitness evaluation in adults following total knee replacement.

Full answer →

Examiners want both the preoperative fitness/risk criteria and the postoperative fitness-for-progression criteria, using validated tools.

  • Fitness evaluation has two parts: before surgery (is the patient fit for the operation?) and after surgery (is the patient fit to progress and go home?).
  • Pre-op: assess cardiovascular and clot risk (DVT, PE, heart attack, stroke) within 30 days of surgery.
  • Screen functional capacity with a validated tool like the Duke Activity Status Index.
  • If reduced, do an objective test — cardiopulmonary exercise testing (gold standard) or 6-minute walk / sit-to-stand / Timed Up and Go.
  • Optimise comorbidities: diabetes, blood pressure, anaemia, heart and lung disease, obesity, smoking.
  • Check thrombosis and infection risk; review pain medicines.
  • Screen mood and provide education and prehabilitation.
  • Post-op: stable vital signs, controlled pain, no infection/DVT, healing wound.
  • Post-op function: safe transfers, safe walking with the aid, enough knee movement and quadriceps control, good balance.
  • Use outcome measures: Oxford Knee Score or KOOS, range of motion, Timed Up and Go, 6-minute walk test.
  • Improving fitness before surgery (prehabilitation) shortens hospital stay and reduces complications.

Memory hook: Fitness for TKR is H-E-A-R-T-S — History, Exercise capacity, Anaemia, Risk (cardiac), Thrombosis risk, Screening & function.

Glossary of difficult terms (76)

Dotted-underlined words also show the definition on hover or tap.

  • allodynia — Pain from a stimulus that is not normally painful.
  • arthrogenic muscle inhibition — Reflex weakness of a muscle caused by a problem inside its joint (abbreviated AMI).
  • arthrokinematics — The small gliding, rolling and spinning movements between joint surfaces.
  • atrophy — Wasting or shrinking of muscle or tissue.
  • biomechanics — The study of the mechanical laws relating to the movement of living organisms.
  • biopsychosocial — An approach that considers biological, psychological and social factors together.
  • capsular pattern — The characteristic order in which a joint loses range when the whole capsule is involved.
  • capsule — The fibrous sleeve that surrounds and stabilises a joint.
  • catastrophising — Interpreting pain in an exaggerated, worst-case way.
  • central sensitisation — Increased excitability of the central nervous system that makes normal inputs feel painful.
  • collagen — The main structural protein in tendon, ligament, skin and bone.
  • concentric — Muscle work while it shortens under load (the lifting phase).
  • contracture — A permanent tightening or shortening of tissue that restricts movement.
  • contraindication — A condition that makes a treatment unsafe or inadvisable.
  • creep — Slow progressive lengthening of tissue under a constant sustained load over time.
  • cryotherapy — Treatment using cold.
  • dermatome — The area of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • dorsal horn — The rear part of the spinal cord's grey matter where sensory nerves first relay pain signals.
  • dorsiflexion — Bending the ankle or wrist so the angle at the front decreases (e.g. lifting the toes up).
  • eccentric — Muscle work while it lengthens under load (the lowering phase).
  • effleurage — A smooth gliding massage stroke.
  • effusion — Fluid collecting inside a joint.
  • electrotherapy — Treatment using electrical currents or electromagnetic energy.
  • end-feel — The quality of resistance felt at the very end of a joint's movement, used to judge what limits it.
  • eversion — Turning the sole of the foot outward.
  • fear-avoidance — Avoiding activity because of fear of pain, which over time worsens disability.
  • gait — The manner of walking.
  • gate control theory — The idea that non-painful input (rubbing, TENS) can 'close a gate' in the spinal cord and reduce pain.
  • golgi tendon organ — A sensor in tendon that detects tension and helps regulate muscle force.
  • goniometry — Measuring joint angles with a goniometer.
  • hyperalgesia — An increased sensitivity to pain.
  • hypermobility — Excessive movement at a joint, usually from lax or torn ligaments.
  • hypertrophy — An increase in muscle or tissue size.
  • hypomobility — Reduced movement at a joint, usually from tight or stiff tissue.
  • ICF — The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health.
  • inflammation — The body's protective response to injury - heat, redness, swelling and pain.
  • inversion — Turning the sole of the foot inward.
  • isometric — A muscle contraction with no change in length (no joint movement).
  • joint play — The small accessory movement available at a joint beyond voluntary control.
  • kinesiophobia — Fear of movement or of re-injury.
  • laser therapy — Red/near-infrared light therapy that stimulates cell repair (photobiomodulation).
  • ligament — Strong fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises a joint.
  • manipulation — A quick, small thrust applied to a joint by a clinician.
  • manual muscle testing — Grading a muscle's strength by resisting a voluntary contraction (abbreviated MMT).
  • mechanoreceptors — Sensory receptors that detect mechanical stimuli such as touch, pressure and joint position.
  • mechanotransduction — How cells turn mechanical load into chemical signals that change the tissue.
  • moment arm — The perpendicular distance from a force to the joint axis; a longer moment arm produces more torque.
  • muscle spindle — A stretch sensor inside muscle that helps control posture and movement.
  • myofascial — Relating to muscle and its surrounding fascia.
  • myotome — The group of muscles supplied by a single spinal nerve root.
  • neurodynamic — Relating to the mechanical and physiological function of nerves; neural mobilisation treats nerve sensitivity.
  • nociceptive — Relating to the detection of painful stimuli.
  • nociceptor — A sensory nerve ending that detects painful or tissue-damaging stimuli.
  • oedema — Swelling caused by fluid trapped in the tissues.
  • osteokinematics — The visible movements of bones at a joint, such as flexion and extension.
  • outcome measure — A standardised tool used to measure a patient's status or change over time.
  • palpation — Examining the body by touch to feel for tenderness, swelling or tissue change.
  • plantarflexion — Pointing the foot downward, as when standing on tiptoe.
  • posture — The position of the body and its parts relative to gravity.
  • precaution — A situation requiring extra care during treatment.
  • proprioception — The sense of body and joint position and movement.
  • proprioceptive — Relating to the body's sense of position and movement.
  • radiculopathy — A nerve-root problem causing pain, numbness or weakness along a limb.
  • range of motion — How far a joint can move (abbreviated ROM).
  • red flag — A sign or symptom suggesting serious pathology that needs medical referral.
  • ROM — Short for range of motion - how far a joint can move.
  • sensitivity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who have the condition.
  • special test — A clinical test used to confirm or rule out a specific structure or condition.
  • specificity — A test's ability to correctly identify people who do not have the condition.
  • synovial — Relating to the fluid-filled lining of a joint.
  • tendinopathy — A tendon disorder causing pain and reduced function.
  • tendon — Strong fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.
  • TENS — Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation - a mild current passed through the skin to relieve pain.
  • torque — A turning force around an axis - the product of force and its moment arm.
  • traction — A gentle pulling force applied to a joint or the spine to relieve pressure.
  • trigger point — A tender, tight knot in a muscle that can refer pain elsewhere.
